# Civic Operator — full reference text

> Civic Operator publishes an independent reference layer for the CMS Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP) — the $50B state-awarded program created by Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. For all 50 states it records the exact Year-1 federal award, the administering agency, how each state defines "rural", the performance metrics each state committed to CMS, official .gov sources, and a dated activity log.

Generated from the Markdown companions of every public page.

---

# About

Source: https://www.civicoperator.com/about/

Daniel X. O'Neil · Chicago

# Creator across domains

A public-interest technologist who turns advanced data capability into systems people actually use — across private industry, public health, media, government, and civic organizations.

Throughout my career I've invented civic systems — and then built the organizations, methods, and tools to make them last. I co-founded EveryBlock, one of the first platforms to turn municipal data into news for your block. I founded Smart Chicago Collaborative and, inside it, created the Civic User Testing Group — paying everyday residents to test civic apps — and co-created Documenters, which pays community members to cover the public meetings that shape their cities.

The pattern repeats across private industry, public health, media, and government: find where data and public life meet, build the thing that connects them, and design it so the people it serves actually use it. Today that work runs through the Rural Health Transformation Grant Tracker and the consulting practice of Civic Operator.

## Select projects

A few of the systems I've invented, founded, or co-created.

Co-founder

### Rural Health Transformation Grant Tracker

State-by-state tracking of RFPs, contracts, and implementation activity for the $50B CMS Rural Health Transformation Program.

[Visit ↗](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/)

Co-creator

### Documenters

A program that pays and trains community members to document public meetings — created at Smart Chicago and now running in cities across the country.

[Read the history ↗](https://www.danielxoneil.com/2018/03/22/history-of-the-documenters-program-at-city-bureau/)

Inventor

### Civic User Testing Group

A model for everyday Chicago residents paid to test civic apps — pairing UX research with community participation and digital-skill building.

[Read the book ↗](https://www.cutgroupbook.com/)

Founding Executive Director

### Smart Chicago Collaborative

A tech philanthropy and incubator devoted to improving lives in Chicago through technology — expanding access, building digital skills, and shipping data-driven public products.

[Visit ↗](https://www.smartchicagocollaborative.org/)

Co-founder

### OpenGovChicago meetup

First-ever meetup for residents who treat government as "us, not them," organizing around open-government and civic-tech principles.

[Visit ↗](https://www.smartchicagocollaborative.org/contact-us/meetups/opengovchicago-meetups/)

Co-founder

### EveryBlock

A pioneering hyperlocal platform that filtered municipal data and local news down to your block — launched in 2008, spread to 14 cities, sold to msnbc.

[Read the story ↗](https://www.danielxoneil.com/2008/01/18/the-launch-of-everyblock/)

monday CRM

# Speed up your sales cycle with an intuitive, AI-powered CRM your team will love

Customizable pipelines, centralized communication, and real-time dashboards — set up and handed over by a certified monday.com partner.

[Book a working call](https://calendar.app.google/XruT8HoUjnKLCkwD8)

Flexible and intuitive

### Customizable to fit your sales cycle

Easily tailor your CRM to work for you, without any development help. Edit deal stages, add as many columns as you'd like, manage multiple pipelines at once, and more.

Communication

### Centralize client communication

Communicate efficiently with your contacts by integrating your email. Automatically log sent emails, keep track of interactions, and use personalized email templates to save you time.

Automations

### Save valuable time by automating sales processes

Keep every stakeholder updated with real-time data. Effortlessly communicate project statuses, roadblocks, and deadlines while collaborating across teams on one centralized platform.

Dashboards

### Increase visibility with customizable dashboards

Easily build dashboards in real time with no development help. Gain insights into where deals stand, expected revenue, your team's performance, and more.

Overviews

### Get an instant overview of each deal

With a single click, quickly access all the information you need to close deals. View contact details, understand deal progress, and what needs to be done next.

# AI Systems

Source: https://www.civicoperator.com/work/ai/

AI Systems

# Emerging AI tools, put to work immediately.

Secure generative-AI built around your operation — without your data being used to train anyone's model.

[Start with one private workflow](https://calendar.app.google/XruT8HoUjnKLCkwD8)

## What I build

Three ways AI shows up as real, usable systems on your stack.

### Environments & agents

AI workspaces on your stack, with agents that run long jobs on a schedule and skills tuned to your work.

### Mine your own data

Turn your email, files, and PDFs into clean, structured data that feeds your systems and sharpens reporting.

### Custom intelligence tools

Purpose-built tools that answer one real question for one real audience.

## Proof

Systems already running in the world.

### Intelligence that compounds overnight

An unattended agent that reads government documents nightly, sorts and files them into structured boards, and drafts the newsletter. Downloads and processes original documents, adding them to the data product.

### A nightly finance data pipeline

An automated, scheduled ETL for a multi-location business: every night it pulls each site's operational database and its payment processor, builds validated finance workbooks, and lands them where dashboards refresh against them — with reconciliation gates that abort the run if recognized revenue doesn't tie out to the penny.

### A purpose-built mapping tool

An interactive mapping tool built for a public-media network's congressional funding application. Pulls from U.S. Census data and custom shapefiles while calculating impact on the fly.

## Some of the tools behind it

I leverage current advances in software to examine processes, build strategy, and automate repetitive tasks. Here are some of the valuable tools I work in.

Great for data-heavy applications, offering the flexibility of a database with the ease of a spreadsheet. Its AI-powered "Build an App" feature can extract value from existing datasets.

Leading AI platforms like Claude Enterprise, OpenAI Enterprise, and Google Gemini for Workspace all have enterprise offerings. Let's talk about what works for you.

Integrating Google's suite of enterprise apps with Gemini and scripting tools can enhance business operations and unlock growth.

Speed up your sales cycle with an intuitive, AI-powered CRM that your team will love.

[Read more](/monday-service.html)

## Selected work

Connected systems that replaced a coalition's worth of spreadsheets, inboxes, and paper.

### A national public-health nonprofit

Built one connected directory of 4,600+ contacts and syndicated it as live, login-free views to 30+ member cities, each kept current by a self-service form. One system replaced a coalition's worth of spreadsheets.

### A regional behavioral-health support nonprofit

Turned a paper-and-inbox intake into one connected program: a family registers through a public form and the system creates their records, assigns an advisor, and opens an intake automatically — then tracks every client through to outcome against a 277-organization referral network.

### A major county health department

Gave field-based community health workers a simple way to file weekly reports that roll straight up into the executive dashboard metrics, with bilingual intake and rolling outcomes analysis.

### A multi-site sports-registration platform

Stabilized a fragile legacy platform end to end — modern hosting, a fixed core defect, a real deploy pipeline — so a business that runs on seasonal registration stopped fearing every release. Data pipelines and dashboards built on unlocked legacy systems.

# Rural Health Transformation

Source: https://www.civicoperator.com/work/rht/

Rural Health Transformation

# Everything I do on the $50B rural health program — in three layers

A free, neutral state-by-state reference; the newsletter that interprets it; and consulting that maps *your* organization to the money — from a one-time State Fit Brief to a standing, verified intelligence arrangement. Start free, go as deep as you need.

[Browse the States — free](/work/rht/states)
[Become a client — $480](/work/rht/brief#consulting)

## Three layers to RHTP

Each layer stands on its own — and builds on the one before it.

The reference — understand

### State-by-state profiles

A neutral, independently maintained profile of every state's program — the award, the administering agency, official source links, and a dated activity log. Public and free, with no login or paywall — the same source data behind everything else on this page.

[Browse the States →](/work/rht/states)

Always free

The newsletter — analyze

### The Grant Tracker

Daily commentary, interpretation and reporting on what the $50B is actually doing — the [Grant Tracker](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/). It comes at several subscription levels, from a free tier to the $480 Founding Member plan that includes your starter consulting — a one-time State Fit Brief.

[Read the Tracker →](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/)

Free – $480/year

The subscription — operate

### RHTP Verified Intelligence

Your State Fit Brief, kept alive. A digest, by email, most business days — the RHTP opportunities that match your organization, read by a person before they reach you, with the contacts the state has published. [See how it works](/work/rht/intelligence).

[Start a conversation →](/work/rht/intelligence)

Scoped retainer · from $2,000/mo

The gateway — customize

### Start with a one-time State Fit Brief

Get the map first. A one-time, ranked **State Fit Brief** shows where your organization fits the program across up to ten states — matched dollars, procurement windows, enabling legislation, and named contacts. It's the point-in-time analysis most clients start with, and the on-ramp to [RHTP Verified Intelligence](/work/rht/intelligence).

[See what's in a brief — $480](/work/rht/brief)

# 2026 Q2 Newsletter Activity Index

Source: https://www.civicoperator.com/work/rht/activity/

# 2026 Q2 Newsletter Activity Index

Every state activity item we logged this quarter — 438 items across 48 states — each linked to the exact section of its newsletter brief. Covering briefs from Feb 22 – Jul 2, 2026.

Headlines are reproduced verbatim from each dated brief. No logged activity this period in MA, VA.

**Dated archive.** This is a fixed Q2 2026 snapshot, kept as an artifact of the newsletter. Current activity lives in the [state profiles](/work/rht/states) and the [Tracker](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/).

[All posts, videos & newsletter sign-up →](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/archive)

# What's in a State Fit Brief · RHT Data Consulting

Source: https://www.civicoperator.com/work/rht/brief/

RHT Data Consulting

# What's in a State Fit Brief

A ranked, ten-state document that tells you where your platform fits the $50B Rural Health Transformation Program — why, what's being procured, when it opens, and who to talk to.

[Become a Founding Member — $480](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/subscribe)
[See the six components](#components)

## Why it matters now

The opportunity is real and time-boxed. The hard part is that it's scattered across 50 separate state plans.

### $50B over five years

The Rural Health Transformation Program is moving roughly $50 billion into the states. Every state has a published plan, a budget, and a procurement calendar.

### A hard October 30, 2026 deadline

States must obligate their first year of funds by October 30, 2026. The windows are open right now, and most of them close inside this fiscal year.

### Scattered across 50 plans

Each state has its own naming conventions, its own procurement portal, and its own legislative backdrop. Reading all of it and ranking it by where you can win is weeks of analyst time.

A State Fit Brief collapses that into a single ranked document — up to ten states where your platform is the strongest fit against published RHTP initiatives, drawn entirely from an existing RHTP intelligence database. No original-research lag, no guesswork.

## How it works

One input from you, one ranked document back.

1

### You provide a profile

A document explaining your company, organization, product, services, or needs — include any and all details that help with matching.

2

### You get direction

A ranked, ten-state brief assembled against your platform's profile — built so the whole thing reads consistently and you can compare states side by side.

## Six components per state

Every state entry is built from the same six components, so the whole document is consistent and comparable.

01

### The fit narrative

A short, plain-English explanation of why this state matches your specific platform — which funded initiatives your product maps into, and where it's the literal infrastructure other funded work depends on. This is what turns a list of grants into a reason to act.

02

### Matched RHTP topics

The named initiatives and themes in the state's published plan that your offering fits, with dollar figures attached wherever the state has published them — so you see the size of the fundable surface at a glance.

03

### Procurement signals

The actual RFPs, RFAs, RFIs, and NOFOs the state has published or forecast — with dates. The highest-fit, soonest-closing opportunities are flagged first.

04

### Enabling legislation

The bills behind the money — appropriations, authorizing statutes, scope-of-practice changes — and their status, so you know whether the funding is locked or still moving.

05

### Budget signal

The state's first-year federal award and, where published, the total plan size across program areas — so you can size the prize.

06

### Named contacts

Up to five publicly identifiable contacts per state — program offices and, where they exist in the public record, named individuals with titles and emails. The shortest path from "interesting state" to "first conversation."

### And a summary recommendation

The brief closes with the three states to attack first — the specific reasoning and the near-term procurement windows that make them urgent — plus honorable mentions and a clear scope note on what's included and what can be added later.

## What's included, and what's not

A fixed-fee, fixed-turnaround engagement, assembled against your platform's profile from existing database intelligence.

### Included

- Up to ten ranked states
- All six components for every state
- The summary recommendation — the three states to attack first
- Honorable mentions
- A clear scope note on what can be added later

### Priced separately if useful later

- Custom research on individual directors, procurement officers, or competing vendors
- Ongoing monitoring or a refresh after delivery
- Coverage beyond the top ten states
- Prime / sub / partnering strategy
- Deep-dive response framework for any single state's RFP or NOFO

The consulting layer

# Q2 RFP Review / Q3 RFP Watcher · Rural Health Transformation

Source: https://www.civicoperator.com/work/rht/dashboard/

Rural Health Transformation Program · Q2 2026 Quarterly Report

# Q2 RFP Review / Q3 RFP Watcher

Every procurement that published this quarter, the near-term contracting outlook for next, and where the federal money actually stands — across the $50B CMS Rural Health Transformation Program.

**Dated archive · Q2 2026.** A fixed quarterly snapshot. The quarterly report is evolving toward tracking the *goals* each state committed to — what they promised to measure and deliver. For now, current procurement activity lives in the [state profiles](/work/rht/states) and the [Tracker](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/).

Q3 Watch — what's coming
Q2 Review — what published
Analytics

WATCH

## Open & upcoming procurements — Q3 2026

Live targets: procurements open or upcoming with deadlines July–October 2026. Sort by deadline or ceiling; filter by month. Ceilings are program maximums *as reported* and often fund multiple awards — always confirm on the state portal before bidding.

REVIEW

## Published procurements catalog — through Q2 2026

The full tracker: every procurement we captured this quarter — RFPs, RFAs, NOFOs, awards and more — with links to the source document. Filter by state or type; sort any column, including the extracted dollar amount.

01

## The map

All 50 states by **implementation maturity** or **rural-geography tier**. A ring marks frontier-tier states; an inner border marks regional-hub operators. Click a state to open its profile below.

02

## The quarter in one view

Every state cleared the starting line — all 50 have a program page and a submitted plan. The spread is in *procurement velocity*.

### Implementation maturity

By procurements issued this cycle (tracker, cross-checked vs. Rural Care Journey). A few states run a letter-of-intent model rather than RFPs (e.g. Alaska: 1,787 LOIs, 430 advanced) and show full maturity with few listed procurements.

### Quarter pulse

State activity events per week across the daily briefs.

03

## The money starts to move

Federal obligations vs. federal outlays, from USAspending (CFDA 93.798). The full FY2026 tranche is obligated; as of early July most states have begun recording outlays — though still well under one percent of the total.

Obligated · FY26

→

Federal outlays

04

## State intelligence & profiles

Maturity, geography, and federal dollars per state. Sort any column; filter by stage. **Click any state** for its profile, its dated activity log, and a link to the deep dive. The **Procurements** column shows the higher of our tracked count and the cross-checked total, so its sum exceeds the deduplicated catalog above.

05

## Geography — the operating models

How a state defines “rural” for RHTP reveals how it administers the program. Tier 1 delineated its own operational rural geography; Tier 3 defers to the federal HRSA definition.

06

# RHTP Verified Intelligence · RHT Data Consulting

Source: https://www.civicoperator.com/work/rht/intelligence/

RHT Data Consulting

# RHTP Verified Intelligence

You already know the work. This is what it looks like as a standing arrangement — a machine trained on one program, and a person who reads everything before it reaches you.

[Start a conversation](mailto:danx@civicoperator.com?subject=RHTP%20Verified%20Intelligence)
[How it works](#how)

## One program, all the way down

Civic Operator runs a single instrument pointed at a single program. The Rural Health Transformation Program, the fifty state programs underneath it, the agencies administering them, the organizations winning the money, and the vendors selling into those organizations. Solicitations, awards, legislation, budget movements, governance changes, named people. It has been fed every day since the program started, and it doesn't do anything else.

That depth is the whole asset. A general-purpose tracker knows a little about a lot of programs. This one knows a single program the way you know your own product.

## What you actually get

A digest, by email, most business days. Not an alert per item — one piece of writing you can read in a few minutes and act on.

Every item tells you what it is, why it matched you, and where to read the source. Most tell you considerably more: when it's due, where it sits in that state's timeline, which organizations are already working the topic, and who to call — by name, with title, and with the email and phone number that have been published.

Contacts aren't a separate product and they aren't rationed. Knowing who to call is most of what this is for.

## Nothing reaches you unread

The machine finds. The operator vouches.

Matching runs automatically across everything fifty states publish. Then I read what it surfaced and decide what's worth your attention. You don't get "probably relevant." You get the things I'd walk down the hall to tell you about, which is the arrangement this is meant to approximate.

That judgment is the part that can't be automated, and it's the part you're paying for.

## It takes the shape you need

Nobody buys this the same way.

Some clients want the daily read and nothing else. Some want everything moving in three states and don't care about the other forty-seven. Some want the awardee side — every organization that has won money in a state, and the people at each one who buy what they sell. Some want the rubric retuned every few weeks as their strategy moves, and some set it once and leave it.

All of that is the same instrument, pointed differently. We work out the shape in the first month and change it whenever it stops fitting. There's no tier you have to buy your way into and no configuration you're locked out of.

## Where it sits

Most clients arrive here after the map is already drawn.

Rung one — The newsletter

### What the money is doing

Daily commentary on the whole program, across the country. Free, and the reason most people know the work. [Read the Tracker →](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/)

Rung two — A State Fit Brief

### Where you fit, once

A one-time ranked document: the states where your organization fits, as of today. The map. [What's in a brief →](/work/rht/brief)

# Rural Health Transformation Program — State-by-State Reference

Source: https://www.civicoperator.com/work/rht/states/

# Rural Health Transformation Program State-by-State Reference Guide

The **Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP)** is a $50 billion, five-year CMS program — created by Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025) — that awarded every U.S. state a share to transform rural health care. Each state administers its own award through a designated agency, on its own timeline, with its own procurements.

This is an **independent reference** to that program, state by state. Each profile collects the facts that are otherwise scattered across dozens of web sites: the state’s CMS award, its administering agency and contacts, its official program and procurement pages, and a dated log of activity — each entry deep-linked to the source. It is maintained by Civic Operator LLC as a neutral archive; commentary and analysis live separately on the newsletter.

## How this works

Primary source

Federal and state government pages — CMS, each state’s .gov RHTP program and procurement portals, and Governor newsrooms. Every profile links out to these. Also relies on [KFF Health News](https://kffhealthnews.org/rural-health/tracking-state-rural-health-transformation-plans/) for many approved plans.

Reference layer

This site. A neutral, structured, independently maintained profile of each state’s program — award, administering agency, official sources, and a dated activity log.

Analysis layer

The [Rural Health Transformation Grant Tracker](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/) newsletter — commentary, interpretation and reporting. Profiles link into its dated briefs; the analysis lives there, not here.

## Compare across states

Single-dimension reference tables that cut across all 50 states, each linking back to the full profiles.

[How states define “rural” →](/work/rht/states/rural-definitions/)

# Alabama Rural Health Transformation Program — CMS award, lead agency, committed metrics & activity

Source: https://www.civicoperator.com/work/rht/states/alabama/

# Alabama Rural Health Transformation Program State Profile

Alabama's **$203.4M** Year-1 Rural Health Transformation Program (ARHTP) award — the eleven-initiative hub strategy, the administering agency, live NOFOs, with a dated log of official activity for vendors, providers, and consultants tracking the program.

## What Alabama committed to measure

The subjects Alabama’s funded application pledges to track and report to CMS — the yardsticks its progress will be measured against. Extracted from the state’s own project narrative; the detailed baselines and targets behind each are tracked in the [newsletter](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/).

Health IT interoperabilityCybersecurity alert responseTelehealth consultationsMaternal and fetal healthCancer screening accessRural workforce trainingEMS trauma diversionEMS treat-in-placeBehavioral health integrationRural clinic capacity

Source: Alabama’s CMS-approved RHTP project narrative. These are the state’s self-declared objectives; CMS weighs each state’s progress against its own commitments.

## Questions & answers

What is Alabama's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Alabama's Year-1 budget under the Alabama Rural Health Transformation Program (ARHTP) is **approximately $203.4 million**, its share of the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program — 100% CMS/HHS-funded. CMS structures the program over five years, and Alabama's approved narrative pairs Year-1 estimates with larger five-year totals for each initiative (for example, Collaborative EHR/IT/Cybersecurity shows $31.6M in Year 1 against a $125M five-year total).

Which agency administers Alabama's RHTP, and who leads it?

The [Alabama Department of Economic and Community Affairs (ADECA)](https://adeca.alabama.gov/about/funding-opportunities/) administers the program and runs the competitive subaward process. Program information is published at the [ARHTP website](https://alabamarhtp.com/). A dedicated program contact email is not published in the primary sources reviewed; ADECA directs applicants to the ARHTP portal and its NOFO workshops for questions.

What is Alabama's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

Alabama's strategy moves beyond short-term stabilization toward long-term system redesign, built around **Regional Referral Center Hubs** — larger regional hospitals or health systems that serve as central resource points for smaller rural providers, offering shared IT, cybersecurity, and specialty telehealth while letting independent providers keep their autonomy. The state identified **11 interrelated initiatives**, 10 of which launch in Year 1 (the Community Medicine Initiative is deferred to Year 2).

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Alabama funding, and at what share?

- **Collaborative EHR, IT & Cybersecurity** — $31.6M Year 1 ($125M over five years); modernizes infrastructure and integrates EHRs with the Alabama One Health Record (ALOHR).
- **Rural Health Initiative** — $60.9M Year 1 ($275M over five years); tele-stroke, tele-behavioral health, and remote patient monitoring.
- **Rural Workforce Initiative** — $60.9M Year 1 ($309.75M over five years); GME expansion, remote EMT training, and relocation incentives.
- **Maternal and Fetal Health** — $7.1M Year 1; telerobotic ultrasound and emergency L&D stabilization carts.
- **Rural Health Practice Initiative** — $30M over five years.

Recurring focuses on record include digital obstetrics, regional cancer hubs, and mobile behavioral health. The full initiative-by-initiative breakdown is in Alabama's approved Project Narrative.

What has Alabama procured so far, and what's open right now?

ADECA's application portal went live June 1, 2026, and the first batch of five NOFOs posted the first week of June — EHR IT & Cybersecurity, Rural Health, Rural Workforce, Mental Health, and Rural Health Practice — with applications due June 26, 2026 and first award notices scheduled for July 17. A second round of five NOFOs followed, together making about **$24.2 million** available across cancer screening, EMS, maternal health, and clinical training: **Cancer Digital Regionalization, EMS Trauma and Stroke, EMS Treat-in-Place, Maternal and Fetal Health, and Simulation Training** — all due August 7, 2026 at 5:00 PM Central through the ARHTP portal. The running record is in the dispatch list below.

[ADECA Funding Opportunities →](https://adeca.alabama.gov/about/funding-opportunities/)

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Alabama?

The most recent hard deadline on the record is **August 7, 2026 at 5:00 PM Central** for the second round of five NOFOs. ADECA is running in-person application workshops (with a virtual Microsoft Teams option) that walk through each NOFO's goals, eligibility, funding details, and the application process. Earlier round-one applications were due June 26 with award notices from July 17. Current per-NOFO dates surface first in the dated dispatches below and on the ADECA funding page.

What legislation or state action enables Alabama's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. Alabama administers its award through ADECA under a CMS-approved Project Narrative, distributing funds through a competitive subaward process. Notably, Alabama operates a **modified reimbursement model**: subrecipients run a formal procurement, select a vendor, and the state draws down federal funds to pay the vendor once an approved invoice is received, rather than providing up-front liquidity.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Alabama's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** are awarded competitively, where firms bid as **prime contractors**. **Subawards** flow to rural providers — hospitals, clinics, EMS agencies, and health systems — and it is here that technology vendors and consultants most often engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners**, since Alabama's model requires subrecipients to procure vendors and the state reimburses against approved invoices. The Regional Referral Center Hubs, typically led by larger regional hospitals, are natural anchor points for vendors offering shared IT, cybersecurity, and telehealth. Track opportunities and workshop schedules on the ARHTP site and the ADECA funding portal.

[ARHTP hub →](https://alabamarhtp.com/) [ADECA Funding Opportunities →](https://adeca.alabama.gov/about/funding-opportunities/)

# Alaska Rural Health Transformation Program — CMS award, lead agency, committed metrics & activity

Source: https://www.civicoperator.com/work/rht/states/alaska/

# Alaska Rural Health Transformation Program State Profile

**Alaska**'s roughly **$272.2 million** Rural Health Transformation Program award — the plan, the administering agency, the six initiative tracks, the Letter-of-Interest pipeline, with a dated log of official activity.

[Alaska’s official RHTP hub →](https://health.alaska.gov/en/education/rural-health-transformation-program/)

Alaska’s official Rural Health Transformation Program page — [health.alaska.gov](https://health.alaska.gov/en/education/rural-health-transformation-program/), captured 2026-07-18.

## At a glance

FY26 award (Year 1)

$272,174,856 · CMS obligated

Program name

Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP)

[Alaska program page](https://health.alaska.gov/en/education/rural-health-transformation-program/)

## What Alaska committed to measure

The subjects Alaska’s funded application pledges to track and report to CMS — the yardsticks its progress will be measured against. Extracted from the state’s own project narrative; the detailed baselines and targets behind each are tracked in the [newsletter](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/).

Prenatal and infant healthPrimary care accessBehavioral health accessCancer screening ratesOverdose and suicide mortalityValue-based payment adoptionHealth workforce pipelineTelehealth utilizationHealth information exchangeChronic disease prevention

Source: Alaska’s CMS-approved RHTP project narrative. These are the state’s self-declared objectives; CMS weighs each state’s progress against its own commitments.

## Questions & answers

What is Alaska's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Alaska's Budget Period 1 award is approximately **$272.2 million**, its share of the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program and among the largest per-capita awards in the country. It is a five-year program; the state opened its funding pipeline with a Letter-of-Interest round rather than immediate RFPs, and demand vastly outstripped supply — roughly $2.5 billion in year-one asks were submitted against the available funding.

Which agency administers Alaska's RHTP, and who leads it?

The [Alaska Department of Health (DOH)](https://health.alaska.gov/en/education/rural-health-transformation-program/) administers the program, led by Commissioner **Heidi Hedberg**. DOH has contracted with the **Alaska Community Foundation (ACF)** as its grant administration partner to run the application and award process. Program inquiries go to [RHTP@alaska.gov](mailto:RHTP@alaska.gov); application-status questions to ACF go to RHTP@alaskacf.org.

What is Alaska's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

Alaska is organizing its plan around six RHTP initiative tracks: Healthy Communities, Strengthen Workforce, Healthy Beginnings (maternal health), Spark Technology & Innovation, Health Care Access, and Pay for Value (fiscal sustainability). Recurring themes include retention over recruitment in the workforce, maternal-care access across vast geography (with a Texas-style insurer-partnership sustainability play discussed for maternal health), Indigenous traditional healing, and mobile specialist teams.

[Alaska RHTP hub →](https://health.alaska.gov/en/education/rural-health-transformation-program/)

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Alaska funding, and at what share?

Detailed dollar allocations have not been published as competitive line items yet — Alaska's Letter-of-Interest process is still resolving which of ~1,800 submissions advance to funded awards. Spending is being shaped across the six initiative tracks, with key project tags including **Indigenous Traditional Healing** and **Mobile Specialist Teams**. The full breakdown will follow in Alaska's budget narrative and the state-level RFPs that the LOI round tees up.

What has Alaska procured so far, and what's open right now?

Alaska's first pathway was a **Letter of Interest (LOI)** round: registration opened February 17, 2026 and closed March 11, with ACF receiving **1,797 LOIs from 864 unique organizations** (about 81% Alaska-based). After initial ACF review and an in-depth DOH assessment, outcomes were communicated by email on May 22, 2026, sorting each submission into: advance to full application under the implementation pathway; advance for planning-pathway consideration; deferred (recommended for resubmission); or declined. DOH has cautioned that advancing does not guarantee funding — more applications are advancing than there is money to fund. State-level RFPs are expected to follow. The running record is in the dispatches below.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Alaska?

Many of the LOI-phase milestones are now past — the LOI window (through March 11, 2026), public comment on the evaluation frameworks (due March 12), and notifications (late May). Alaska has run a heavy calendar of **RHTP Impacts Series** webinars, organized initiative-by-initiative, as its main engagement channel. Upcoming application windows, full-application deadlines and new webinars surface first in the dispatches below and on the DOH RHTP hub and Funding Opportunities & Applicant Information Center.

What legislation or state action enables Alaska's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. Alaska administers its award through the Department of Health, which contracted the Alaska Community Foundation as grant administrator and posted an **RHTP Advisory Council Charter** along with draft Project Evaluation and Portfolio Analysis Review Frameworks for public comment. Detailed allocation figures are set out in Alaska's CMS-approved budget narrative.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Alaska's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** will go out as competitive RFPs where firms bid as **prime contractors**. **Subgrants and subawards** flow to rural providers — hospitals and Tribal health organizations, clinics, EMS and community organizations — and it is here that technology vendors and consultants most often engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners** rather than direct grantees. DOH has explicitly used its Impacts Series webinars as a brokerage layer — framed as a “dating session” where Alaskan providers and outside vendors find each other by initiative track.

Grant administration and applications run through the [Alaska Community Foundation grants portal](https://alaskacf.org/grants/); contribute ideas via the DOH Community Input Form and track updates on the [Alaska RHTP hub](https://health.alaska.gov/en/education/rural-health-transformation-program/).

# Arizona Rural Health Transformation Program — CMS award, lead agency, committed metrics & activity

Source: https://www.civicoperator.com/work/rht/states/arizona/

# Arizona Rural Health Transformation Program State Profile

Arizona's **$166,988,956** Rural Health Transformation Program award — the plan, the three administering agencies, the budget split, live procurements, with a dated log of official activity.

[Arizona’s official RHTP hub →](https://www.azahcccs.gov/AHCCCS/Initiatives/RHTP/)

Arizona’s official Rural Health Transformation Program page — [azahcccs.gov](https://www.azahcccs.gov/AHCCCS/Initiatives/RHTP/), captured 2026-07-28.

## At a glance

FY26 award (Year 1)

$166,988,956

RHTCMS332059-01-00 (Dec 29, 2025)

5 years — through Oct 30, 2030

9 dated briefs

## What Arizona committed to measure

The subjects Arizona’s funded application pledges to track and report to CMS — the yardsticks its progress will be measured against. Extracted from the state’s own project narrative; the detailed baselines and targets behind each are tracked in the [newsletter](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/).

Rural workforce developmentClinician retentionBehavioral health crisis servicesSubstance use treatment accessChronic disease screeningMaternal-fetal healthTelehealth adoptionCare coordinationProvider credentialing timeShared-service networks

Source: Arizona’s CMS-approved RHTP project narrative. These are the state’s self-declared objectives; CMS weighs each state’s progress against its own commitments.

## Questions & answers

What is Arizona's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Arizona received **$166,988,956** in Year 1 funding under CMS Notice of Award **RHTCMS332059-01-00**, dated December 29, 2025, with a five-year period of performance running through October 30, 2030. The award is Arizona's share of the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program.

Which agency administers Arizona's RHTP, and who leads it?

[AHCCCS](https://www.azahcccs.gov/AHCCCS/Initiatives/RHTP/) (the Arizona Health Care Cost Containment System) is the single CMS awardee. The Governor's Office named **three lead agencies** to administer distinct slices: the Office of Economic Opportunity (OEO) runs workforce; the Department of Health Services (ADHS) runs maternal health and chronic-disease work; and AHCCCS runs everything else. Program coordination runs through the **Arizona Center for Rural Health** ([manand@arizona.edu](mailto:manand@arizona.edu)).

What is Arizona's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

Arizona is using RHTP dollars to strengthen the rural health workforce, expand access through telehealth, mobile care and satellite sites, and make rural providers financially and operationally resilient through diagnostic equipment, EHR modernization and shared-services consortiums — coordinated across three state agencies rather than a single office.

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Arizona funding, and at what share?

- **Rural Health Education & Training (OEO)** — 28% (≈$47M), the single largest slice.
- **Maternal Health (ADHS)** — 3%; **Chronic Disease Prevention & Management (ADHS)** — 7%.
- **Behavioral Health & SUD (AHCCCS)** — 6%.
- **Making Rural Health Care Accessible (AHCCCS)** — 23% (telehealth/digital 10%, rural-health innovation 13%).
- **Making Rural Health Resilient (AHCCCS)** — 23% (diagnostic/EHR tech 18%, shared-services consortiums 3%, operational/fiscal TA 2%).

What has Arizona procured so far, and what's open right now?

Arizona's first live solicitation was the **AHCCCS Opioid Antagonist Distribution Initiative RFGA**, released July 10, 2026 — targeting rural counties, Tribal communities, fire districts and frontier clinics. OEO (workforce) and ADHS (maternal/chronic disease) previewed their procurement calendars at the June Arizona Rural Health Conference, with the bulk of solicitations expected across the back half of 2026. Every dated dispatch covering Arizona is listed below, newest first.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Arizona?

The Opioid RFGA's application deadline is posted on the AHCCCS grant application page (confirm it there — it is not printed on the toolkit card). AHCCCS is also hosting three regional “Share Your Voice on Rural Health” public meetings, with dates on the RHTP hub. Live procurement dates surface first in the dated dispatches below.

What legislation or state action enables Arizona's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. Arizona's participation is administered through AHCCCS under its CMS-approved project and budget narratives, with the Governor's Office designating the three lead agencies. Detailed state appropriation and allocation figures are set out in Arizona's approved Project Narrative and Budget Narrative.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Arizona's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out as competitive RFPs, where firms bid as **prime contractors**. **Subgrants and subawards** flow to rural providers — hospitals, Rural Health Clinics, FQHCs, Tribal health organizations, EMS agencies, counties and fire districts — and it is here that technology vendors and consultants most often engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners** rather than as direct grantees.

Track opportunities on the [AHCCCS RHTP hub](https://www.azahcccs.gov/AHCCCS/Initiatives/RHTP/) and the [Grants Administration portal](https://www.azahcccs.gov/Resources/Grants/GrantsAdministration.html); attend the regional “Share Your Voice” meetings to shape priorities before more solicitations drop; and request a letter of support from the **Arizona Center for Rural Health** (as State Office of Rural Health) by sending them a link to an open funding opportunity.

# Arkansas Rural Health Transformation Program State Profile

Arkansas's **$208.8M** Rural Health Transformation Program award — the “Healthy. Connected. Local” plan, its four initiative tracks, live NOFOs, with a dated log of official activity for vendors, providers, and consultants tracking the program.

## What Arkansas committed to measure

The subjects Arkansas’s funded application pledges to track and report to CMS — the yardsticks its progress will be measured against. Extracted from the state’s own project narrative; the detailed baselines and targets behind each are tracked in the [newsletter](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/).

Nutrition and preventionCommunity health partnershipsRural specialty accessMobile and telehealth servicesScope-of-practice expansionClinically integrated networksHealth workforce recruitmentLeadership trainingEMS response timesRemote patient monitoring

Source: Arkansas’s CMS-approved RHTP project narrative. These are the state’s self-declared objectives; CMS weighs each state’s progress against its own commitments.

## Questions & answers

What is Arkansas's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Arkansas's FY2026 allocation is **approximately $208.8 million** (reported by the state as roughly $209 million), its share of the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program. CMS structures the program over five years; Arkansas's initiatives carry both Year-1 ceilings and larger five-year totals (its HEART pillar, for example, is about $27.6M in Year 1 against roughly $151.9M over five years), and — per CMS rules — every Year-1 dollar must be obligated by October 30, 2026.

Which agency administers Arkansas's RHTP, and who leads it?

Arkansas runs its program — branded **“Healthy. Connected. Local”** — through the Arkansas Department of Health, with the Arkansas Department of Finance and Administration handling funding administration for tracks such as HEART. Program contact is [adh.ruralhealth@arkansas.gov](mailto:adh.ruralhealth@arkansas.gov) (applicants are also directed to Info@arkansasrhtp.com for application questions), and program information lives at the [Arkansas RHTP site](https://arkansasrhtp.com/).

What is Arkansas's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

Arkansas structures its award into four named initiative tracks that together modernize the rural health system: **PACT** (Promoting Access, Coordination, and Transformation) for access, coordinated care, and clinically integrated networks; **THRIVE** (Telehealth, Health-Monitoring, and Response Innovation for Vital Expansion) for telehealth, remote patient monitoring, and EMS/emergency response; **RISE AR** (Recruitment, Innovation, Skills, and Education) for workforce and leadership; and **HEART** (Healthy Eating, Active Recreation, and Transformation) for prevention, nutrition, and chronic-disease work. No matching funds are required on these tracks.

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Arkansas funding, and at what share?

- **THRIVE** — $55.6M for telehealth, remote patient monitoring, EMS/emergency-response modernization, and IT infrastructure.
- **PACT** sub-initiatives — ACCESS up to $24.4M, SAFE (facility enhancement) up to $63M, CINC up to $3.69M, SCOPE up to $1.5M, ROADMAP up to $1M.
- **RISE AR** sub-initiatives — RETAIN up to $14.4M, PATHWAY up to $7M (GME, scholarships), LEAD up to $4.3M, SKILL UP up to $1.6M.
- **HEART** — up to $27,557,600 in Year 1 across six sub-initiatives (IMPACT $8.42M, GROW Kids $6M, FARM $5.7M, MOVE $5.04M, HEAL $1.3M, FAITH $1.1M).

Recurring focuses on record include EMS stabilization, rural maternal health, and data interoperability.

What has Arkansas procured so far, and what's open right now?

All four tracks are now in market. **THRIVE** ($55.6M) opened its application portal May 11, 2026, with dollars flowing from June. **PACT** opened June 8 with applications closing July 10 across its five sub-initiatives. **RISE AR** ran a June 22–July 24 window. **HEART** (up to $27.56M) opened June 29 with a deadline extended to August 7 (from July 31). The running record of every posting is in the dispatch list below.

[Arkansas RHTP Resources & Application Portal →](https://arkansasrhtp.com/resources/)

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Arkansas?

The most recent hard deadline on the record is **August 7, 2026** for HEART (extended from July 31); RISE AR closed July 24 and PACT closed July 10. Every Year-1 dollar must be **obligated by October 30, 2026**, and the NOFOs flag that a new SAM.gov registration can take up to eight weeks — a real planning constraint for these short windows. Current per-track dates surface first in the dated dispatches below and on the resources page.

What legislation or state action enables Arkansas's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. Arkansas administers its award through the Arkansas Department of Health (with the Department of Finance and Administration handling funding for tracks such as HEART) under its CMS-approved plan; every subaward carries standard federal grant requirements, including 2 CFR Part 200 capacity and an active SAM.gov UEI.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Arkansas's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out competitively, where firms bid as **prime contractors**. **Subawards** flow to rural providers and partners — hospitals, FQHCs, community clinics, EMS agencies, pharmacies, licensed practitioners, behavioral health providers, and clinically integrated networks — and it is here that technology vendors and consultants most often engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners**. Arkansas's eligibility is unusually wide, especially on HEART, which also opens the door to state agencies, employers, schools, higher-ed and academic research partners, community and faith-based organizations, community health workers, and nonprofit or public entities serving rural Arkansas. All applicants must clear 2 CFR Part 200 capacity and hold an active SAM.gov UEI.

[Arkansas RHTP hub →](https://arkansasrhtp.com/) [Application portal →](https://arkansasrhtp.com/resources/)

# California Rural Health Transformation Program — CMS award, lead agency, committed metrics & activity

Source: https://www.civicoperator.com/work/rht/states/california/

# California Rural Health Transformation Program State Profile

California's **$233,639,308.46** Budget Period 1 Rural Health Transformation Program award — the largest in the country — including the CalRHT plan, the HCAI team administering it, the initiatives, the live grants, with a dated log of official activity.

[California’s official RHTP hub →](https://hcai.ca.gov/rural-health/calrht/)

California’s official Rural Health Transformation Program page — [hcai.ca.gov](https://hcai.ca.gov/rural-health/calrht/), captured 2026-07-29.

California’s own state-published rural map — HCAI Medical Service Study Area (MSSA) Definition Map — frontier/rural/urban. Source: [hcai.ca.gov](https://hcai.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/MSSADefinitionMap.pdf). See [how every state defines rural](/work/rht/states/rural-definitions/#map-california).

## What California committed to measure

The subjects California’s funded application pledges to track and report to CMS — the yardsticks its progress will be measured against. Extracted from the state’s own project narrative; the detailed baselines and targets behind each are tracked in the [newsletter](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/).

Blood pressure controlDiabetes glycemic controlColorectal cancer screeningPrenatal care accessVaginal birth after cesareanRural workforce capacityTime to hireHealth information exchangeCybersecurity risk assessmentTelehealth utilization

Source: California’s CMS-approved RHTP project narrative. These are the state’s self-declared objectives; CMS weighs each state’s progress against its own commitments.

## Questions & answers

What is California's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

California's Budget Period 1 award is **$233,639,308.46**, 100% funded by CMS/HHS — the largest Rural Health Transformation Program award in the country and its share of the federal $50 billion program, which runs five years with additional annual awards expected. CMS's February 27, 2026 Notice of Award approved a revised budget and lifted restriction on $183,639,308.47; a $50,000,000 line for **Transformative Payments to Support Strategically Located Hospitals** initially remained restricted in the "Other" cost category pending additional information.

Which agency administers California's RHTP, and who leads it?

The [Department of Health Care Access and Information (HCAI)](https://hcai.ca.gov/rural-health/calrht/) administers the program, branded **California Rural Health Transformation (CalRHT)**, through its own dedicated hub and contact inbox ([CalRHT@hcai.ca.gov](mailto:CalRHT@hcai.ca.gov)), separate from the older California State Office of Rural Health page. HCAI's Director of California Rural Health Transformation staffs the program, advised by the **Rural Health Policy Council (RHPC)**, whose members the HCAI Director appoints.

What is California's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

CalRHT is built around three thrusts: a **Transformative Care Model (TCM)** using regional care collaboratives and hub-and-spoke relationships to strengthen primary and maternity care; **Technology and Tools**, focused on EHR modernization, telehealth/eConsult, interoperability and revenue-cycle management; and **Workforce Development**, including doula/midwife training, community health worker expansion, and rural residencies. The plan explicitly excludes broadband expansion; telehealth work targets clinical tools and workflows, not connectivity.

Where is the money going — which initiatives is California funding, and at what share?

Money moves through grant funding opportunities tied to the three initiatives. Named tags include **doula/midwife training, community health worker (CHW) expansion, and rural residency**, and $50,000,000 is set aside for Transformative Payments to Support Strategically Located Hospitals. HCAI has not published a single public percentage split; the full initiative-level breakdown is in the [CalRHT Project and Budget Narratives](https://hcai.ca.gov/rural-health/calrht/) (posted March 27, 2026).

What has California procured so far, and what's open right now?

The first grants are live. The **Accelerator Partner Program RFA** (Transformative Care Model testing sites) and the **Family Medicine Obstetrics (FM-OB) Fellowship Subaward Program** (workforce) both close **August 14**. The **EHR Modernization Grant** — funding first-time certified-EHR adoption or full replacement only, upgrades excluded — closes **August 21 at 3:00 p.m. PT**, with subaward notifications expected in September. A **Workforce Development Recruitment and Retention (WDRR)** opportunity is also on the runway. The dispatch list below carries the running record.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in California?

Key dates: the first **Rural Health Policy Council meeting** was July 28, 2026; informational webinars ran for the EHR Modernization Grant (July 27), WDRR (July 23 and August 4), and the Accelerator Partner Program (July 20). Application deadlines land **August 14** (Accelerator and FM-OB) and **August 21** (EHR Modernization). Confirm current windows on the [CalRHT funding page](https://hcai.ca.gov/rural-health/calrht/funding/); live dates surface in the dispatches below.

What legislation or state action enables California's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. California administers its award through HCAI under CMS-approved project and budget narratives; on January 30, 2026, as required by CMS, the state submitted a revised budget, and CMS's February 27, 2026 Notice of Award approved it and lifted most restrictions.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with California's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out as competitive RFAs, where firms bid as **prime contractors** — and California's is unusually open: out-of-state organizations can apply directly with no California partner required, as long as they can meet state contracting requirements and deliver services in rural California, and "rural serving" is keyed to who benefits (per the HRSA Rural Health Grants Eligibility Analyzer), not where the applicant sits. **Subawards** flow to rural providers — CAHs, FQHCs (including Tribal), Rural Health Clinics, health care districts and county behavioral-health sites — where vendors and consultants engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners**. Note two limits: county public health departments cannot be primary recipients (only State-selected partners or subrecipients), and broadband expansion is not permissible.

Track opportunities on the [CalRHT funding page](https://hcai.ca.gov/rural-health/calrht/funding/), join the [HCAI mailing list](https://hcai.ca.gov/mailing-list/), and email a resume and expression of interest to [CalRHT@hcai.ca.gov](mailto:CalRHT@hcai.ca.gov) to be considered for the Rural Health Policy Council.

# Colorado Rural Health Transformation Program — CMS award, lead agency, committed metrics & activity

Source: https://www.civicoperator.com/work/rht/states/colorado/

# Colorado Rural Health Transformation Program State Profile

Colorado's **$200,105,604.17** Rural Health Transformation Program award — the plan, the administering agency, the budget guardrails, live procurements, with a dated log of official activity.

[Colorado’s official RHTP hub →](https://hcpf.colorado.gov/rural-health-transformation-program)

Colorado’s official Rural Health Transformation Program page — [hcpf.colorado.gov](https://hcpf.colorado.gov/rural-health-transformation-program), captured 2026-07-29.

Colorado’s own state-published rural map — HCPF Rural & Frontier Counties map — 52 of 64 counties. Source: [hcpf.colorado.gov](https://hcpf.colorado.gov/sites/hcpf/files/52%20Rural%20%26%20Frontier%20Counties%20%28for%20publication%29.pdf). ## What Colorado committed to measure

The subjects Colorado’s funded application pledges to track and report to CMS — the yardsticks its progress will be measured against. Extracted from the state’s own project narrative; the detailed baselines and targets behind each are tracked in the [newsletter](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/).

Chronic disease programsRural care accessHospital collaborationsEMS expansionRural workforce pipelineValue-based care modelsTelehealth accessData exchange (HIE)Cybersecurity readinessRemote patient monitoring

Source: Colorado’s CMS-approved RHTP project narrative. These are the state’s self-declared objectives; CMS weighs each state’s progress against its own commitments.

## Questions & answers

What is Colorado's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Colorado's Year 1 award is **$200,105,604.17**, fully funded by CMS as its share of the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program. The approved project narrative narrows an original 5-year, roughly $1 billion draft down to **Budget Period 1** only, with those first-year funds to be fully expended by **September 30, 2027**. Spending guardrails cap direct provider payments at 15% (Budget Period 1 lands at 11%, or $21,524,573.22) and hold state administrative overhead to 2.65%.

Which agency administers Colorado's RHTP, and who leads it?

The [Colorado Department of Health Care Policy & Financing (HCPF)](https://hcpf.colorado.gov/rural-health-transformation-program) administers the program through its **Rural Health Transformation Division**, led by Division Director **Courtney Roy**. Program questions go to [hcpf\_rhtp@state.co.us](mailto:hcpf_rhtp@state.co.us).

What is Colorado's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

Colorado is steering RHTP dollars toward provider stabilization, rural workforce retention, and Medicaid alignment, alongside chronic-disease prevention and management, EMS transport coordination and coverage, community health worker and rural-clinician training, telehealth participation, and whole-person and alternative care models. A guiding principle set by the RHTP Advisory Committee is to fund fewer, larger, collaborative projects tied directly to program goals rather than many small grants.

[Colorado RHTP hub →](https://hcpf.colorado.gov/rural-health-transformation-program)

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Colorado funding, and at what share?

- **Direct provider payments** — capped at 15% of the grant; Budget Period 1 sits at 11% ($21,524,573.22).
- **EHR replacement** — capped at 5% ($205,280) under Initiative 5.
- Priority themes include **provider stabilization**, **workforce retention**, and **Medicaid alignment**, plus chronic-disease prevention, EMS transport coordination and coverage, CHW and rural-clinician continuing education, telehealth support, and the Whole Person Health and Alternative Care Models program.

The full line-by-line allocation is set out in Colorado's approved Budget Narrative.

What has Colorado procured so far, and what's open right now?

Colorado's competitive **Request for Applications (RFA)** opened June 18, 2026 through the state's [RFA application portal](https://coloradorhtp-rfa.my.site.com/apply/s/), with applications due **11:59 p.m. on August 3, 2026**. Each application is led by a **Lead Applicant Organization (LAO)** that serves as fiscal agent for state payments. HCPF separately contracted the **Colorado Rural Health Center (CRHC)**, the State Office of Rural Health, to provide free application training and technical assistance ([CRHC\_RHTP@coruralhealth.org](mailto:CRHC_RHTP@coruralhealth.org)). Every dated dispatch covering Colorado is listed below, newest first.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Colorado?

- **August 3, 2026, 11:59 p.m.** — RFA application deadline.
- Final LAO office hours: **July 23, July 27, and July 29, 2026**.
- RHTP Advisory Committee meeting: **July 27, 2026, 10:00–11:30 a.m.**
- **September 30, 2027** — Budget Period 1 funds must be fully expended.

Live dates surface first in the dated dispatches below.

What legislation or state action enables Colorado's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. In Colorado, the State Controller approved a **waiver of Fiscal Rule 3-1**, letting HCPF make case-by-case advance payments (rather than reimbursement only) through June 30, 2027; after that date the blanket waiver expires. State allocation figures are detailed in Colorado's approved Project and Budget Narratives.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Colorado's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out as competitive RFAs, where firms bid as **prime contractors**. **Subgrants and subawards** flow to rural providers — hospitals, Rural Health Clinics, FQHCs, Tribal health organizations, EMS agencies, counties and special districts physically located in one of Colorado's 52 rural or frontier counties — and it is here that technology vendors and consultants most often engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners**. Colorado explicitly names technology vendors and consultants among the non-eligible lead applicants that may still join an application as partners.

Track opportunities on the [HCPF RHTP hub](https://hcpf.colorado.gov/rural-health-transformation-program) and the [RFA application portal](https://coloradorhtp-rfa.my.site.com/apply/s/), and complete the state's vendor interest survey to be listed for partnerships.

# Connecticut Rural Health Transformation Program — CMS award, lead agency, committed metrics & activity

Source: https://www.civicoperator.com/work/rht/states/connecticut/

# Connecticut Rural Health Transformation Program State Profile

Connecticut's **$154,249,105.53** Rural Health Transformation Program award — the DSS-led administration, the 30-plus projects across 11 state agencies, the first AI/remote-patient-monitoring NOFO, with a dated log of official activity.

[Connecticut’s official RHTP hub →](https://portal.ct.gov/dss/rural-health-transformation-program)

Connecticut’s official Rural Health Transformation Program page — [portal.ct.gov](https://portal.ct.gov/dss/rural-health-transformation-program), captured 2026-07-24.

## At a glance

FY26 award (Year 1)

Connecticut Rural Health Transformation

## What Connecticut committed to measure

The subjects Connecticut’s funded application pledges to track and report to CMS — the yardsticks its progress will be measured against. Extracted from the state’s own project narrative; the detailed baselines and targets behind each are tracked in the [newsletter](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/).

Maternal health servicesBehavioral health accessChronic disease managementRural workforce recruitmentProvider retentionHealth information exchangeTelehealth adoptionED utilization reductionValue-based paymentCare coordination

Source: Connecticut’s CMS-approved RHTP project narrative. These are the state’s self-declared objectives; CMS weighs each state’s progress against its own commitments.

## Questions & answers

What is Connecticut's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Connecticut's Year 1 award is **$154,249,105.53** from CMS under Notice of Award RHTCMS332073, its share of the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program. The program is a five-year CMS cooperative agreement, and Connecticut's grants are renewable for up to five years pending CMS continuation funding.

Which agency administers Connecticut's RHTP, and who leads it?

The [Connecticut Department of Social Services (DSS)](https://portal.ct.gov/dss/rural-health-transformation-program) is the lead agency, operating a new **Division of Rural Health Transformation**, with **Daniel Sinclair** confirmed as Project Director per CMS's April 16 revised Notice of Award. General questions route to [RHTP-Questions@ct.gov](mailto:RHTP-Questions@ct.gov). The first NOFO was issued by the **Office of Health Strategy (OHS)** — though, per Public Act 26-68 (effective July 1, 2026), OHS is being dissolved and its functions absorbed into the Office of Policy and Management (OPM), which the NOFO names as successor Grantor.

What is Connecticut's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

Connecticut's plan encompasses **30-plus named projects across 11 state agencies**, organized into four initiatives: **Population Health Outcomes, Workforce, Data & Technology, and Care Transformation & Stability**. The last bucket is the largest, absorbing **$85.6 million** in Year 1, and includes rural hospital right-sizing grants anticipated for Charlotte-Hungerford, Day Kimball, Sharon and Windham hospitals. AHEAD Model Readiness and Health Equity Data are core project tags.

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Connecticut funding, and at what share?

The single biggest Year 1 concentration is **Care Transformation & Stability at $85.6 million**, anchored by rural hospital right-sizing grants for Charlotte-Hungerford, Day Kimball, Sharon and Windham hospitals. The remainder is spread across the Population Health Outcomes, Workforce, and Data & Technology initiatives — including the first funded project, AI-enabled remote patient monitoring and care coordination. The full breakdown of the 30-plus projects across 11 agencies is set out in Connecticut's project and budget narratives.

What has Connecticut procured so far, and what's open right now?

Connecticut's first live procurement is the OHS **Health Care Coordination and Remote Patient Monitoring Using Artificial Intelligence NOFO (#26OHS001)**, posted May 22, 2026 — a **$1.8 million** Year 1 solicitation for AI-enabled remote patient monitoring and care coordination, with applications due July 7, 2026. Awards range from $100,000 to $1,000,000, with up to five grants in Year 1, renewable for up to five years pending CMS continuation funding. Every funded project must integrate bidirectionally with **Connie**, the state's health information exchange. Every dated dispatch covering Connecticut is listed below, newest first.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Connecticut?

The AI/remote-patient-monitoring NOFO (#26OHS001) set applications due **July 7, 2026**. Because most published dates are now past and the issuing agency is mid-transition (OHS to OPM, effective July 1, 2026), upcoming deadlines and new solicitations surface first in the dated dispatches below and on the [DSS RHTP hub](https://portal.ct.gov/dss/rural-health-transformation-program).

What legislation or state action enables Connecticut's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. In Connecticut, the award is administered through DSS under CMS Notice of Award RHTCMS332073, via a new Division of Rural Health Transformation. A state-specific action shapes the administrative landscape: **Public Act 26-68** (effective July 1, 2026) dissolves the Office of Health Strategy and transfers its functions to the Office of Policy and Management, which is named successor Grantor on the first NOFO.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Connecticut's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out as competitive NOFOs, where firms bid as **prime contractors**. For the first NOFO, however, eligibility is limited to **Connecticut-licensed providers** — hospitals, FQHCs, behavioral health providers, EMS, pharmacists, oral health, maternity programs, municipal health agencies, academic medical centers, multi-entity consortia, and federally recognized Tribes — with **technology vendors restricted to subcontractor roles**. That is the clearest possible signal of the two-track model: rural providers apply for the subawards, and vendors and consultants engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners** underneath them. Every funded project must integrate bidirectionally with the state HIE, Connie.

Track opportunities on the [DSS RHTP hub](https://portal.ct.gov/dss/rural-health-transformation-program) and the [OHS NOFO page](https://portal.ct.gov/ohs/press-room/press-releases/2025-press-releases/notice-of-funding-opportunity-rural-health-transformation-program), and [sign up for program updates](https://confirmsubscription.com/h/j/230BA14F52E2EB66).

[Connecticut DSS Rural Health Transformation Program →](https://portal.ct.gov/dss/rural-health-transformation-program)

# Delaware Rural Health Transformation Program — CMS award, lead agency, committed metrics & activity

Source: https://www.civicoperator.com/work/rht/states/delaware/

# Delaware Rural Health Transformation Program State Profile

**Delaware**'s approximately **$157.4M** Year-1 Rural Health Transformation Program award — the administering agency, the 15-initiative plan for Kent and Sussex counties, live RFPs, with a dated log of official activity.

[Delaware’s official RHTP hub →](https://dhss.delaware.gov/dph/rural-health-transformation-program/)

Delaware’s official Rural Health Transformation Program page — [dhss.delaware.gov](https://dhss.delaware.gov/dph/rural-health-transformation-program/), captured 2026-07-21.

## At a glance

## What Delaware committed to measure

The subjects Delaware’s funded application pledges to track and report to CMS — the yardsticks its progress will be measured against. Extracted from the state’s own project narrative; the detailed baselines and targets behind each are tracked in the [newsletter](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/).

Emergency department utilizationChronic disease screeningSchool-based health servicesFood is medicineValue-based care participationTelehealth and remote monitoringDiabetes managementMedical workforce pipelineRural provider recruitmentHealth information exchange

Source: Delaware’s CMS-approved RHTP project narrative. These are the state’s self-declared objectives; CMS weighs each state’s progress against its own commitments.

## Questions & answers

What is Delaware's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Delaware was awarded approximately **$157.4 million** (reported as nearly $160 million) for federal fiscal year 2026 under the Rural Health Transformation Program — the floor amount every state received. Year 1 is the first tranche of a much larger multi-year plan; Delaware's own Executive Budget Summary puts the total estimated direct cost of its plan at **$721,329,131.03**, with a 9.1% indirect cost rate for statewide oversight. The award is structured by CMS as an annual award across a five-year performance period, and is Delaware's share of the federal $50 billion program.

Which agency administers Delaware's RHTP, and who leads it?

The program is administered by the **Delaware Department of Health and Social Services (DHSS)** through the [Division of Public Health](https://dhss.delaware.gov/dph/rural-health-transformation-program/). Governor **Matt Meyer** has framed the effort as a generational rural healthcare overhaul. Program contact: [nichole.moxley@delaware.gov](mailto:nichole.moxley@delaware.gov).

What is Delaware's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

Delaware's plan unites **15 integrated initiatives** designed to expand access, strengthen the workforce, modernize technology, and improve population health in rural **Sussex and Kent counties** — directly impacting roughly 400,000 rural residents, about 38–40% of the state's population. The Delaware Health Information Network (DHIN) provides the technology backbone, linking mobile health units to patient EMRs and the state Health Information Exchange.

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Delaware funding, and at what share?

Money is spread across 15 initiatives detailed in Delaware's Executive Budget Summary. Named projects include:

- **Workforce** — a vendor-managed technology product supporting SB122 and related workforce data needs ($2,685,200).
- **Delaware Diabetes Wellness Pilot Program** — a three-year observational study using care management and continuous glucose monitoring (enabled by HB305).
- **Rural Community Health Hubs**, **School-Based Health Centers Expansion**, **Rural Library-Based Health Access**, and a **Food is Medicine Infrastructure Initiative**.
- **Creation of a medical school** (rural med-school track).

The full project-by-project breakdown and budgets are in Delaware's [RHTP Executive Budget Summary](https://dhss.delaware.gov/wp-content/uploads/sites/10/2026/02/Final-RHTP-Revised-Budget-1.30.26.pdf).

What has Delaware procured so far, and what's open right now?

Delaware opened its initial RFPs against its RHTP allocation on **February 9, 2026**, formalizing the procurement track. The state is now accepting RFP applications for the **Workforce** program ($2,685,200), with additional RFPs identified for Rural Community Health Hubs, School-Based Health Centers Expansion, Rural Library-Based Health Access, the Food is Medicine Infrastructure Initiative, and the medical school. The Diabetes Wellness Pilot (HB305) is one of the 15 projects and will plug into this procurement track. The dispatch list below carries the running record.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Delaware?

Delaware's initial RFP track opened February 9, 2026, and specific application windows for each of the 15 initiatives are being posted on a rolling basis. Because most early dates have passed or vary by RFP, live deadlines surface first in the dated dispatches below and on the state procurement portal.

[Delaware bids portal →](https://bids.delaware.gov)

What legislation or state action enables Delaware's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. Delaware has paired its award with enabling state legislation: **HB305** establishes the Delaware Diabetes Wellness Pilot Program inside DHSS (its fiscal note states the act is "to be federally funded through the Federal Rural Health Transformation Program"), and **SB122** expands health-care workforce data collection to support workforce research and planning. Delaware submitted its full application, with 15 projects, to CMS in November 2025.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Delaware's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out as competitive RFPs (for example, the workforce technology product and other vendor-managed initiatives), where firms bid as **prime contractors**. **Subgrants and subawards** flow to rural providers and community partners — hospitals, health clinics, school-based health centers, libraries, and community organizations serving Kent and Sussex counties — where technology vendors and consultants most often engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners** rather than direct grantees. Because DHIN provides the technology backbone, vendors whose solutions integrate with the state Health Information Exchange are well positioned.

Track and respond to opportunities on the [Delaware bids portal](https://bids.delaware.gov) and follow the [RHTP hub](https://dhss.delaware.gov/dph/rural-health-transformation-program/).

# Florida Rural Health Transformation Program — CMS award, lead agency, committed metrics & activity

**Florida**'s roughly **$209.9 million** Rural Health Transformation Program award — the plan, the administering agency, the bundled-and-standalone RFA slate, with a dated log of official activity.
