## Questions & answers

What is Florida's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Florida's Year-1 award is approximately **$209.9 million**, its share of the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program. It is a five-year program; Florida's spending authority to expend the first-year federal award is carried in the state's Fiscal Year 2027 General Appropriations Act, and Year-1 dollars are being released through a slate of Requests for Applications administered by the Agency for Health Care Administration.

Which agency administers Florida's RHTP, and who leads it?

The [Agency for Health Care Administration (AHCA)](https://ahca.myflorida.com/rural-health-transformation-program.html) administers Florida's RHTP. Program inquiries go to [RHTP@AHCA.myFlorida.com](mailto:RHTP@AHCA.myFlorida.com), and solicitations are posted through MyFloridaMarketplace.

What is Florida's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

Florida's plan pushes care beyond traditional clinical walls — mobile health units, community paramedicine, remote patient monitoring, pharmacy-based retail clinics, satellite clinics and telehealth — while strengthening rural facilities' capacity for specialty and acute care, workforce pipelines, and value-based purchasing. A load-bearing technology thread is **Florida HIE/ENS onboarding**: the plan targets raising EHR and diagnostic interoperability among rural facilities from a 2024 baseline of about 73% to at least 83% by FY2030. Key project tags include Satellite Clinic Expansion, Mobile Maternal and Pharmacy Tech.

[Florida RHTP hub →](https://ahca.myflorida.com/rural-health-transformation-program.html)

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Florida funding, and at what share?

Florida structured its Year-1 funding as two bundled RFAs plus four standalone RFAs:

- **Preventive Care & Care-at-Home Bundle (RFA 033-25/26)** — five integrated initiatives (mobile units, community paramedicine, remote telemonitoring, pharmacy retail clinics, mandatory Florida HIE connectivity).
- **Specialty & Acute Care Bundle (RFA 034-25/26)** — HIE integration, diagnostic support, and a lead telehealth initiative (specialty, eICU, telestroke, or behavioral health).
- **Value-Based Purchasing (RFA 035-25/26)**, Initiative 11.
- **Rural Satellite Clinics (RFA 036-25/26)**, Initiative 1.
- **Workforce Development (RFA 037-25/26)**, Initiative 8.
- **Health & Lifestyle (RFA 038-25/26)**, Initiative 9.

The full breakdown is in Florida's budget narrative.

What has Florida procured so far, and what's open right now?

Florida's first live procurement round was the six-RFA slate (033-25/26 through 038-25/26). The application due date was extended to **Wednesday, June 17, 2026 at 2:00 p.m. EST**. AHCA also published grant-writing resources for applicants and an expanded definition of “rural” eligibility (four qualifying pathways). RFAs are posted and searchable on MyFloridaMarketplace under “RHTP.” The running record of solicitations and awards is in the dispatches below.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Florida?

The headline RFA deadline — June 17, 2026 — has passed. As new solicitations, amendments and award notices are posted, the dates surface first in the dispatches below and on MyFloridaMarketplace (search “RHTP”).

[MyFloridaMarketplace bids (search RHTP) →](https://vendor.myfloridamarketplace.com/search/bids)

What legislation or state action enables Florida's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. In Florida, spending authority flows through **HB 5001-E, the Fiscal Year 2027 General Appropriations Act** ($113.575 billion), which carries AHCA's authority to expend the state's ~$209 million first-year federal award; it was presented to Governor Ron DeSantis on June 23, 2026. Detailed allocation figures are set out in Florida's CMS-approved budget narrative.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Florida's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out as competitive RFAs where firms bid as **prime contractors**. **Subgrants and subawards** flow to rural providers — hospitals, clinics and satellite sites, pharmacies, community paramedicine and EMS programs, and workforce/education partners — and it is here that technology and connectivity vendors most often engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners**, particularly around the mandatory Florida HIE/ENS onboarding component. Applicants must clear AHCA's expanded rural eligibility definition.

Find and respond to solicitations on [MyFloridaMarketplace](https://vendor.myfloridamarketplace.com/search/bids) (search “RHTP”), and track updates on the [AHCA RHTP hub](https://ahca.myflorida.com/rural-health-transformation-program.html).

# Georgia Rural Health Transformation Program State Profile

## Questions & answers

What is Georgia's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Georgia is receiving approximately **$218.8 million** in Year-1 funding (the state cites $218.9M) under the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program, branded **GREAT Health** (Georgia Rural Enhancement And Transformation of Health). Year 1 is the first tranche of a proposed **$1.428 billion** five-year plan spanning 29 projects across 126 rural counties; only the Year-1 slice is presently obligated. The award is structured by CMS as an annual award across a five-year performance period.

Which agency administers Georgia's RHTP, and who leads it?

The program is administered by the **Georgia Department of Community Health (DCH)** under the [GREAT Health](https://greathealth.georgia.gov/) banner, with Director of Provider Services **James Peoples** among the named leads. DCH has hired **RSM** as its grants management vendor, running the applicant portal and a live technical-assistance inbox (greatgrant@rsmus.com). Program contact: [GREATHealth@dch.ga.gov](mailto:GREATHealth@dch.ga.gov).

What is Georgia's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

GREAT Health is organized around five initiatives DCH proposed to CMS: a sustainable health system, continuum of care, access, workforce, and information technology. The program is already in active deployment — running multiple competitive rounds concurrently, each with its own Notice of Funding Opportunity per initiative and applicant tier — with a clear tilt toward stabilizing rural hospitals and building workforce and technology capacity.

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Georgia funding, and at what share?

Georgia has been writing checks fast. Committed RHT dollars reached about **$43.3 million** by late July, with a $30.6M Phase 2 to 26 organizations:

- **Workforce** — $12.5M (GME expansion, nursing pathways, dementia-care training via the University System of Georgia, the GA Board of Health Care Workforce, and the Alzheimer's Association).
- **Technology** — $7M (hospital cybersecurity via Augusta University's Georgia Cyber Center; an EMS "Treat-versus-Transport" telehealth model).
- **Connecting to Care / Rural Stabilization Grants** — $6.5M to 17 rural hospitals.
- **Point-of-Care Telepods** — ~$4.3M across eight awards, scaling in units of $356,465 per telepod deployment.

The full breakdown across 29 projects is in Georgia's budget narrative and searchable application overview.

What has Georgia procured so far, and what's open right now?

Georgia is running four competitive grant rounds concurrently, each with its own NOFO. Named solicitations include **Care to Consumer: Telepods** ($356,465 per award, up to 20 awards; open May 15–June 15), **Telehealth Enhancements** and **Workforce Retention Technology (Surgical Robots)** (Round 4, June 15–July 15), and hospital **Rural Stabilization Grants**. On July 24 DCH posted its **Notice of Intent to Award for Initiative 3: Connecting to Care — Point-of-Care Telepods**, naming eight awards totaling about $4.3M (an intent to award, not a final commitment; no protest deadline was printed). The dispatch list below carries the running record.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Georgia?

Georgia's rounds have run on tight, sequential windows: Care to Consumer: Telepods (May 15–June 15), and Round 4 Telehealth Enhancements and Workforce Retention Technology (June 15–July 15, 2026). Because GREAT Health runs multiple rounds concurrently on a rolling basis, live application windows and technical-assistance webinars surface first in the dated dispatches below and on the [funding opportunities](https://greathealth.georgia.gov/find-funding-opportunities) page.

What legislation or state action enables Georgia's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. Georgia administers its award through the Department of Community Health under its CMS-approved GREAT Health project and budget narratives, with RSM engaged as the named grants management vendor.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Georgia's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out competitively (RSM runs DCH's grants management), where firms bid as **prime contractors**. **Subgrants and subawards** flow to rural providers — hospitals (including critical access hospitals), health systems, EMS agencies, academic and workforce partners, and community organizations — through the per-initiative NOFOs, and it is here that technology vendors and consultants most often engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners** rather than direct grantees. Because Georgia runs concurrent rounds each with its own NOFO and applicant tier, review the searchable application overview to identify which initiative fits, and use RSM's live TA inbox ([greatgrant@rsmus.com](mailto:greatgrant@rsmus.com)) for application questions.

Apply through the [GREAT Health grants portal](https://portal.greathealth.georgia.gov/) and track opportunities on the [funding opportunities](https://greathealth.georgia.gov/find-funding-opportunities) page and the [program hub](https://greathealth.georgia.gov/).

## Questions & answers

What is Hawaii's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Hawaii's award is **approximately $188.9 million** in Year-1 funding, its share of the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program. CMS structures the program over five years, with a Year-1 allocation followed by additional annual funding across the period. Hawaii's detailed Year-1 versus five-year budget structure is set out in the state's CMS-approved application and budget narrative.

Which agency administers Hawaii's RHTP, and who leads it?

Hawaii's program is administered by the **Hawaii Department of Health**, through its Office of Primary Care and Rural Health. Program contact is [doh.opcpdh@doh.hawaii.gov](mailto:doh.opcpdh@doh.hawaii.gov), and program information is published on the state's engagement hub.

[Hawaii RHTP hub →](https://engage.hawaii.gov/rhtp/)

What is Hawaii's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

Based on the state's published focus areas, Hawaii's plan centers on **Native Hawaiian health hubs** and **tele-robotic surgery** — signaling an emphasis on culturally grounded rural care delivery and on extending specialty surgical capacity to remote and island communities. Fuller detail on the plan's priorities and initiatives is published on the state's RHTP hub.

[Hawaii RHTP hub →](https://engage.hawaii.gov/rhtp/)

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Hawaii funding, and at what share?

The focus areas on record for Hawaii are **Native Hawaiian health hubs** and **tele-robotic surgery**. The state has not yet published a detailed public initiative-by-initiative budget breakdown in the primary sources reviewed; the full allocation is set out in Hawaii's CMS-approved budget narrative, and specific spending categories will surface as the state posts them to its hub.

[Hawaii RHTP hub →](https://engage.hawaii.gov/rhtp/)

What has Hawaii procured so far, and what's open right now?

As of this writing, Hawaii has **not published a dedicated RHTP funding or RFP portal** in the primary sources reviewed, and no live solicitations are on record on record. Procurements, NOFOs, and awards will be tracked here as the state posts them; the state's engagement hub is the primary place to watch for the first opportunities.

[Hawaii RHTP hub →](https://engage.hawaii.gov/rhtp/)

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Hawaii?

There are no confirmed application windows, technical-assistance calls, or webinar dates for Hawaii on record yet. Key upcoming deadlines will surface first in the dated activity log as the state publishes them, and on the state's RHTP hub.

[Hawaii RHTP hub →](https://engage.hawaii.gov/rhtp/)

What legislation or state action enables Hawaii's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. Hawaii administers its award through the Hawaii Department of Health under its CMS-approved application. No additional Hawaii-specific enabling statute is named in the primary sources reviewed.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Hawaii's program?

Eligibility is expected to run on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out as competitive RFPs, where firms bid as **prime contractors**. **Subgrants and subawards** flow to rural providers — hospitals, Rural Health Clinics, FQHCs, Native Hawaiian and Tribal health organizations, EMS agencies, and counties — and it is here that technology vendors and consultants most often engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners**. Until Hawaii posts its first solicitations, the best move is to monitor the state's engagement hub and reach the Department of Health's Office of Primary Care and Rural Health directly.

Tracker dispatches

12 dated briefs

## How Idaho defines rural

Idaho designates rural at the **census tract**, not the county. Its RHTP eligibility map applies the federal Office of Rural Health Policy definition of rural to 2020 Census tract population estimates, under which 655,070 residents — 36 percent of the state — live in eligible rural tracts covering roughly 96 percent of Idaho’s land area. County boundaries appear on the map as a display frame only; no Idaho RHTP document designates a county as rural or ineligible.

Sitting on top of the tract layer is a list of 225 named eligible places in two classes: 196 *eligible rural cities*, and 29 cities of fewer than 25,000 residents that fall *inside* an urban area and are individually eligible on that population test. The second class is the substance of the 27 August 2026 revision, when the Department of Health and Welfare replaced the eligibility map and the accompanying list of eligible cities across every open funding opportunity and described the earlier versions as incorrect. Nineteen cities named as ineligible in the withdrawn appendix — among them Chubbuck, Ammon, Hayden, Rathdrum, Kimberly and Garden City — are eligible under the replacement.

Two cautions for anyone reading the list as a target list. Thirty-one of the 196 eligible rural cities are unincorporated — census-designated places, and in one case an Air Force base — so they are eligible geography with no municipal government to receive a subgrant. And a place is not always contained by one county: Star spans Ada and Canyon, and the withdrawn appendix listed it as ineligible under Ada and eligible under Canyon at the same time. Applicants scoping a service area should work from the 27 August map rather than from an appendix inside a solicitation packet downloaded before that date.

See [how every state defines “rural”](/work/rht/states/rural-definitions/) for the cross-state comparison and source.

## What Idaho committed to measure

The subjects Idaho’s funded application pledges to track and report to CMS — the yardsticks its progress will be measured against. Extracted from the state’s own project narrative; the detailed baselines and targets behind each are tracked in the [newsletter](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/).

telehealth accesshealth alert networkEHR upgradesEMS capacitypreventable ED visitsrural workforce trainingphysician recruitmentchronic disease preventionbehavioral health mortalitytribal partnershipsmobile service deliverypatient experience

Source: Idaho’s CMS-approved RHTP project narrative. These are the state’s self-declared objectives; CMS weighs each state’s progress against its own commitments.

## Questions & answers

What is Idaho's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Idaho's total award is **$185,974,367.81**, its share of the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program under CMS federal award RHTCMS332084 (ALN 93.798). The program is a five-year CMS cooperative agreement. Idaho's published Year 1 milestone is a hard one: **all Year 1 funds must be obligated by October 30, 2026** — a deadline that is now visibly shaping how the state designs, times and routes its procurements.

Which agency administers Idaho's RHTP, and who leads it?

The [Idaho Department of Health and Welfare (DHW)](https://healthandwelfare.idaho.gov/providers/rural-health-transformation-program-grant/about-rural-health-transformation-program-grant) administers the program, with questions routed to [IdahoRHTP@dhw.idaho.gov](mailto:IdahoRHTP@dhw.idaho.gov). Specific pieces run through DHW divisions — for example, the Division of Behavioral Health leads the Pediatric Psychiatry Access Line procurement. A legislative RHT Oversight Committee reviews the program, and DHW holds regular lobbyist and stakeholder calls.

What is Idaho's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

Idaho organizes its plan around five initiatives: (1) improving rural access to care through technology — facility technology assessments, telehealth, digital health, cybersecurity and AI tools, emergency communications, data analytics and EHR upgrades; (2) innovative care-delivery models — diagnostic and care-access innovations, health extenders, and EMS expansion; (3) sustaining the rural workforce through ladder payments, career pathways, work-based learning and graduate medical education; (4) population-specific, evidence-based projects in chronic disease, behavioral health, and maternal and child health; and (5) rural health infrastructure and partnerships — facility renovations, pharmacy solutions, clinical equipment, patient-transport vehicles, safety-code compliance and Tribal support. The five initiatives contemplate roughly 23 targeted procurements.

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Idaho funding, and at what share?

The single largest Year 1 vehicle is an **$83,700,800 competitive subgrant pool** for technology, equipment, renovation and vehicle enhancements — telehealth pods, diagnostic and telepharmacy kiosks, AI-enabled cybersecurity, clinical equipment, mobile health units, patient-transport vehicles and targeted renovations — open to rural health clinics, FQHCs, hospitals, Tribes, long-term care and local public health districts. Direct-to-state RFPs in the pipeline include Data Analytics & Outcomes Evaluation (~$2M), Project Management Support (~$1.3M), Facility Renovation Independent Verification (~$2M), a Facility/Technology Assessment (~$2.2M), workforce/care-gap needs assessments (~$2.79M), and a Ladder Payments third-party administrator (~$800K overseeing $13.72M in Year 1 incentive payments). Workforce Residency, Broadband and Pharmacy Support are core project tags; the full breakdown is in Idaho's procurement overview and budget narrative. Federal caps apply: infrastructure ≤20%, EHR replacement ≤5%, administrative ≤10%.

What has Idaho procured so far, and what's open right now?

Idaho has posted a steady stream of solicitations. Live and recent items include the **Technology Assessment RFP (RHRFP2606 / IPRO RFP1375)** — posted July 10, proposals due August 21 — whose winner effectively drafts the requirements for downstream technology procurements; the **Pediatric Psychiatry Access Line (RHTPPAL1)**; two Maternal & Child Health subawards (OB Readiness RHTPMCH1 and Perinatal Quality Collaborative RHTPMCH2); a Ladder Payments TPA RFP; and Facility Renovation Independent Verification. Notably, Idaho has routed several connective-tissue contracts through **cooperative-contract vehicles rather than open bid** — Project Management Support (~$1.3M), a Rural Cybersecurity Modernization Assessment, and, after canceling its open RFP on July 13, the Data Analytics & Outcomes Evaluation contract (~$2M). Every dated dispatch covering Idaho is listed below, newest first.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Idaho?

Key recent dates: the Technology Assessment RFP held its pre-proposal conference July 17, with questions due July 24, **proposals due August 21 (5:00 p.m. MT)** and public opening August 24; its anticipated contract term runs October 1, 2026 through September 30, 2028, extendable to five years. The Pediatric Psychiatry Access Line held a pre-application webinar August 4, and the Maternal & Child Health subawards (OB Readiness, Perinatal Quality Collaborative) closed July 10. Everything is pinned to the **October 30, 2026** Year 1 obligation deadline. Live windows surface first in the dated dispatches below and on the funding page.

What legislation or state action enables Idaho's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. In Idaho, the award is administered through DHW under CMS federal award RHTCMS332084, with legislative review by an RHT Oversight Committee. State law shapes specific procurements: Idaho's interagency-contracting authority under **Idaho Code §67-2332A** is what limits the Pediatric Psychiatry Access Line to the state's public universities, and Idaho procurement rules underpin its use of cooperative-contract vehicles for several infrastructure contracts.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Idaho's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks, and Idaho splits them explicitly. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out as competitive RFPs (or cooperative contracts), where firms bid as **prime contractors** — project management, data/evaluation, technology and facility assessments, cybersecurity and the Ladder Payments administrator; some are narrowed to Idaho universities or public entities by statute. **Subgrants and subawards** flow to rural providers — critical access hospitals, rural health clinics, the state's rural emergency hospital, FQHCs, Tribal health organizations, pharmacies, EMS agencies and long-term care — and vendors of telehealth pods, diagnostic kiosks and analytics tools should market to these funded recipients as **subcontractors or implementation partners**. Bidders route through Idaho's Infor/LUMA state supplier portal.

Track opportunities on the [Idaho RHTP funding-opportunities page](https://healthandwelfare.idaho.gov/providers/rural-health-transformation-program-grant/funding-opportunities-rural-health) and the program hub.

[Idaho DHW Rural Health Transformation Program →](https://healthandwelfare.idaho.gov/providers/rural-health-transformation-program-grant/about-rural-health-transformation-program-grant)

# Illinois Rural Health Transformation Program State Profile

Illinois's **$193.4M** Transforming Rural Health Delivery award — the plan, the administering agency, where the money is headed, the NOFO pipeline, with a dated log of official activity.

## Questions & answers

What is Illinois's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Illinois's annual award is **approximately $193.4 million**, its share of the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program, structured by CMS as a five-year program. The state has branded its plan **Transforming Rural Health Delivery**.

Which agency administers Illinois's RHTP, and who leads it?

The [Illinois Department of Healthcare and Family Services (HFS)](https://hfs.illinois.gov/info/fedresctr/ruralhealthtp.html) administers the award, working with the Illinois Department of Public Health (IDPH) and its Center for Rural Health on eligibility and hospital analysis. Program questions go to [dph.crh@illinois.gov](mailto:dph.crh@illinois.gov).

What is Illinois's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

Illinois has been one of the quieter states publicly, but its plan centers on a **Hospital Transformation Program** (with planning grants for eligible rural hospitals), a statewide **Health Data Utility**, and a workforce **pipeline**. It is building a governance structure with monthly partner meetings and a Rural Health Advisory Workgroup to guide investments.

[Illinois RHTP hub →](https://hfs.illinois.gov/info/fedresctr/ruralhealthtp.html)

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Illinois funding, and at what share?

Illinois has published less initiative-level budget detail than most states so far. Its named priorities are **Hospital Transformation**, a **Health Data Utility**, and a workforce **pipeline**. The Hospital Transformation Program will begin with planning grants for hospitals meeting the state's rurality-threshold eligibility criteria. The full line-by-line allocation will be set out in Illinois's budget narrative and forthcoming Notices of Funding Opportunity.

What has Illinois procured so far, and what's open right now?

Illinois is **actively drafting Notices of Funding Opportunity (NOFOs)** rather than posting live solicitations to a central portal yet. In May 2026 it published its **Eligibility Criteria and Rurality Threshold Methodology** plus a full tabular list of eligible hospitals for the Hospital Transformation Program's planning-grant opportunity — a significant signal from an otherwise quiet state, based on IDPH discharge and ED data (2022–2024) and HRSA rural definitions. An April 2026 HFS presentation laid out an aggressive 2026 schedule for workforce funding, governance, initial collaborative-entity awards, and Hospital Transformation grant standards. The dispatch list below carries the running record.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Illinois?

Per HFS's April 2026 timeline, Illinois planned to launch workforce-funding stakeholder processes in March, stand up its governance structure in March/April, make initial funding awards to collaborative entities in April–May, and develop Hospital Transformation grant standards by July/August 2026. Concrete application windows will surface as the NOFOs are released; watch the HFS hub and the dated dispatches below.

What legislation or state action enables Illinois's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. In Illinois, spending authority for the $193.4M award is carried by **HB0111**, the omnibus Fiscal Year 2027 appropriations bill, which passed both chambers June 1, 2026 and was signed by Governor JB Pritzker on June 16, 2026 — now **Public Act 104-0464**.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Illinois's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** and NOFOs (now in development) go out as competitive solicitations where firms and collaborative entities bid as **prime applicants**. **Subgrants and subawards** flow to rural providers — principally rural hospitals through the Hospital Transformation Program's planning grants, plus workforce and data-utility partners — and it is here that technology vendors and consultants most often engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners** rather than as direct grantees.

Illinois has not yet stood up a single central RFP portal; watch the [HFS RHTP hub](https://hfs.illinois.gov/info/fedresctr/ruralhealthtp.html) for NOFO releases and direct questions to the IDPH Center for Rural Health at [dph.crh@illinois.gov](mailto:dph.crh@illinois.gov).

## What Indiana committed to measure

The subjects Indiana’s funded application pledges to track and report to CMS — the yardsticks its progress will be measured against. Extracted from the state’s own project narrative; the detailed baselines and targets behind each are tracked in the [newsletter](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/).

First-trimester prenatal carePrimary & preventative care access pointsCardiometabolic (BP & diabetes) careRegional health coalitionsTravel time to care (30-minute access)Lifestyle medicine trainingMaternal & infant health outcomes

Source: [Indiana’s RHTP project narrative](https://www.in.gov/grow-rural-health/files/rhtp-narrativein.pdf). These are the state’s self-declared objectives; CMS weighs each state’s progress against its own commitments.

## Questions & answers

What is Indiana's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Indiana received **approximately $206.9 million** in Year 1 funding under the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program, part of the CMS awards announced December 29, 2025. As with every state, the award is disbursed by CMS annually over five years, with each year's payment tied to performance.

Which agency administers Indiana's RHTP, and who leads it?

The [Indiana Department of Health (IDOH)](https://www.in.gov/grow-rural-health/) owns the program, branded **GROW: Cultivating Hoosier Health**. Competitive procurements are run for IDOH by the Indiana Department of Administration (IDOA), with IDOA's Mike Huth serving as buyer on several RHTP RFPs. Program contact: [lbouza@health.in.gov](mailto:lbouza@health.in.gov).

What is Indiana's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

GROW: Cultivating Hoosier Health brings the federal program to the state with a locally driven design — Indiana's premise is that rural communities know their own needs best, and it has stood up regional committees with dozens of members to shape local solutions. Early initiatives span a statewide Medical Operations Coordinator Center for transfer and EMS coordination, alternate Medicaid payment models (including a rural ACO), a rural clinical-training and preceptor pipeline, and a telehealth landscape assessment. Tracked priorities include cardiac access, pediatric telehealth, and a rural connectivity build-out.

[Indiana GROW hub →](https://www.in.gov/grow-rural-health/)

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Indiana funding, and at what share?

Indiana's spending picture is emerging through its numbered RHTP initiatives rather than published percentage shares. Visible initiatives include Initiative 1 (Medical Operations Coordinator Center), Initiative 7 (Teleconsult/Telehealth Landscape Assessment), and Initiative 10 (Clinical Training and Readiness — rural physician and preceptor stipends plus a centralized preceptor registry), alongside an ACO feasibility study and a program-evaluator contract. Tracked project tags are cardiac access, pediatric telehealth, and rural connectivity. The full breakdown is set out in Indiana's RHTP application and budget narrative to CMS.

What has Indiana procured so far, and what's open right now?

Indiana issued a cluster of RHTP RFPs through the IDOA bids portal: RFP 26-87448 (MOCC Operations, a 5-year contract, due June 15); RFP 26-87556 (Clinical Training and Readiness / preceptor registry, Initiative 10, due June 15); RFP 26-87667 (ACO Feasibility Study, with a June 11 pre-proposal conference); RHTP07 (Teleconsult/Telehealth Landscape Assessment, due May 18); and an RHTP Admin Program Evaluator (due May 18). Watch the broad IDOA Current Business Opportunities portal, not just the regional grants page — that is where these post. The dispatch list below carries the running record.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Indiana?

Indiana's early RFP deadlines (May 18 and June 15, 2026) and pre-proposal conferences (May 20 and June 11) are now past. Additional solicitations post to the [IDOA Current Business Opportunities portal](https://www.in.gov/idoa/procurement/current-business-opportunities/) on a rolling basis; live dates surface first in the dated dispatches below. Subscribe to Indiana's RHTP updates to be notified as new opportunities open.

What legislation or state action enables Indiana's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. Indiana administers its award through IDOH under its CMS-approved application and budget, with procurement run through IDOA; no separate enabling state statute is named in the record. Note a key structural rule Indiana added to its FAQ: primary subrecipients are prohibited from awarding funds to other subrecipients via sub-awards or sub-grants, though they may still engage contractors.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Indiana's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out as competitive IDOA RFPs, where firms bid as **prime contractors** — the route for most of Indiana's early administrative and infrastructure work (MOCC, evaluator, telehealth assessment, preceptor registry). **Subgrants and subawards** flow to rural providers — hospitals, Rural Health Clinics, FQHCs, EMS agencies and community organizations — where technology vendors and consultants most often engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners**. Note Indiana bars subrecipients from re-granting funds onward, so partners engage as contractors, not sub-subgrantees.

Indiana maintains a self-service vendor intake list (add your firm via the state's form) and publishes it weekly. Track opportunities on the IDOA portal and subscribe for GROW updates.

[Indiana IDOA opportunities →](https://www.in.gov/idoa/procurement/current-business-opportunities/) [Subscribe to GROW updates →](https://cloud.subscription.in.gov/signup?depid=546006748)

## What Iowa committed to measure

The subjects Iowa’s funded application pledges to track and report to CMS — the yardsticks its progress will be measured against. Extracted from the state’s own project narrative; the detailed baselines and targets behind each are tracked in the [newsletter](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/).

telehealth infrastructurecenters of excellencecancer screeningradon mitigationoncology care accesscommunity health workersco-located carechronic disease managementhealth information exchangemobile integrated healthEMS modernizationmaternal neonatal transport

Source: Iowa’s CMS-approved RHTP project narrative. These are the state’s self-declared objectives; CMS weighs each state’s progress against its own commitments.

## Questions & answers

What is Iowa's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Iowa's five-year federal award is **$209,040,063.71**, its share of the $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program. The program is a five-year CMS cooperative agreement (opportunity CMS-RHT-26-001); contracts on Iowa's first big wave of RFPs run **October 31, 2026 through September 30, 2031**. Note that Iowa's anticipated funding across its four July RFPs totals $328,345,729 — larger than the single-year award — because those figures span the full multi-year program period, with Year 1 across the four totaling roughly $89.2M.

Which agency administers Iowa's RHTP, and who leads it?

The [Iowa Department of Health and Human Services (Iowa HHS)](https://hhs.iowa.gov/initiatives/healthy-hometowns-iowas-rural-health-transformation-plan) administers the program under the **Healthy Hometowns** banner, with questions routed to [healthyhometowns@hhs.iowa.gov](mailto:healthyhometowns@hhs.iowa.gov). Iowa HHS has named statewide technical-assistance providers to prepare applicants: **University of Iowa Health Care** for the Health Hub (hub-and-spoke) work ([HealthHubs-TA@uiowa.edu](mailto:HealthHubs-TA@uiowa.edu)), and the **Iowa Primary Care Association** for Communities of Care co-location.

What is Iowa's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

Healthy Hometowns is built around restructuring rural care delivery through partnerships and hub-and-spoke networks. The centerpiece is an expansion of Governor Kim Reynolds's Centers of Excellence Program into enhanced **Health Hubs** — investing in telehealth, specialized equipment, provider recruitment/retention and efficient space use — alongside **Communities of Care** co-location of rural provider types, community health workers as system navigators, and heavy investment in chronic-disease prevention and management. Named initiatives span maternal health, cardiovascular care, cancer care, mobile integrated (EMS-led) health, high-risk OB and neonatal transport, school-based services, and a rural residency program.

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Iowa funding, and at what share?

The four RFPs Iowa issued July 14 carry the largest anticipated dollars to date:

- **Communities of Care Co-Location (COMPADM26005)** — program total $168,234,514 (Year 1 $39,558,631; ~7 awards), the single biggest initiative.
- **Maternal Health Hub and Spoke (COMPADM26006)** — program total $119,783,328 (Year 1 $38,591,059).
- **High-Risk OB and Neonatal Transport (PHTHOET27002)** — program total $20,127,987 (Year 1 $6,000,000; ~3 awards).
- **Mobile Integrated Health (PHTHOET27001)** — program total $20,199,900 (Year 1 $5,049,975; ~7 awards).

Innovation Grants, OB/GYN Recruitment and Regional EMS are core project tags; further categories (cancer care, cardiovascular, school-based services, workforce recruitment) appear in the state's funding-opportunity documents.

What has Iowa procured so far, and what's open right now?

Iowa has moved through Requests for Information (maternal and cardiovascular hub-and-spoke), Notices of Intent to Release, and now live RFPs. Beyond the four July 14 procurements, the state ran a **Combat Cancer Health Hub Program (COMPADM26008, Round 2)**, a **rural workforce recruitment RFP (PHTHORC260120)** posted in February, and issued a Notice of Intent for a **rural residency program** (Internal Medicine or OB/GYN). The University of Iowa's Health Hub TA and the Iowa PCA's Communities of Care TA operate in an open Phase 1 through October 2026, with competitive site selection to follow. Every dated dispatch covering Iowa is listed below, newest first.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Iowa?

For the four July 14 RFPs, the calendar is firm: **mandatory letters of intent were due August 10** for Communities of Care and Maternal Health Hub and Spoke (miss the LOI and you cannot apply); **all four applications close September 1, 2026**; notices of intent to award land on or around **October 16**; and contracts run October 31, 2026 through September 30, 2031. Because Year 1 has a CMS obligation clock, dates are compressed. Live windows surface first in the dated dispatches below and on the Iowa HHS funding page.

What legislation or state action enables Iowa's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS under opportunity CMS-RHT-26-001. Iowa administers its award through Iowa HHS under the Healthy Hometowns plan, with the initiative anchored in an expansion of Governor Kim Reynolds's Centers of Excellence Program. Detailed allocation figures are set out in Iowa's approved project and budget narratives.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Iowa's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out as competitive RFPs through iowagrants.gov, where lead applicants bid as **prime contractors**. **Subgrants and subawards** flow to rural providers — and Iowa's co-location and hub-and-spoke designs make partnership central: Communities of Care requires each applicant to bring at least two other service-delivery entities under one rural roof, with **signed MOUs due with the application**. Eligible partners run from FQHCs and rural health clinics to pharmacies, dentists, behavioral health, nutrition services, aging/disability organizations, labs and community-based organizations — the natural entry points for vendors and consultants engaging as **subcontractors or implementation partners**.

Track opportunities on the [Iowa HHS funding-opportunities portal](https://hhs.iowa.gov/about/funding-opportunities), work with the named TA providers ([HealthHubs-TA@uiowa.edu](mailto:HealthHubs-TA@uiowa.edu) and the Iowa PCA), and [sign up for Healthy Hometowns updates](https://forms.office.com/pages/responsepage.aspx?id=TXssjVoIF0aFNjinbRmw2sbuYlanKX1HvvQN-2lxpgNUMTg5U0FHNTBGR1MzN1VTMUM5WlRXWUU2Vi4u&route=shorturl).

[Healthy Hometowns — Iowa RHTP →](https://hhs.iowa.gov/initiatives/healthy-hometowns-iowas-rural-health-transformation-plan)

# Kansas Rural Health Transformation Program State Profile

Kansas's **$221,890,000** Rural Health Transformation Program award — the plan, the KDHE-led administration, where the money is going, the wave of live procurements, with a dated log of official activity.

## Questions & answers

What is Kansas's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Kansas's award totals **$221,890,000**, 100 percent funded by CMS/HHS as its share of the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program. The Rural Health Transformation Program is a five-year CMS cooperative agreement, and Kansas's approved initial Budget Period 1 runs Dec. 31, 2025 through Oct. 30, 2026 — a compressed 10-month Year 1 in which the state is racing to obligate roughly $221M before that October deadline, with the remaining years funded through annual CMS budget periods.

Which agency administers Kansas's RHTP, and who leads it?

The [Kansas Department of Health and Environment (KDHE)](https://www.kdhe.ks.gov/2361/Rural-Health-Transformation-Program) is the lead agency and CMS awardee, with program questions routed to [kdhe.primarycare@ks.gov](mailto:kdhe.primarycare@ks.gov). KDHE runs many grant programs directly, but has also delegated significant pieces to partners: **Healthworks** (a nonprofit housed at the KHA Foundation) is running the state's finance-and-revenue and credentialing RFPs, the **University of Kansas Health System Care Collaborative** operates the Evidence-Based Practice Program, and the **Kansas Health Institute** facilitates the Emerging Technology Committee.

What is Kansas's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

Kansas's dominant thrust is the **financial survival of rural hospitals** — revenue cycle, denied-claims recovery, CFO capacity and centralized credentialing — rather than new clinical programs alone. Alongside that finance backbone, the plan funds regional partnerships, Rural Emergency Hospital conversion and capital investment, workforce (loan repayment), evidence-based practice infrastructure, community health workers paired with food-as-medicine, and a technology track aiming by 2031 for universal remote patient monitoring, seamless telehealth, and secure AI adoption across rural providers.

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Kansas funding, and at what share?

Kansas has already put roughly $79.1M on the street across two flagship programs plus a string of targeted grants:

- **Regional Partnerships Grant Program (RPGP)** — ~$50M to 22 recipients (KDHE reallocated an extra $20M after demand ran ~5x supply).
- **REH Conversion / Transformative Capital Investment (REH/CAP)** — ~$31.3M to 18 providers.
- **Emerging Technology Program** — $9.5M to 5–10 providers for scaling proven patient-facing tech, including AI.
- **CHW + Accountable Food is Medicine** — $1,029,405 for ~7 rural clinics.
- **Interfacility Transport Project** — $870,958.97 for 1–2 awards.

Loan Repayment, Facility Modernization and Mental Health are core project tags; the full breakdown is in the state's [approved budget narrative](https://www.kdhe.ks.gov/2361/Rural-Health-Transformation-Program).

What has Kansas procured so far, and what's open right now?

Kansas has been one of the most active states in the country. Recent finance-and-revenue solicitations run by Healthworks include the Revenue Technical Support Organization (RTSO) umbrella, CFO Mentoring & Financial Leadership Support, a Revenue Support Program, and an All-Payers Scorecard Program, plus a Centralized Verification Organization (CVO) RFP for the statewide credentialing pilot. On the KDHE side, the Interfacility Transport Project RFA and the Emerging Technology RFA have run, following the RPGP, REH/CAP, CHW+AFIM and Evidence-Based Practice solicitations. Every dated dispatch covering Kansas is listed below, newest first, and it carries the running procurement record.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Kansas?

The finance-RFP cluster carried compressed end-of-July deadlines — CFO Mentoring due July 29, the Revenue Support Program July 30, and the All-Payers Scorecard and the Interfacility Transport RFA both July 31 — with the Healthworks CVO RFP proposals due August 4 and IFTp awards anticipated on or around August 28. CMS officials are scheduled for a Kansas site visit September 22–23, 2026, and the Year 2 budget and Year 1 annual report are due to CMS in August. Because Year 1 dollars must be obligated by October 30, 2026, deadlines are tight; live dates surface first in the dated dispatches below and on the [KDHE RHTP page](https://www.kdhe.ks.gov/2361/Rural-Health-Transformation-Program).

What legislation or state action enables Kansas's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. In Kansas, the award is administered through KDHE under its CMS-approved budget narrative. State oversight runs through **House Bill 2555**, under which KDHE files monthly expenditure updates to the State Finance Council and the Legislative Budget Committee.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Kansas's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out as competitive RFPs — the finance, revenue-cycle, credentialing (CVO), data and technology procurements — where firms bid as **prime contractors** (several are administered through Healthworks/KHA Foundation). **Subgrants and subawards** flow to rural Kansas providers — FQHCs and FQHC look-alikes, Rural Health Clinics, hospitals, local health departments, Tribal health facilities, CCBHCs and primary care clinics — and it is here that technology vendors and consultants most often engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners**. Applicants for subawards must hold a UEI, FEIN and a Kansas SMART Vendor ID.

Track opportunities on the [KDHE RHTP hub](https://www.kdhe.ks.gov/2361/Rural-Health-Transformation-Program) and its open funding opportunities, and join the [RHTP application-update mailing list](https://public.govdelivery.com/accounts/KSDHE/subscriber/new?topic_id=OOS_1) to be first to see new solicitations.

[KDHE Rural Health Transformation Program →](https://www.kdhe.ks.gov/2361/Rural-Health-Transformation-Program)

# Kentucky Rural Health Transformation Program State Profile

Kentucky's **$212.9M** Rural Health Transformation Program award — the five-track plan, the administering agency, the budget split, live procurements, with a dated log of official activity.

## What Kentucky committed to measure

The subjects Kentucky’s funded application pledges to track and report to CMS — the yardsticks its progress will be measured against. Chronic disease preventionRural community hubsMaternal & infant healthBehavioral health crisis careRural dental accessEMS & trauma capacityTelehealth utilizationPreventable ED visitsData sharing & interoperabilityCommunity paramedicine

Source: [Kentucky’s RHTP project narrative](https://ruralhealthplan.ky.gov/documents/ky%20rhtp%20project%20narrative_cms-rht-26-001.pdf). These are the state’s self-declared objectives; CMS weighs each state’s progress against its own commitments.

## Questions & answers

What is Kentucky's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Kentucky's award is **approximately $212.9 million** in Budget Year 1 under the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program, and the state has confirmed the project is 100% funded by CMS/HHS. The grant spans five budget periods aligned with federal fiscal years (FY2026–FY2030), disbursed annually by CMS based on achievement of performance metrics.

Which agency administers Kentucky's RHTP, and who leads it?

The [Kentucky Department for Public Health (KDPH)](https://ruralhealthplan.ky.gov/Pages/index.aspx) administers the state's Rural Health Transformation Program, including its Office of Community Health Workers, which approves the workforce certificates the plan depends on. General inquiries go to [ruralhealthplan@ky.gov](mailto:ruralhealthplan@ky.gov).

What is Kentucky's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

Kentucky's plan is organized into **five named program tracks**: PoWER (perinatal and infant health), From Crisis to Care (EMS transformation and training), Rapid Response to Recovery (behavioral-health crisis and safety net), Rooted in Health (dental and oral health), and Rural Community Hubs. After procuring services across those tracks in the spring, the state moved to build the non-clinical workforce — community health workers — those services will need to run. Related priorities include vaccine confidence, primary-care extension, and substance-use disorder.

[Kentucky RHTP hub →](https://ruralhealthplan.ky.gov/Pages/index.aspx)

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Kentucky funding, and at what share?

Named Year-1 allocations from Kentucky's RFAs so far: about **$9.9M** to establish or expand accredited dental hygiene programs (Rooted in Health), and up to **$800,000** for four Community Health Worker specialized certificates ($200,000 each). The From Crisis to Care and Rapid Response to Recovery tracks fund EMS agencies and community mental health centers through additional RFAs. Priorities across the tracks include vaccine confidence, primary-care extension, and substance-use disorder. The full program-by-program breakdown is set out in Kentucky's approved Project Narrative and the six [APPROVED] initiative info sheets.

What has Kentucky procured so far, and what's open right now?

Kentucky has been procuring in waves through its Request for Applications page. Notable RFAs: Establish or Expand Accredited Dental Hygiene Programs ($9.9M, due May 29); the From Crisis to Care EMS set — Community Paramedicine, EMS Training Equipment/Mobile Units, and EMS Transformation (Treat-No-Transport and Transport to Alternate Destination, Wave 1 closed June 15, with more waves coming); Rapid Response to Recovery's CMHC Support and Telebehavioral Health Support RFAs (due July 3); and the Community Health Worker Specialized Certificates RFA (up to $800K, due August 5). That CHW RFA notably requires content be authored by subject-matter experts and not by AI. The dispatch list below carries the running record.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Kentucky?

The live deadline to watch is the Community Health Worker Specialized Certificates RFA: applications are due **August 5, 2026**, with awards announced **August 26** and the funding period opening **October 7**. KDPH has signaled additional EMS funding waves are coming. Live dates surface first in the dated dispatches below and on the [Request for Applications page](https://ruralhealthplan.ky.gov/Pages/Request_For_Applications.aspx).

What legislation or state action enables Kentucky's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. In Kentucky, RHTP funds flow at the state level through the biennial executive-branch budget (HB500), and the CMS Notice of Award issued December 29, 2025 required Kentucky to submit a Type 6 budget revision — reallocating an "other" category into detailed budget lines and filing a revised Project Narrative, reflected in the state's [APPROVED] info sheets.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Kentucky's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out as competitive RFAs, where organizations bid as **prime applicants** — but note Kentucky often hard-walls eligibility to Kentucky-based non-profits (the CHW certificates RFA, for example, excludes out-of-state organizations even if they currently serve Kentucky). **Subgrants and subawards** flow to rural providers — hospitals, KBEMS-licensed EMS agencies, community mental health centers, FQHCs and training institutions — where technology vendors and consultants most often engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners**. A May amendment made for-profit entities eligible as Rural Community Hub Lead Organizations.

Track open opportunities on the [Request for Applications page](https://ruralhealthplan.ky.gov/Pages/Request_For_Applications.aspx).

[Kentucky RHTP funding opportunities →](https://ruralhealthplan.ky.gov/Pages/Request_For_Applications.aspx)

# Louisiana Rural Health Transformation Program State Profile

**Louisiana**'s **$208,374,448** Rural Health Transformation Program award — a top-five national award — the plan, the administering office, the dense NOFO calendar, with a dated log of official activity.

[Louisiana’s official RHTP hub →](https://ldh.la.gov/page/rural-health-transformation-program)

## How Louisiana defines rural

An organization does not have to be located in rural Louisiana to be eligible for the state's Rural Health Transformation Program. Rather than defer to the federal default, the Louisiana Department of Health published its own rural eligibility methodology (RHTP: Rural Eligibility Definition and Methodology, v1.0, May 13, 2026), under which an applicant qualifies as rural-serving through any one of three pathways — and two of the three are not geographic at all.

The first pathway is location: a provider in a non-metro parish, or in a RUCA-aligned rural census tract inside a metro parish, verified through HRSA's Rural Health Grants Eligibility Analyzer. The second is a CMS rural hospital designation — Critical Access Hospital, Sole Community Hospital, Medicare Dependent Hospital, or a hospital in a rural-designated area. The third is patient share: an organization more than half of whose patients live in ZIP codes classified RUCA 4–10 qualifies, measured either across the whole organization by its headquarters or at a single site such as a clinic or office. LDH's stated intent is to reach high-impact providers that may not be geographically rural but still serve rural populations — telehealth, mobile delivery, regional hubs — and it reserves the right to validate submissions against federal datasets.

See [how every state defines “rural”](/work/rht/states/rural-definitions/) for the cross-state comparison and source.

## Questions & answers

What is Louisiana's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Louisiana drew **$208,374,448** in Year-1 funding under the CMS Rural Health Transformation Program — a top-five national award — and is positioned to pull down roughly $1.4 billion across the program's five years. It is Louisiana's share of the federal $50 billion program, with Year-1 dollars released through a fast-moving series of Notices of Funding Opportunity funded via Cooperative Endeavor Agreements.

Which agency administers Louisiana's RHTP, and who leads it?

The [Louisiana Department of Health (LDH)](https://ldh.la.gov/page/rural-health-transformation-program) administers the program through its new **Office of Rural Health Transformation and Sustainability (ORHTS)**, which absorbed the former State Office of Rural Health. Program inquiries go to [RuralHealthTransformation@la.gov](mailto:RuralHealthTransformation@la.gov).

What is Louisiana's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

Louisiana's plan is built around numbered initiatives spanning workforce, innovative and collaborative care, telehealth/access (MRAHA), and sustainable access to care. A centerpiece is a data-driven rural Medicaid **Alternative Payment Model**: working from a Milliman review of Medicaid claims, LDH found rural parishes run higher per-member cost but lower inpatient and readmission rates — a pattern it reads as a physical-access problem, not overutilization — and is funding a primary-care-led, provider-owned APM in response. Key project tags include Value-Based Shift, Clinical Pipeline and Rural EMS Tech.

[Louisiana RHTP hub →](https://ldh.la.gov/page/rural-health-transformation-program)

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Louisiana funding, and at what share?

- **Rural Health Facilities Capital Improvement** (Initiative 5, Sustainable Access) — $39.9M, the largest opportunity, prioritizing ready-to-implement projects; awards $100,000–$10M.
- **Rural Medicaid Alternative Payment Model** (Innovative Care) — roughly $30M Year 1.
- **Telehealth Infrastructure for Rural Access** (Initiative 4, MRAHA) — $5M, awards $50,000–$500,000.
- **Rural Clinician Credit Bank** (Initiative 1, Workforce) — $5.63M.
- Plus **Collaborative Provider Models**, **Food is Medicine**, **Regional Care Conveners**, and the vendor-facing **Rural Tech Catalyst Fund**.

The full breakdown is in Louisiana's budget narrative.

What has Louisiana procured so far, and what's open right now?

Louisiana ran an unusually dense NOFO calendar and is now moving from solicitation into award. The **Rural Clinician Credit Bank** ($5.63M) closed June 25; **Telehealth Infrastructure** ($5M) and **Capital Improvement** ($39.9M) closed July 10; **Collaborative Provider Models** closed August 5; the **Rural Medicaid APM** (~$30M) closed August 7; and **Food is Medicine** and **Regional Care Conveners** closed August 14. As of late July, LDH's page showed several programs as Closed with **Notices of Intent to Contract** slated for late July through mid-August, and Rural Tech Catalyst Fund Cohort 1 awardees expected mid-September. The running record is in the dispatches below.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Louisiana?

Most Year-1 application windows have now closed (deadlines ran July 10, August 5, August 7 and August 14, 2026), and the state is in its award phase — watch for **Notice of Intent to Contract** announcements across late July into mid-August and RTCF Cohort 1 awards in mid-September. LDH holds a monthly RHTP webinar (the next was August 6). Upcoming deadlines, webinars and vendor showcases surface first in the dispatches below and on the funding-opportunities page.

[LA RHTP funding opportunities →](https://ldh.la.gov/page/rhtp-funding-opportunities)

What legislation or state action enables Louisiana's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. In Louisiana, Gov. **Jeff Landry** signed an executive order creating the Office of Rural Health Transformation and Sustainability inside LDH and a RHTP Advisory Council that seats the chairs of the House and Senate Health and Welfare committees. The legislature added a standing oversight hook via **Senate Resolution 198** (passed 36-0 on June 1, 2026), directing LDH to report to the legislature on its implementation of the award.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Louisiana's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out as competitive NOFOs where firms bid as **prime contractors**. **Subgrants and subawards** flow to rural providers — hospitals, FQHCs/RHCs, ACOs and clinically integrated networks, EMS, and rural hospital-led partnerships. On the Medicaid APM, LDH is explicit that funding flows to Medicaid-enrolled provider entities and that vendors (it cites Equality Health and Azara as examples) can support implementation but are not the default recipients — the classic **subcontractor / implementation-partner** lane. The Rural Tech Catalyst Fund is a more directly vendor-facing vehicle.

Track opportunities on the [LA RHTP funding-opportunities page](https://ldh.la.gov/page/rhtp-funding-opportunities), watch for vendor showcases co-hosted with the Louisiana Rural Health Association, and monitor the [program hub](https://ldh.la.gov/page/rural-health-transformation-program).

# Maine Rural Health Transformation Program — CMS award, lead agency, committed metrics & activity

# Maine Rural Health Transformation Program State Profile

Maine's **$190,008,051** Rural Health Transformation Program award — the plan, the administering agency and its nonprofit administrator, the budget split, live procurements, with a dated log of official activity.

## What Maine committed to measure

The subjects Maine’s funded application pledges to track and report to CMS — the yardsticks its progress will be measured against. Extracted from the state’s own project narrative; the detailed baselines and targets behind each are tracked in the [newsletter](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/).

school-based health centersopioid treatment accessbehavioral health accesscommunity paramedicinerural workforce recruitmenthealth career pathwaysclinical preceptorstelehealth utilizationspecialty teleconsultationuninsured pool carepreventive screeningvalue-based paymentPRTF in-state services

Source: Maine’s CMS-approved RHTP project narrative. These are the state’s self-declared objectives; CMS weighs each state’s progress against its own commitments.

## Questions & answers

What is Maine's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Maine received **$190,008,051** in Year 1 funding under the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program. As with every state, the award is disbursed by CMS annually across five years, with each year's payment tied to performance; Maine adjusted its budget to meet federal requirements and the final award.

Which agency administers Maine's RHTP, and who leads it?

The [Maine Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS)](https://www.maine.gov/dhhs/ruralhealth) leads the program, in partnership with the Governor's Office of Policy Innovation and the Future. Day-to-day administration is contracted to **MCD Global Health**, an Augusta nonprofit; Danielle Louder directs its technology and innovation work. Program contact: [kyle.kagele@maine.gov](mailto:kyle.kagele@maine.gov).

What is Maine's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

Maine is treating technology modernization as the foundation for everything else: its program leaders frame the work as groundwork for population health, augmented intelligence, telehealth, interoperability, and cybersecurity, starting with getting rural providers off aging electronic medical record systems. Alongside that, tracked priorities include small hospital support, oral health, and tele-emergency care.

[Maine RHTP hub →](https://www.maine.gov/dhhs/ruralhealth)

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Maine funding, and at what share?

Maine's first provider funding opportunity is a roughly **$30M** EMR/EHR modernization program, and its structure is unusually explicit. The money splits three ways: about **$9M** to hospitals (minimum ~$306K rural, ~$204K non-rural per site), **$20.4M** to comprehensive care providers including primary care practices and CCBHCs (~$81K rural, ~$54K non-rural per site), and **$600K** to opioid treatment programs (~$42K/~$28K per site) — with rural sites receiving roughly 50% more than comparable non-rural sites. Other tracked priorities are small hospital support, oral health, and tele-emergency. The full program-by-program breakdown lives in Maine's budget narrative.

What has Maine procured so far, and what's open right now?

Maine's first provider opportunity is the ~$30M EMR/EHR funding program, and notably it is **not an RFP**: every eligible organization that submits a qualifying application is expected to receive an award, on a formula basis. Applications run through MCD Global Health and were expected to open in mid-July 2026. Eligible uses run wide — system replacements, upgrades, hardware, and the staff or consultant hours to implement any of it. The dispatch list below carries the running record as more opportunities post.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Maine?

The EMR/EHR application was expected to open in **mid-July 2026** through MCD Global Health. Maine's RHTP Advisory Committee — providers, community organizations, Tribal partners, employers and educators — meets periodically to guide implementation (its most recent meeting was July 1, 2026, open to the public in listen-mode). Concrete application deadlines surface first in the dated dispatches below and on the program's funding page.

What legislation or state action enables Maine's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. Maine administers its award through DHHS (with the Governor's Office of Policy Innovation and the Future) under its CMS-approved budget, adjusted to meet federal requirements and the final award; no separate enabling state statute is named in the record.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Maine's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out competitively, where firms bid as **prime contractors** — and in Maine, MCD Global Health is itself the state's contracted RHTP administrator. **Subgrants and formula awards** flow to rural providers — hospitals, primary care practices, CCBHCs, opioid treatment programs, FQHCs and Tribal partners — where technology vendors and consultants most often engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners**. Maine's EMR program explicitly makes consultant and staff implementation hours an allowable use, a direct on-ramp for EHR, interoperability, and cybersecurity vendors.

Track opportunities through the program hub and MCD Global Health's RHTP page.

[Maine RHTP application portal (MCD Global Health) →](https://www.mcd.org/focus-areas/maine-rural-health-transformation-program)

## Activity log · 4 dated briefs

# Maryland Rural Health Transformation Program — CMS award, lead agency, committed metrics & activity

Source: https://www.civicoperator.com/work/rht/states/maryland/

# Maryland Rural Health Transformation Program State Profile

Maryland's **$168.18M** first-year Rural Health Transformation Program award — the largest per-rural-resident award in the country — including the three-pillar plan, the MDH team and issuing partners, the RFA wave, with a dated log of official activity.

[Maryland’s official RHTP hub →](https://health.maryland.gov/pophealth/Pages/Rural-Health-Transformation-Program.aspx)

Maryland’s official Rural Health Transformation Program page — [health.maryland.gov](https://health.maryland.gov/pophealth/Pages/Rural-Health-Transformation-Program.aspx), captured 2026-07-25.

Maryland’s own state-published rural map — State-designated rural counties — 18 of 24 jurisdictions. Source: [health.maryland.gov](https://health.maryland.gov/pophealth/Pages/Rural-health.aspx). See [how every state defines rural](/work/rht/states/rural-definitions/#map-maryland).

## What Maryland committed to measure

The subjects Maryland’s funded application pledges to track and report to CMS — the yardsticks its progress will be measured against. Extracted from the state’s own project narrative; the detailed baselines and targets behind each are tracked in the [newsletter](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/).

workforce pipeline programshealth training programsworkforce credentialingclinical rotation infrastructureprimary care capacitybehavioral health capacityhealth information exchangeadvanced care modelsnutrition educationhealthy food distributionhealthy food purchasing

Source: Maryland’s CMS-approved RHTP project narrative. These are the state’s self-declared objectives; CMS weighs each state’s progress against its own commitments.

## Questions & answers

What is Maryland's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Maryland's Budget Period 1 Notice of Award came in at **$168.18 million** (about $168.2M), 100% CMS-funded — 84 percent of what the state requested, and roughly double the national average measured per rural resident. CMS released the funds on February 25, 2026. It is Year 1 of the five-year federal $50 billion program, part of a proposed roughly $1 billion Maryland allocation over five years.

Which agency administers Maryland's RHTP, and who leads it?

The [Maryland Department of Health (MDH)](https://health.maryland.gov/pophealth/Pages/Rural-Health-Transformation-Program.aspx), through its State Office of Rural Health, administers the program, with a designated **Rural Health Transformation Committee** reviewing and approving funding requests quarterly. Maryland delegates delivery to issuing partners — the Maryland Health Care Commission (primary care), CRISP the state HIE (telehealth and connectivity), Garrett County Health Department (revenue-cycle TA), and the Maryland Department of Labor (workforce). Program contact: [jamie.cardillo@maryland.gov](mailto:jamie.cardillo@maryland.gov); general questions route to [mdh.transformruralhealth@maryland.gov](mailto:mdh.transformruralhealth@maryland.gov).

What is Maryland's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

Maryland's plan runs on three pillars: **Transform the Rural Health Workforce** (apprenticeships, AHEC expansions including a first-ever Southern Maryland AHEC, physician and advanced-practice recruitment); **Promote Sustainable Access and Innovative Care** (primary, specialty and behavioral health capacity, school-based health centers, HIT connectivity, telehealth infrastructure, mobile health, and value-based care); and **Empower Rural Marylanders to Eat for Health** (post-harvest infrastructure, food hubs, and healthy-food access in rural "hunger hot spots"). The through-lines are the state's global-budget transition and population health.

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Maryland funding, and at what share?

- **Pillar 2 — Sustainable Access and Innovative Care: ~$126M (about 75% of Year 1)**, with state-designated HIE CRISP positioned across health-information exchange, AI clinical-workflow pilots, and centralized telehealth infrastructure.
- **Pillar 1 — Workforce: ~$26M**, funding the first Southern Maryland AHEC (St. Mary's, Calvert, Charles counties).
- **Pillar 3 — Eat for Health: ~$15M**.
- **Governance: ~$1M**.

As of mid-July roughly $134.5M of the competitive-procurement pool had yet to be solicited. The full breakdown is in Maryland's budget narrative.

What has Maryland procured so far, and what's open right now?

Procurement has come in waves through the issuing partners. Currently open: a Maryland Department of Labor RFA covering **Pathways to Health Careers ($3.7M)** and **RISE ($16.4M)** across 18 designated rural counties, plus CRISP's first-come, first-served **Rural Health Connectivity Program** paying rural HIPAA-covered providers up to $40,000 each for new ADT, CCD and InContext connections. Earlier solicitations included PHPA 3936 (Pillar 2), Rural Maryland Council food-system grants (Pillar 3), an MHCC primary-care expansion opportunity ($6.3M), a CRISP telehealth-blueprint consultant, and a Garrett County revenue-cycle TA contract; the MDA Post-Harvest Cold Storage grant (closed June 14) and Garrett County Insurance Contracting RFA (closed June 15) have expired. The dispatch list below carries the running record.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Maryland?

Near-term dates: on the Maryland Department of Labor RFA, the **Notice of Intent to Apply is due August 7 (1:00 p.m.)** and **proposals are due August 9 (11:59 p.m.)**, with awards in September. CRISP held a Rural Health Connectivity webinar July 21. The Rural Health Transformation Committee meets quarterly, with sessions on **September 10 and December 11, 2026**. Confirm windows on the [RHTP procurement page](https://health.maryland.gov/pophealth/Pages/RHTP-Procurement.aspx); live dates surface in the dispatches below.

What legislation or state action enables Maryland's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. In Maryland, **Senate Bill 282** — the $70.8 billion FY2027 operating budget — serves as the appropriations vehicle for the Maryland Department of Health, which received the $168.2M first-year award; MDH's State Office of Rural Health manages implementation under that budget authority, with the oversight committee approving funding requests quarterly.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Maryland's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out as competitive RFAs and RFPs through the issuing partners (MDH, MHCC, CRISP, Garrett County Health Department, Maryland Department of Labor, Rural Maryland Council), where firms bid as **prime contractors or consultants**. **Subawards** flow to rural providers — rural hospitals, local health departments, area agencies on aging, FQHCs, school-based health centers, EMS and food-system organizations — where technology vendors and consultants most often engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners**. With roughly $134.5M still to be solicited against an October 30 obligation deadline, the backlog is the opportunity.

Track opportunities on the [RHTP procurement page](https://health.maryland.gov/pophealth/Pages/RHTP-Procurement.aspx), monitor the [program hub](https://health.maryland.gov/pophealth/Pages/Rural-Health-Transformation-Program.aspx), and route questions to [mdh.transformruralhealth@maryland.gov](mailto:mdh.transformruralhealth@maryland.gov).

## What Massachusetts committed to measure

Source: Massachusetts’s CMS-approved RHTP project narrative. These are the state’s self-declared objectives; CMS weighs each state’s progress against its own commitments.

## Questions & answers

What is Massachusetts's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Massachusetts is receiving approximately **$162.0 million** in Year-1 funding under the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program. Like every RHTP award, it is structured by CMS as an annual award across a five-year performance period. Detailed allocation figures live in the state's CMS-approved budget narrative; program updates are posted on the state's [RHTP hub](https://www.mass.gov/rural-health-transformation-program).

Which agency administers Massachusetts's RHTP, and who leads it?

Massachusetts's Rural Health Transformation Program is led by an **interagency team** rather than a single agency: the **Executive Office of Health and Human Services (EOHHS)**, the **Department of Public Health (DPH)**, **MassHealth** (the state Medicaid program), DPH's **Office of Rural Health**, and the Executive Office of Economic Development's **Office of Rural Affairs**, among other state agencies. Program contact: **Kirby Lecy** ([kirby.lecy@mass.gov](mailto:kirby.lecy@mass.gov)).

[Massachusetts RHTP overview →](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/rural-health-transformation-in-massachusetts)

What is Massachusetts's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

Early signals point to a plan focused on rural workforce housing, pharmacy access, and tele-emergency care. Massachusetts has not yet published detailed public plan documents in the sources reviewed, so this profile is kept brief and pointing you to the source of record.

[Massachusetts RHTP hub →](https://www.mass.gov/rural-health-transformation-program)

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Massachusetts funding, and at what share?

The key project areas signaled so far are **Workforce Housing**, **Pharmacy Access**, and **Tele-ED** (tele-emergency care). Specific dollar shares by initiative are not yet public in the primary sources reviewed; the full breakdown will appear in Massachusetts's budget narrative and on the [RHTP hub](https://www.mass.gov/rural-health-transformation-program).

What has Massachusetts procured so far, and what's open right now?

No source has yet tracked a live Massachusetts RHTP solicitation (RFP, NOFO, RFA, or award). As the state stands up its procurement track, opportunities and awards will surface first on the [RHTP hub](https://www.mass.gov/rural-health-transformation-program) and in the activity log on this page.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Massachusetts?

No firm application windows or deadlines have been posted in the primary sources reviewed. Because all RHTP awardees face a hard federal obligation timeline for Year-1 funds, expect Massachusetts to post solicitations in the coming months. Live dates will surface first in the dispatches below and on the [RHTP hub](https://www.mass.gov/rural-health-transformation-program); the Governor's office also posts related [news](https://www.mass.gov/orgs/governor-maura-healey-and-lt-governor-kim-driscoll/news).

What legislation or state action enables Massachusetts's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. Massachusetts administers its award under its CMS-approved project and budget narratives. No source confirms a Massachusetts-specific enabling statute or executive action from a primary source, and none is asserted here until it's documented.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Massachusetts's program?

Eligibility for RHTP funds generally runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out as competitive RFPs, where firms bid as **prime contractors**. **Subgrants and subawards** flow to rural providers — hospitals, Rural Health Clinics, FQHCs, EMS agencies, pharmacies, and community organizations — where technology vendors and consultants most often engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners** rather than direct grantees. Massachusetts hasn't yet published its specific eligibility rules in the primary sources reviewed, so watch the hub for those details.

The best entry point today is to monitor the [Massachusetts RHTP hub](https://www.mass.gov/rural-health-transformation-program) and reach the program contact, Kirby Lecy, at [kirby.lecy@mass.gov](mailto:kirby.lecy@mass.gov).
