# Methodology & Sources — RHTP State Reference

Source: https://www.civicoperator.com/work/rht/states/methodology/

Rural Health Transformation Program · Reference

# Methodology & Sources

How the Civic Operator Rural Health Transformation Program reference is compiled, sourced, and maintained.

## What this is (and isn’t)

This is an independent, structured **reference** to the CMS Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP) — a $50 billion, five-year program covering all 50 states ($10.1B in Year-1 awards tracked here). It exists to collect, in one predictable place per state, facts that are otherwise scattered across federal and state government sites. It is **not** a government site, and it is not the program’s commentary layer — interpretation, opinion and reporting live on the separate [Rural Health Transformation Grant Tracker](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/) newsletter.

## Sources we monitor

- **CMS** — the federal program, Notices of Award, and guidance (cms.gov/RHTProgram).
- **USAspending.gov** — the federal record of award obligations; each profile links to a state-scoped search.
- **State .gov program pages** — each state’s official RHTP hub.
- **State procurement portals** — RFPs, NOFOs, RFAs and award postings.
- **Governor newsrooms** — press releases, monitored for rural-health announcements.
- **Primary documents** — CMS-approved project and budget narratives.
- **The Tracker’s dated dispatches** — used as a chronological record of what happened and when, each deep-linked to its source brief.

## How facts are derived

Award amounts, administering agencies, procurement details and dates are drawn from the primary sources above and from the program’s own dated reporting. Where a precise figure appears in a primary source, we use it; otherwise we label a figure as approximate. We do not invent figures, agencies, or dates.

The **Year-1 award** shown on each profile is the state’s exact obligated amount from [USAspending.gov](https://www.usaspending.gov/) (CFDA 93.798), not a rounded estimate.

The **“Rural geography”** fact records how each state itself defines “rural” for its RHTP — a state-published rural definition or map, a fixed county list, or the default federal (HRSA/FORHP) designation. It is a factual classification of the state’s own methodology, drawn from its program materials; it is not a ranking, score, or judgment of the program.

## Update cadence

- **Nightly** — official-source links and the dated activity log refresh automatically.
- **Weekly (Sundays)** — state profiles are regenerated from the latest reporting; material changes are reviewed before publication.
- Every page carries a **“last reviewed”** date.

## Inclusion & corrections

A state is profiled once it has a CMS RHTP award. An activity-log entry is included when the program’s reporting covers that state by name. Spotted an error or omission? Corrections are welcome — the fastest path is the newsletter contact channel; verified corrections are applied at the next regeneration.

## Reference vs. analysis

We keep a strict line between **facts** (award amounts, agencies, official documents, procurements, dates — here) and **analysis** (interpretation, trends, implications — on the newsletter). Profiles link into the newsletter’s dated briefs for context, but the reference layer stays neutral.

## Editorial ownership

Compiled and maintained by **Civic Operator LLC**. Last reviewed 2026-09-18.

---
Source: https://www.civicoperator.com/work/rht/states/methodology/

# Michigan Rural Health Transformation Program — CMS award, lead agency, committed metrics & activity

Source: https://www.civicoperator.com/work/rht/states/michigan/

# Michigan Rural Health Transformation Program State Profile

Michigan's **$173.1 million** Rural Health Transformation Program award — the MDHHS administration, the four-part “Care Closer to Home” blueprint, the themed grant funding opportunities, the subrecipient roster, with a dated log of official activity.

[Michigan’s official RHTP hub →](https://www.michigan.gov/mdhhs/assistance-programs/medicaid/rural-health-transformation-program)

Michigan’s official Rural Health Transformation Program page — [michigan.gov](https://www.michigan.gov/mdhhs/assistance-programs/medicaid/rural-health-transformation-program), captured 2026-07-29.

Tracker dispatches

10 dated briefs

## What Michigan committed to measure

The subjects Michigan’s funded application pledges to track and report to CMS — the yardsticks its progress will be measured against. Extracted from the state’s own project narrative; the detailed baselines and targets behind each are tracked in the [newsletter](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/).

Rural partnership agreementsCare coordination accessHospital readmission reductionCommunity-based health projectsRural workforce recruitmentHealth professions pipelineCommunity health workersHealth IT interoperabilityMobile & home-based careTransportation & delivery access

Source: [Michigan’s RHTP project narrative](https://www.michigan.gov/mdhhs/-/media/project/websites/mdhhs/assistance-programs/medicaid/rht-project-narrative-final_cover.pdf). These are the state’s self-declared objectives; CMS weighs each state’s progress against its own commitments.

## Questions & answers

What is Michigan's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Michigan's award is **approximately $173.1 million** in Year 1 federal funds — its share of the $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program (CMS assistance listing 93.798). The program is a five-year CMS cooperative agreement. The state's enacted FY2026-2027 budget carries the appropriation at $173.2 million after the legislature reduced a $250 million base by $76.8 million to align it with Michigan's actual CMS award. So far MDHHS is releasing the money as a series of themed, mid-size grant funding opportunities rather than a few large ones.

Which agency administers Michigan's RHTP, and who leads it?

The [Michigan Department of Health and Human Services (MDHHS)](https://www.michigan.gov/mdhhs/assistance-programs/medicaid/rural-health-transformation-program) administers the program, with questions routed to [MDHHS-RHTP@michigan.gov](mailto:MDHHS-RHTP@michigan.gov). In July 2026 MDHHS established an **RHT Advisory Council** to strengthen engagement with rural health partners, community leaders and residents, and to make recommendations that inform strategic direction across the program.

What is Michigan's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

Michigan's plan is organized as a four-part “**Care Closer to Home**” blueprint, built from feedback MDHHS gathered from rural providers, community partners, Medicaid beneficiaries and residents. Its pillars, reflected in the state's grant funding opportunities and subrecipient awards, are **Care Closer to Home** (hub-and-spoke and access, including transportation), **Transforming Rural Health Through Partnerships** (collaborative care integration and chronic-disease work), **Workforce for Wellness** (recruitment, retention and training), and **Interoperability in Action** (health IT and cybersecurity). The aim is to make one-time federal dollars build durable, sustainable capacity for rural providers.

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Michigan funding, and at what share?

Michigan has released money in themed batches:

- **Workforce for Wellness** — $34,231,500 across five competitive GFOs (~73 awards), heavily weighted toward the MSW social-work pipeline ($14.5M), plus a $14,731,500 Rural Health Provider Recruitment & Retention fund and $5.0M for Maternal Health Provider Training.
- **Improving Care Delivery and Access through Transportation** — $12M across ~15 awards.
- **Chronic Disease Collaborative Care (Diabetes and Hypertension Management and Education)** — ~$2.5M across ~8 awards.
- **Subrecipient awards to date** — 124 awards totaling roughly $65M across the four initiatives plus Tribal government awards.

Quality Improvement, Clinical Residency and Cybersecurity are core project tags; the full breakdown is in Michigan's budget narrative and its subrecipient award page.

What has Michigan procured so far, and what's open right now?

Michigan procures through its **EGrAMS** grant system as competitive grant funding opportunities. Recent GFOs include the five Workforce for Wellness funds ($34.2M), the Improving Care Delivery and Access through Transportation Grant Program ($12M), and the Chronic Disease Collaborative Care Fund (~$2.5M). MDHHS also maintains a public subrecipient award page listing 124 awards (~$65M) and an earlier tranche of ~$15M to six entities, led by the Michigan Health and Hospital Association's hub-and-spoke work. Every dated dispatch covering Michigan is listed below, newest first, and it carries the running procurement record.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Michigan?

Michigan's GFOs run on tight, paired clocks — a project-director access-request step a few days before the application deadline, then submission through EGrAMS. For example, the Transportation grant set access requests due August 7 and applications due August 12; the Chronic Disease Collaborative Care Fund set access due August 6 and applications due August 11; and the Workforce for Wellness funds set access due July 30 and applications due August 4. Award periods generally run October 1, 2026 through September 30, 2027. Because access and application dates are separate, missing the earlier step blocks the filing. Live windows surface first in the dated dispatches below and via the [MDHHS RHTP listserv](https://public.govdelivery.com/accounts/MIDHHS/subscriber/new?topic_id=MIDHHS_960).

What legislation or state action enables Michigan's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. In Michigan, the appropriation was enacted through **Senate Bill 878 (Public Act 21 of 2026)** — the FY2026-2027 MDHHS omnibus signed by Governor Gretchen Whitmer on July 21, 2026 — which set the RHTP line at $173.2 million in federal funds, transferred 2.0 positions, and designated the federal grant as a separate fund source.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Michigan's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** would go out competitively, where firms bid as **prime contractors**. In practice, Michigan is running most of its money as competitive **grant funding opportunities and subawards** to a deliberately wide field — 501(c)(3) nonprofits, for-profits, local municipalities, transit agencies, local health departments, health systems, health plans, community-based coalitions, community foundations, universities, and federally recognized Michigan Tribes or Indian Health Clinic programs. That breadth (the Transportation GFO in particular opens the door to the transit-and-access layer that usually sits outside RHTP) is where technology vendors and consultants most often engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners**.

Track opportunities in **EGrAMS** via the [MDHHS RHTP hub](https://www.michigan.gov/mdhhs/assistance-programs/medicaid/rural-health-transformation-program), and [sign up for the RHTP listserv](https://public.govdelivery.com/accounts/MIDHHS/subscriber/new?topic_id=MIDHHS_960) to be first to see new GFOs.

[MDHHS Rural Health Transformation Program →](https://www.michigan.gov/mdhhs/assistance-programs/medicaid/rural-health-transformation-program)

# Minnesota Rural Health Transformation Program State Profile

**Minnesota**'s roughly **$193.1 million** Rural Health Transformation Program award — the plan, the administering agency, the early RFP and grant slate, with a dated log of official activity.

[Minnesota’s official RHTP hub →](https://www.health.state.mn.us/facilities/ruralhealth/ruraltrans/index.html)

## Questions & answers

What is Minnesota's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Minnesota's Year-1 award is approximately **$193.1 million**, its share of the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program. It is a five-year program; Minnesota's early Year-1 activity has flowed through competitive RFPs for advisory services and grant opportunities aimed at rural providers.

Which agency administers Minnesota's RHTP, and who leads it?

The [Minnesota Department of Health (MDH)](https://www.health.state.mn.us/facilities/ruralhealth/ruraltrans/index.html) administers the program through its **Office of Rural Health and Primary Care**. Program inquiries go to [roble.aden@state.mn.us](mailto:roble.aden@state.mn.us).

What is Minnesota's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

Minnesota's plan is aimed at strengthening rural health care through workforce development, capital improvement, and modernized health information technology — building rural clinical training pipelines, upgrading facilities and equipment, and supporting rural EMS. Early solicitations emphasize preparing and retaining advanced-practice, behavioral-health and oral-health providers to deliver comprehensive rural care. Key project tags include Capital Improvement, Workforce Grants and Rural EMS.

[Minnesota RHTP hub →](https://www.health.state.mn.us/facilities/ruralhealth/ruraltrans/index.html)

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Minnesota funding, and at what share?

Minnesota's published Year-1 spending so far centers on workforce and technology. It includes a **Rural Clinical Rotations Expansion Grant Program** funding rural clinical fellowships (12–18 months) for advanced-practice, behavioral-health and oral-health providers, and a **Health Information Technology (HIT) Advisory Services** engagement to guide subgrantees' technology purchases. MDH also opened four Notices of Grant Opportunity targeting rural hospitals, rural FQHCs, rural Tribal Nations, and rural CCBHCs/CMHCs. Key project tags include Capital Improvement, Workforce Grants and Rural EMS; the full breakdown is in Minnesota's budget narrative.

What has Minnesota procured so far, and what's open right now?

Minnesota's named solicitations to date include the **Rural Clinical Rotations Expansion Grant Program RFP** (applications due July 31, 2026, with an informational webinar July 1); the **HIT Advisory Services RFP** (SWIFT Event #2000018129, responses due April 20, 2026, submitted through the State's SWIFT Supplier Portal); and **four Notices of Grant Opportunity** published in March 2026 for rural hospitals, FQHCs, Tribal Nations and CCBHCs/CMHCs. The running record of solicitations and awards is in the dispatches below.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Minnesota?

Recent named dates include the Rural Clinical Rotations Expansion Grant application deadline of **July 31, 2026, 4:30 p.m.** (with a July 1 informational webinar) and the HIT Advisory Services response deadline of April 20, 2026. As those windows close, new deadlines and webinars surface first in the dispatches below and on MDH's grants and funding-opportunities page.

[MN RHTP grants & funding →](https://www.health.state.mn.us/facilities/ruralhealth/funding/grants)

What legislation or state action enables Minnesota's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. Minnesota administers its award through the Department of Health's Office of Rural Health and Primary Care. Detailed allocation figures are set out in Minnesota's CMS-approved budget narrative.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Minnesota's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out as competitive RFPs where firms bid as **prime contractors** — the HIT Advisory Services RFP, run through the State's SWIFT Supplier Portal, is a clear example for technology-advisory firms. **Subgrants and subawards** flow to rural providers — rural hospitals, rural clinics, FQHCs, CCBHCs/CMHCs, rural Tribal Nations, and accredited clinical training programs — and it is here that technology vendors and consultants most often engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners**. Firms responding to state RFPs must register and bid through the SWIFT Supplier Portal.

Track opportunities on the [MDH grants and funding page](https://www.health.state.mn.us/facilities/ruralhealth/funding/grants) and the [Minnesota RHTP hub](https://www.health.state.mn.us/facilities/ruralhealth/ruraltrans/index.html).

# Mississippi Rural Health Transformation Program — CMS award, lead agency, committed metrics & activity

# Mississippi Rural Health Transformation Program State Profile

**Mississippi**'s **$205,990,180.16** Year-1 Rural Health Transformation Program award — the administering office, the initiatives, live provider grant programs, with a dated log of official activity.

[Mississippi’s official RHTP hub →](https://mississippirhtp.com)

Mississippi’s official Rural Health Transformation Program page — [mississippirhtp.com](https://mississippirhtp.com), captured 2026-07-29.

Tracker dispatches

11 dated briefs

## Questions & answers

What is Mississippi's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Mississippi's total RHTP award is roughly **$206 million** — precisely **$205,990,180.16**, and about 99.96% CMS-funded. This is Mississippi's Year-1 share of the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program, structured by CMS as an annual award across a five-year performance period (the program's obligation deadline for Year-1 funds is October 30, 2026).

Which agency administers Mississippi's RHTP, and who leads it?

The program is administered by the **Mississippi State Department of Health (MSDH)** through the Mississippi Rural Health Transformation Office, under the [Mississippi Rural Health Transformation Program](https://mississippirhtp.com) banner. Program contact: [info@mississippirhtp.com](mailto:info@mississippirhtp.com).

What is Mississippi's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

Mississippi's plan concentrates on stabilizing and modernizing rural provider capacity — hospital stabilization, maternal health hubs, and care coordination — delivered through provider-facing grant programs across capital, technology, telehealth, workforce, and behavioral-health crisis care. A defining design choice: MSDH has deliberately built its applications to be completed **without a grant writer**, using pull-down selections and limited narrative responses so that providers, not consultants, fill out the forms.

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Mississippi funding, and at what share?

Mississippi opened its first competitive phase in June 2026 with three provider grant programs making about **$91.2 million** available in Year 1:

- **Rural Capital Project Care Gap Closure (RCGC)** — $28.5M for facility renovations, upgrades, clinic expansion and equipment; 20–30 awards of up to $3M each (excludes new construction, telehealth, cybersecurity, EHRs, and broadband).
- **Rural Provider Technology Grant (RTG)** — $57M.
- **Telehealth Hub Connectivity, Equipment, and Education (TCE)** — telehealth adoption.

Additional initiatives include the Workforce Expansion Initiative (four opportunities) and the Psychiatric Emergency Services (PES) EmPATH Units program. The full breakdown is in Mississippi's budget narrative and on the [funding page](https://mississippirhtp.com/funding/).

What has Mississippi procured so far, and what's open right now?

Mississippi's first funding phase (RCGC, RTG, and TCE) opened June 15 and closed July 15, 2026. A second wave followed: four **Workforce Expansion Initiative (WEI)** opportunities and the **PES – EmPATH Units Grant Program** opened July 15, 2026. On the direct-contract side, MSDH issued a Notice of Intent to Award on June 9, 2026 naming **Premier Healthcare Solutions, Inc.** as top-ranked offeror for the four-year Comprehensive State Health Plan contract (RFx 3180002944), from a deep field of seven responsive firms. The dispatch list below carries the running record of what's opened and closed.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Mississippi?

Key posted dates: the WEI opportunities and the PES–EmPATH program opened July 15, 2026, with an **application deadline of August 17, 2026 at 5:00 PM CST** and EmPATH award announcements expected in September 2026. Mississippi's first-phase provider grants (RCGC/RTG/TCE) closed July 15, 2026. Because windows are short, live dates surface first in the dated dispatches below and on the [MS RHTP funding page](https://mississippirhtp.com/funding/).

What legislation or state action enables Mississippi's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. Mississippi's legislature attempted to add competitive-bidding and reporting requirements through **SB2477** and companion **HB1067**, but Governor Tate Reeves **vetoed** the bill on April 3, 2026, arguing (citing a CMS letter) that the added requirements would risk the state's ability to obligate funds by the October 30, 2026 deadline. As a result, the program continues to operate under MSDH's CMS-approved project and budget narratives without that statutory procurement overlay.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Mississippi's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out as competitive RFPs (for example, the Comprehensive State Health Plan RFx), where firms bid as **prime contractors**. **Subgrants and subawards** flow to a broad pool of "Eligible Providers" — Mississippi-located hospitals (including critical access hospitals), physician practices and solo practitioners, rural health clinics, FQHCs, local health departments, Native American Sovereign Tribe healthcare facilities, certified community behavioral health clinics, SUD and dental services, and licensed long-term care facilities located in or serving rural populations. Mississippi defines "rural" as counties under 50,000 residents or fewer than 500 people per square mile, or municipalities under 15,000; an organization need not be physically rural but must show meaningful benefit to rural Mississippians. Note the state's stated preference for providers over grant-writing consultants — UEI/MAGIC vendor numbers are required only before award execution, not to apply.

Track opportunities on the [MS RHTP Funding Opportunities](https://mississippirhtp.com/funding/) page and the [program hub](https://mississippirhtp.com).

## What Missouri committed to measure

The subjects Missouri’s funded application pledges to track and report to CMS — the yardsticks its progress will be measured against. Extracted from the state’s own project narrative; the detailed baselines and targets behind each are tracked in the [newsletter](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/).

care hub coveragechronic disease controlmaternal and infant healthbehavioral health utilizationalternative payment modelsdata interoperabilityrural healthcare workforceEMS optimizationremote patient monitoringfacility service-line preservation

Source: Missouri’s CMS-approved RHTP project narrative. These are the state’s self-declared objectives; CMS weighs each state’s progress against its own commitments.

## Questions & answers

What is Missouri's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Missouri's Year 1 award is **approximately $215.9 million**, its share of the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program, structured by CMS as a five-year program. The state has branded its plan **ToRCH Care** (Transformation of Rural Community Health Care).

Which agency administers Missouri's RHTP, and who leads it?

The [Missouri Department of Social Services (DSS)](https://mydss.mo.gov/mhd/rural-health), through its MO HealthNet Division and Rural Health Transformation Office, administers the program on behalf of CMS. It is led by RHT Director **Joseph Miller**, coordinating with the Department of Mental Health (DMH) and the Department of Health and Senior Services (DHSS). Program questions go to [ruralhealth@health.mo.gov](mailto:ruralhealth@health.mo.gov).

What is Missouri's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

Missouri's ToRCH Care model organizes the state into **27 Community Hub Areas**, each led by a competitively selected Hub Anchor organization that convenes local providers and community partners. Underpinning it is a **Digital Backbone** — a foundational technology and data layer (the Missouri Integrated Health Data Fabric, or MOFAB) built on HL7 FHIR R4 and USCDI v3 standards — alongside innovative payment models, talent-pipeline development, and regional networks.

[Missouri ToRCH Care hub →](https://mydss.mo.gov/mhd/rural-health)

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Missouri funding, and at what share?

- **Digital Backbone** — roughly $56 million in Year 1, covering EHR modernization, a statewide Social Care Referral platform, ambient AI, remote patient monitoring, telehealth, and data/AI governance.
- **27 Hub Anchors** — one organization per ToRCH Care Community Hub Area.
- **MEMSA Mobile Integrated Healthcare / Community Paramedicine** — roughly $6.5 million.
- **Missouri Doula Association** — $732,660.43 for rural doula training and integration.
- **Rural home visiting** (via the Children's Trust Fund) — $588,000 annually.

The full breakdown, including talent pipeline, EHR upgrades, and regional networks, is in Missouri's budget narrative.

What has Missouri procured so far, and what's open right now?

Missouri is taking a distinct structural path: rather than run open state RFPs, DSS largely routes RHTP dollars through **named administering intermediaries**. It selected 27 Hub Anchor organizations (from 41 applications) through a competitive review; partnered with the **Missouri Emergency Medical Services Association (MEMSA)** on a roughly $6.5M Mobile Integrated Healthcare build (MEMSA is now recruiting rural EMS agencies directly and this is open now); awarded the **Missouri Doula Association** $732,660.43; and opened **Rural Health Transformation Funding for Home Visiting** through the Children's Trust Fund. The dispatch list below carries the running record.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Missouri?

- **August 23, 2026** — Rural Health Transformation Funding for Home Visiting application period closes (via the Children's Trust Fund).
- **Open now** — MEMSA's Mobile Integrated Healthcare / Community Paramedicine recruitment for rural EMS agencies (funded through July 31, 2027; questions to RHTP@memsa.org or 573-370-1702).
- **July 18, 2026** — 27 Hub Anchor awardees announced.

New dates surface first in the dated dispatches below.

What legislation or state action enables Missouri's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. In Missouri, the Department of Social Services (MO HealthNet Division) administers the award on behalf of CMS, coordinating with the Department of Mental Health and the Department of Health and Senior Services. Detailed allocation figures are set out in Missouri's ToRCH Care project and budget narratives.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Missouri's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** can go out as competitive solicitations where firms bid as **prime contractors** — but Missouri leans heavily on **designated intermediaries** instead: funds flow through MEMSA (for rural EMS), the Missouri Doula Association, the Children's Trust Fund (for home visiting), and the 27 Hub Anchors that lead each Community Hub Area. Rural providers — hospitals, FQHCs, behavioral-health organizations, local public health agencies, EMS agencies, and universities — engage as **subawardees and applicants** to these intermediaries, and technology vendors and consultants most often engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners** to Hub Anchors and the Digital Backbone build.

Missouri does not run a single central RFP portal; watch the [ToRCH Care hub](https://mydss.mo.gov/mhd/rural-health) and DSS announcements, and direct questions to [ruralhealth@health.mo.gov](mailto:ruralhealth@health.mo.gov).

# Montana Rural Health Transformation Program State Profile

Montana's **$233.5M** Rural Health Transformation Program award — the five-initiative plan, the administering agency, the budget split, live procurements, with a dated log of official activity.

[Montana’s official RHTP hub →](https://dphhs.mt.gov/RuralHealthTransformationProgram/)

Montana’s official Rural Health Transformation Program page — [dphhs.mt.gov](https://dphhs.mt.gov/RuralHealthTransformationProgram/), captured 2026-07-18.

## What Montana committed to measure

The subjects Montana’s funded application pledges to track and report to CMS — the yardsticks its progress will be measured against. Extracted from the state’s own project narrative; the detailed baselines and targets behind each are tracked in the [newsletter](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/).

Rural health workforce ratiosProvider retention and turnoverRural facility operating marginsTelehealth utilizationEmergency and EMS care deliveryBehavioral health accessChronic disease controlHealth information exchange and EHR adoptionCommunity and preventive healthYouth mental health and suicide

Source: [Montana’s RHTP project narrative](https://dphhs.mt.gov/assets/ruralhealthtransformation/rhtp-plan.pdf). These are the state’s self-declared objectives; CMS weighs each state’s progress against its own commitments.

## Questions & answers

What is Montana's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Montana received **approximately $233.5 million** in Year 1 funding under the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program, with up to **$1.2 billion over five years**. CMS issued final approval of Montana's first-year budget on February 19, 2026, clearing the way to award funds. As with every state, disbursement is annual across five budget periods (FY2026–FY2030), with each year's payment tied to performance.

Which agency administers Montana's RHTP, and who leads it?

The [Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services (DPHHS)](https://dphhs.mt.gov/RuralHealthTransformationProgram/) administers the program, with Director **Charlie Brereton** and Program Director **Michelle McNamee** leading it. Workforce (Initiative 1) is run through the Montana Department of Labor and Industry (DLI). Program contact runs through the State Office of Rural Health at [montana.sorh@montana.edu](mailto:montana.sorh@montana.edu).

What is Montana's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

Montana's plan is organized around **five core initiatives**, with a Rural Health Center of Excellence (CoE) at its heart. The CoE is built on three objectives: a data-driven strategy that analyzes rural supply and demand at the county and facility level; long-term sustainability, helping facilities reach positive operating margins without ongoing state support; and performance incentives for facilities that opt in and hit measurable improvements. Alongside it, the state is investing in workforce recruitment, EHR/HIE modernization, EMS, and integrated care for the rural dual-eligible population.

[Montana RHTP hub →](https://dphhs.mt.gov/RuralHealthTransformationProgram/)

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Montana funding, and at what share?

Montana's marquee investment is the Center of Excellence, procured as its own administrative initiative. Other visible priorities in the state's tracked project set include drone-based medical delivery, rural EMS, and critical facility repair. Named funding so far includes a $4M rural EMS equipment grant round. Montana published its full budget breakdown alongside the CMS-approved Year-1 budget; the complete program-by-program allocation lives in that budget narrative.

What has Montana procured so far, and what's open right now?

Montana runs competitive procurements through eMACS and bids.mt.gov, and provider grants through Submittable. Activity to date: two Center of Excellence RFPs (one to create the CoE, one to help facilities implement its recommendations), released in April via the Department of Administration; a Rural Physician/APP Recruitment RFP (DLI-RFP-2026-0088DL, opened June 26, closed July 16); a $4M Rural EMS Equipment grant round (portal open through August 15, 2026); and a Medicare/Medicaid duals RFI (May) that will inform a follow-on pilot RFP. The state's July appointment of a 26-member CoE Advisory Council signals its marquee CoE Strategy and Analytics procurement is at or near award. The dispatch list below carries the running record.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Montana?

Concrete near-term dates: the Rural EMS Equipment grant portal is open through **August 15, 2026**, and the summer Stakeholder Advisory Committee (SAC) meeting is set for **August 6, 2026** in Bozeman (register by July 24, in person or virtual). DLI runs its Initiative 1 workforce stakeholder webinars on a quarterly cadence. DPHHS says it will post additional grant opportunities on a rolling basis; live dates surface first in the dated dispatches below and at [ruralhealth.mt.gov](https://ruralhealth.mt.gov).

What legislation or state action enables Montana's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. Montana administers its award through DPHHS under its CMS-approved budget, which CMS finalized on February 19, 2026 after DPHHS submitted a revised budget prioritizing scalable, high-impact programs.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Montana's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out as competitive RFPs through eMACS and [bids.mt.gov](https://bids.mt.gov), where firms bid as **prime contractors**. **Subgrants and subawards** (and inter-agency agreements, e.g. DPHHS to DLI) flow to rural providers — hospitals, Rural Health Clinics, FQHCs, Tribal health organizations, EMS agencies and community organizations, applying via Submittable — where technology vendors and consultants most often engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners**.

Montana has built explicit on-ramps for firms: a Vendor Information page, a vendor-networking directory (around 215 organizations already listed) to find subcontracting partners, and posted vendor-webinar materials and FAQs.

[Montana RHTP funding portal →](https://ruralhealth.mt.gov)

# Nebraska Rural Health Transformation Program — CMS award, lead agency, committed metrics & activity

Source: https://www.civicoperator.com/work/rht/states/nebraska/

# Nebraska Rural Health Transformation Program State Profile

Nebraska's **$218.4M** first-year Rural Health Transformation Program award — the seven-initiative plan, the DHHS team running it, the RFA wave, the early awardees, with a dated log of official activity.

[Nebraska’s official RHTP hub →](https://dhhs.ne.gov/Pages/Rural-Health-Transformation.aspx)

Nebraska’s official Rural Health Transformation Program page — [dhhs.ne.gov](https://dhhs.ne.gov/Pages/Rural-Health-Transformation.aspx), captured 2026-07-16.

Tracker dispatches

12 dated briefs

## What Nebraska committed to measure

The subjects Nebraska’s funded application pledges to track and report to CMS — the yardsticks its progress will be measured against. Extracted from the state’s own project narrative; the detailed baselines and targets behind each are tracked in the [newsletter](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/).

Food as medicine (school meals)Local food producer contractsMaternity desert coverageCommunity paramedicine workforceEMS regionalizationBehavioral health accessChronic disease prevention

Source: [Nebraska’s RHTP project narrative](https://dhhs.ne.gov/documents/ne%20final%20project%20narrative%20rhtp%202025.pdf). These are the state’s self-declared objectives; CMS weighs each state’s progress against its own commitments.

## Questions & answers

What is Nebraska's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Nebraska received **approximately $218.4 million** for the first year of the five-year Rural Health Transformation Program — a revised CMS Notice of Award dated February 27, 2026 put the figure at about $218.5 million, its share of the federal $50 billion program, which runs five years with additional application opportunities in each funding year. The award lets DHHS access federal funds to launch Nebraska's seven initiatives.

Which agency administers Nebraska's RHTP, and who leads it?

The [Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS)](https://dhhs.ne.gov/Pages/Rural-Health-Transformation.aspx) administers the award and releases the Requests for Applications, coordinating with sister agencies such as the Department of Education (school-kitchen grants) and the Department of Agriculture on food-related pieces. General questions go to [dhhs.ruralhealth@nebraska.gov](mailto:dhhs.ruralhealth@nebraska.gov). Region-specific input comes through the program's **Health Care Advisory Regions (HCARs)**.

What is Nebraska's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

Nebraska's plan spans seven initiatives aimed at modernizing Critical Access Hospitals, retaining the rural workforce, and strengthening pharmacy and community-based care. Concrete threads include Critical Access Hospital and Rural Emergency Hospital infrastructure upgrades, a rural workforce pipeline built on SNAP Employment & Training partners, remote patient monitoring, community health workers and community paramedicine, a "Food as Medicine" track, and enhanced Medicaid support for assisted-living facilities serving higher-acuity rural residents.

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Nebraska funding, and at what share?

Money is moving through numbered RHTP initiatives rather than a single published percentage split. Named tags include **CAH modernization, workforce retention, and pharmacy**. Funded examples so far: Initiative 3.3 Rural Health Care Workforce Incentive & Sustainability (SNAP E&T) committed $2M; Initiative 3.2 rural VR/skills training; Initiative 4.4b Remote Patient Monitoring; Initiative 1.2 "Food as Medicine"; and more than $2.2M in school-kitchen modernization grants. The full breakdown is in Nebraska's RFA forecast and budget narrative.

What has Nebraska procured so far, and what's open right now?

Nebraska has been issuing RFAs on a rolling basis and has already named awardees. Under **Initiative 3.3** (SNAP E&T), awardees include Waterfield Health LLC, York County Health Coalition, Lutheran Family Services, and The Well NE. Awards were also made under **Initiative 4.4b Remote Patient Monitoring**. Open or ongoing opportunities include **School Kitchen Modernization** grants (up to $100,000/year, applications through August 31), **Critical Access Hospital and Rural Emergency Hospital** infrastructure funding (ongoing), and the **Rural Health Workforce Incentive Program**. The dispatch list below carries the running record.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Nebraska?

Concrete windows on the calendar: **School Kitchen Modernization** applications are accepted through **August 31, 2026** (or until funds are committed), and **Critical Access Hospital / Rural Emergency Hospital** infrastructure applications are ongoing. Nebraska maintains a regularly updated **RFA Forecast/Timeline** and posts new opportunities on the [RHTP funding page](https://dhhs.ne.gov/Pages/DHHS-Releases-RFAs-for-RHTP-Funding-Opportunities.aspx); live dates surface first in the dispatches below.

What legislation or state action enables Nebraska's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. Nebraska administers its award through DHHS under its CMS-approved plan and budget, refreshed by the revised February 27, 2026 Notice of Award, with additional RFAs planned in each of the five funding years.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Nebraska's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts and RFAs** are open to a deliberately broad field — local governments, Indian tribes, institutions of higher education, and nonprofit or for-profit entities can apply as **prime applicants**. **Subawards** flow to rural providers — rural clinics, FQHCs, certified community behavioral health clinics, local health departments, Critical Access Hospitals, Rural Emergency Hospitals, rural hospitals and Tribal health facilities — where technology vendors and consultants most often engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners**. The Rural Health Workforce Incentive Program ties incentives to a five-year rural service commitment.

Track opportunities on the [Nebraska RHTP hub](https://dhhs.ne.gov/Pages/Rural-Health-Transformation.aspx) and the [RFA funding page](https://dhhs.ne.gov/Pages/DHHS-Releases-RFAs-for-RHTP-Funding-Opportunities.aspx), and direct questions to [dhhs.ruralhealth@nebraska.gov](mailto:dhhs.ruralhealth@nebraska.gov).

# Nevada Rural Health Transformation Program — CMS award, lead agency, committed metrics & activity

Source: https://www.civicoperator.com/work/rht/states/nevada/

# Nevada Rural Health Transformation Program State Profile

Nevada's **$179.9M** Rural Health Transformation Program award — the four funding pillars, the Nevada Health Authority, its tracks-based RFAs, with a dated log of official activity for vendors, providers, and consultants tracking the program.

[Nevada’s official RHTP hub →](https://www.nvha.nv.gov/RHTP/)

Nevada’s official Rural Health Transformation Program page — [nvha.nv.gov](https://www.nvha.nv.gov/RHTP/), captured 2026-07-10.

## What Nevada committed to measure

The subjects Nevada’s funded application pledges to track and report to CMS — the yardsticks its progress will be measured against. Extracted from the state’s own project narrative; the detailed baselines and targets behind each are tracked in the [newsletter](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/).

preventive and primary care accesschronic disease mortalitymaternal and postpartum carebehavioral health and suiciderural hospital financial sustainabilityhealthcare workforce supplymedical transport accessmodern facility infrastructuretelehealth utilizationhealth technology and cybersecurity

Source: Nevada’s CMS-approved RHTP project narrative. These are the state’s self-declared objectives; CMS weighs each state’s progress against its own commitments.

## Questions & answers

What is Nevada's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Nevada's FY2026 allocation is **approximately $179.9 million**, its share of the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program (CMS cooperative agreement **#RHTCMS332074-01**). CMS structures the program over five years, with a Year-1 (Budget Period 1) allocation followed by additional annual funding; Nevada requires all BP1 subawards and contracts to be fully signed and obligated no later than October 30, 2026.

Which agency administers Nevada's RHTP, and who leads it?

The [Nevada Health Authority (NVHA)](https://www.nvha.nv.gov/RHTP/) administers the program, led by Director **Stacie Weeks**. Program contact is [gackerman@med.unr.edu](mailto:gackerman@med.unr.edu). NVHA runs the RHT effort with a standing Steering Committee and a CMS Project Officer, and in early 2026 onboarded two contract vendors to help develop its RFPs and RFAs.

What is Nevada's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

Nevada organizes its rural transformation funding into four main pillars — the **Rural Health Outcomes Accelerator Program (RHOAP)**, the **Nevada Rural Health System Flex Fund**, the **Workforce Recruitment and Rural Access Program (WRRAP)**, and the **Rural Health Innovation and Technology (RHIT)** grant — plus cross-cutting set-asides for Tribal health, Veterans/Corrections, and a school-based fitness initiative. The stated priorities span value-based care, telehealth and remote patient monitoring, behavioral health integration, maternal and infant health, workforce expansion, population-health analytics, and cross-sector care coordination, with heavy emphasis on sustainability, payer alignment, and multi-organization collaboration.

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Nevada funding, and at what share?

- **RHOAP** — roughly $27M made available in Budget Period 1, tiered from Tier 1 pilots ($100k–$250k) up to Tier 4 transformational system-level programs ($1.5M–$2.5M).
- **RHIT** — $26,989,741 (about 15% of the FY2026 allocation), across three tracks: Core Health IT & Interoperability, Provider-Facing Digital Health & Remote Care, and a capped Consumer-Facing Digital Tools & AI track.
- **WRRAP** and the **Flex Fund** — workforce recruitment/retention and rural system flexibility, run through their own RFAs.
- **Presidential Fitness Test** — a $1,298,985 set-aside (85% Nevada Department of Education, 15% State Public Charter School Association).

Recurring focuses on record include a workforce data utility, telehealth infrastructure, and quality. The full multi-year budget is in Nevada's Program Fact Sheet and Project Narrative.

What has Nevada procured so far, and what's open right now?

Nevada is among the first states to publish fully built-out primary funding RFAs. Named solicitations include the **RHOAP RFA** (about $26.99M available in BP1; proposals due June 26, 2026, awards expected by July 27), the **RHIT RFA** ($26,989,741; applications due July 6, 2026, decisions by August 10, subawards in September), the **Flex Fund RFA** (due April 30), **WRRAP** RFAs including a dedicated Workforce Residency RFA (1st/2nd due May 15; 3rd due June 26), a **Rural Tribal Health Transformation RFA** (due May 29), and the **Rural Presidential Fitness Test RFA** ($1,298,985, limited to two state education entities). Upcoming RFPs published in May remain open at least 42 days on Nevada ePro. The running record is in the dispatch list below.

[Nevada RHT NOFOs →](https://www.nvha.nv.gov/RHTP/rht-nofos/)

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Nevada?

Concrete dates on the record include RHOAP proposals due **June 26, 2026** (awards by July 27), RHIT applications due **July 6, 2026** (decisions by August 10), and the Q3 RHT Steering Committee meeting on **September 10, 2026**. All BP1 subawards and contracts must be obligated no later than **October 30, 2026**. Where individual windows have passed, current deadlines surface first in the dated dispatches below and on the NOFO portal.

What legislation or state action enables Nevada's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. Nevada administers its cooperative agreement (#RHTCMS332074-01) through the Nevada Health Authority under its CMS-approved Project Narrative and budget, guided by a state RHT Steering Committee and bi-weekly coordination with the state's CMS Project Officer.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Nevada's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks, and Nevada has been unusually explicit about the line. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out competitively, where firms bid as **prime contractors**. **Subawards** flow to rural and frontier providers, Tribal entities, and provider-led regional consortia. Vendor rules differ by program: under RHIT, NVHA states it “will not own or operate infrastructure” and limits technology vendors, counties, academic institutions, CBOs, and school-based programs to **subgrantee or fiscal-agent** roles rather than prime status. Under RHOAP, by contrast, non-profits, universities, and even out-of-state and technology vendors may apply as the lead applicant if they hold a signed intent-to-contract or MOU with an eligible rural Nevada provider. “Rural” covers the 14 rural counties plus eligible rural census tracts within urban counties (verifiable via the HRSA rural eligibility tool).

[Nevada RHTP hub →](https://www.nvha.nv.gov/RHTP/)

# New Hampshire Rural Health Transformation Program State Profile

**New Hampshire**'s roughly **$204 million** Rural Health Transformation Program award — the plan, the GO-NORTH office that runs it, the hub-organization contracts, the competitive evaluation award, with a dated log of official activity.

[New Hampshire’s official RHTP hub →](https://www.dhhs.nh.gov/programs-services/medicaid/rural-health-transformation-program)

New Hampshire’s official Rural Health Transformation Program page — [dhhs.nh.gov](https://www.dhhs.nh.gov/programs-services/medicaid/rural-health-transformation-program), captured 2026-07-21.

## What New Hampshire committed to measure

The subjects New Hampshire’s funded application pledges to track and report to CMS — the yardsticks its progress will be measured against. Extracted from the state’s own project narrative; the detailed baselines and targets behind each are tracked in the [newsletter](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/).

Avoidable ED and inpatient usePrimary care accessCCBHC certification and accessRural health workforce pipelineTelehealth and closed-loop referralsMaternal and perinatal careValue-based payment readinessRural hospital financial solvencyPreventive dental accessMedication therapy management

Source: [New Hampshire’s RHTP project narrative](https://www.dhhs.nh.gov/sites/g/files/ehbemt476/files/inline-documents/sonh/rhtc-project-narrative.pdf). These are the state’s self-declared objectives; CMS weighs each state’s progress against its own commitments.

## Questions & answers

What is New Hampshire's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

New Hampshire's Year-1 award is approximately **$204 million**, its share of the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program. It is a five-year program, delivered through five initiatives carried out with contracted hub organizations. Federal RHTP dollars flow as sub-awards under 2 CFR Part 200 — the state's independent evaluation contract, for example, runs through September 30, 2031.

Which agency administers New Hampshire's RHTP, and who leads it?

The program is run by **GO-NORTH — Governor Kelly Ayotte's Office of New Opportunities & Rural Transformational Health**, working with the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) under a memorandum of understanding. Program inquiries go to [rhtf@dhhs.nh.gov](mailto:rhtf@dhhs.nh.gov). The GO-NORTH leadership named on recent evaluation panels includes Sarah Goss (Evaluation Lead), David Chorney (Financial Sustainability), Marisa Lara (Population Health) and Tom Broderick (Legal & Contracts).

What is New Hampshire's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

GO-NORTH's stated goals are to make rural New Hampshire healthier through prevention, chronic-disease management, and improved behavioral and maternal health; ensure sustainable access by strengthening rural hospitals, health centers, EMS and telehealth; build and retain a skilled rural workforce; promote financial sustainability through innovative payment and value-based care; and modernize care delivery via technology, interoperability and data security. Key project tags include CCBHC Expansion, SUD Services and Elder Care Models.

[New Hampshire RHTP hub →](https://www.dhhs.nh.gov/programs-services/medicaid/rural-health-transformation-program)

Where is the money going — which initiatives is New Hampshire funding, and at what share?

New Hampshire is delivering its five initiatives largely through **contracted hub organizations** rather than a broad micro-grant slate. The hub organizations approved for grant period one include the Community Behavioral Health Association (CBHA), the Community College System of New Hampshire (CCSNH), the Community Development Finance Authority (CDFA), the Foundation for Healthy Communities (FHC), and the University System of New Hampshire (USNH). Key project tags include CCBHC Expansion, SUD Services and Elder Care Models; the full allocation breakdown is in New Hampshire's budget narrative.

What has New Hampshire procured so far, and what's open right now?

GO-NORTH's first competitive procurement, **RFP 2026-001 (Evaluation Services)**, was awarded to **NORC at the University of Chicago** with a price limitation of **$20,220,274**, running through September 30, 2031; it went before the Governor and Executive Council on June 17, 2026. The field was deep — 15 firms bid, 10 cleared the 500-point technical minimum, and NORC topped the field on technical strength rather than low price. A second procurement, an **Augmented and Virtual Reality (AR/VR) Hardware, Software & Training RFP**, was issued by USNH on behalf of UNH Manchester's Simulation Education Core. Hub-organization contracts for grant period one were approved through the Governor and Executive Council in March 2026. The running record is in the dispatches below.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in New Hampshire?

New Hampshire's early competitive and hub-contract milestones (the March 2026 Governor and Executive Council approvals and the June 17, 2026 evaluation award) are now past. Contracts and awards move through the Governor and Executive Council calendar, and current opportunities post to the GO-NORTH contracts-and-awards and apply-for-funds pages. Upcoming dates surface first in the dispatches below.

[GO-NORTH contracts & awards →](https://www.gonorth.nh.gov/contracts-awards)

What legislation or state action enables New Hampshire's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. In New Hampshire, Governor **Kelly Ayotte** established GO-NORTH to lead the effort, and the Governor and Executive Council approved a GO-NORTH–DHHS memorandum of understanding and an Accept & Expend request for the grant funds. Federal RHTP dollars flow as sub-awards under 2 CFR Part 200. Detailed allocation figures are set out in New Hampshire's CMS-approved budget narrative.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with New Hampshire's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out as competitive RFPs where firms bid as **prime contractors** — RFP 2026-001 (won by NORC) and the USNH AR/VR RFP are examples, and New Hampshire's evaluation award made clear that technical depth, not price, decides. **Subgrants and subawards** flow through the contracted hub organizations to rural providers — hospitals, health centers, behavioral-health and EMS providers — and it is here that technology vendors and consultants most often engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners**.

Watch the [GO-NORTH contracts & awards](https://www.gonorth.nh.gov/contracts-awards) and [apply-for-funds](https://www.gonorth.nh.gov/apply-funds) pages, and track the [DHHS RHTP hub](https://www.dhhs.nh.gov/programs-services/medicaid/rural-health-transformation-program).

## Questions & answers

What is New Jersey's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

New Jersey received **approximately $147.2 million** in Year 1 funding under the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program. As with every state, the award is disbursed by CMS annually across five years, with each year's payment tied to performance.

Which agency administers New Jersey's RHTP, and who leads it?

The [New Jersey Department of Health (NJDOH)](https://www.nj.gov/health/fhs/primarycare/rural-health/) administers the program through its Family Health Services / primary care office. Program contact: [RHTP.Application@doh.nj.gov](mailto:RHTP.Application@doh.nj.gov).

What is New Jersey's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

New Jersey has published relatively little detail publicly so far. The visible thrust is expanding rural primary care and improving access for underserved populations, including migrant health access and rural maternal and child health — the state's first solicitation targets integrating community doulas into rural maternal care. For the fuller picture, watch the program hub.

[New Jersey RHTP hub →](https://www.nj.gov/health/fhs/primarycare/rural-health/)

Where is the money going — which initiatives is New Jersey funding, and at what share?

New Jersey has not published a public percentage-by-initiative breakdown yet. The state's tracked project priorities are migrant health access and rural primary care expansion, with an early spending signal in maternal and child health through its doula-integration RFA. The full program-by-program allocation is set out in New Jersey's approved budget narrative to CMS.

What has New Jersey procured so far, and what's open right now?

New Jersey's first published solicitation is an RFA for **Doula Integration in Rural New Jersey**, released April 10, 2026. NJDOH is seeking proposals to integrate NJ FamilyCare Community doulas into the maternal and child health landscape serving rural residents, with the goal of growing the size and capacity of the community doula workforce and supporting their engagement across health settings. The dispatch list below carries the running record as more opportunities post.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in New Jersey?

No concrete forward deadlines are confirmed in the public record beyond the April 2026 doula RFA. New opportunities and their application windows surface first in the dated dispatches below and on the [NJ DOH Grant Programs Directory](https://healthapps.nj.gov/noticeofgrant/noticegrants.aspx).

What legislation or state action enables New Jersey's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. New Jersey administers its award through NJDOH under its CMS-approved application and budget; no separate enabling state statute is named in the record.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with New Jersey's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out as competitive RFAs, where firms bid as **prime applicants**. **Subgrants and subawards** flow to rural providers — hospitals, Rural Health Clinics, FQHCs, maternal-health providers and community organizations — where technology vendors and consultants most often engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners**. New Jersey posts its opportunities through the NJ DOH grant notices directory.

Track open opportunities on the state's grant directory and the program hub.

[NJ DOH Grant Programs Directory →](https://healthapps.nj.gov/noticeofgrant/noticegrants.aspx)

# New Mexico Rural Health Transformation Program — CMS award, lead agency, committed metrics & activity

# New Mexico Rural Health Transformation Program State Profile

**New Mexico**'s **$211,484,741** Rural Health Transformation Program award — the plan, the administering agency, the outsourced operating model, the live procurements, with a dated log of official activity.

[New Mexico’s official RHTP hub →](https://www.hca.nm.gov/rural-health-transformation-program/)

New Mexico’s official Rural Health Transformation Program page — [hca.nm.gov](https://www.hca.nm.gov/rural-health-transformation-program/), captured 2026-07-29.

## What New Mexico committed to measure

The subjects New Mexico’s funded application pledges to track and report to CMS — the yardsticks its progress will be measured against. Extracted from the state’s own project narrative; the detailed baselines and targets behind each are tracked in the [newsletter](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/).

specialty and primary care accesschronic disease controlbehavioral health screeningmaternal and postpartum healthremote patient monitoringrural workforce pipelineworkforce retentioncommunity-led innovation grantsprovider financial sustainabilityhealth data infrastructure

Source: New Mexico’s CMS-approved RHTP project narrative. These are the state’s self-declared objectives; CMS weighs each state’s progress against its own commitments.

## Questions & answers

What is New Mexico's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

New Mexico was awarded **$211,484,741** for Federal Fiscal Year 2026 (FFY26) through the CMS Rural Health Transformation Program — its share of the federal $50 billion program, and a figure the state confirmed in its Administrative Services Organization RFP. It is a five-year award (roughly $1 billion over the grant period), structured with Year-1 funding released through competitive procurements and subawards, subject to annual CMS approval and a program-wide administrative-cost cap of 10%.

Which agency administers New Mexico's RHTP, and who leads it?

The [New Mexico Health Care Authority (HCA)](https://www.hca.nm.gov/rural-health-transformation-program/) administers the program. HCA is running a deliberately lean internal team — hiring roughly 17 full-time staff plus a wave of program roles (Finance Director, Operations Manager, Data & Evaluation Manager, and initiative managers) — and leaning on outsourced vendors as the operational engines. Federal program inquiries route to [MAHARural@cms.hhs.gov](mailto:MAHARural@cms.hhs.gov).

What is New Mexico's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

New Mexico is implementing five approved RHT initiatives focused on expanding access, strengthening rural health infrastructure, closing maternal-care deserts, and advancing health equity across rural, frontier and Tribal communities. A defining feature is durability: HCA is building a permanent **Center for Rural Health Sustainability & Innovation (CRHSI/RHSIC)** embedded in the agency and designed to outlive the five-year grant via a revenue-sharing model. New Mexico plans to push roughly 95% of its federal RHTP funding out the door through competitive procurements and direct subawards.

[New Mexico RHTP hub →](https://www.hca.nm.gov/rural-health-transformation-program/)

Where is the money going — which initiatives is New Mexico funding, and at what share?

- **Rural Health Innovation Fund (RHIF)** — the primary community-led micro-grant vehicle, ~$187.5M over the grant ($47M in Year 1), for locally designed projects spanning behavioral health, preventive care, equipment/facility upgrades and care-delivery technology.
- **Healthy Horizons** — the specialty-care and chronic-disease initiative (~$393.2M), anchored by Regional Hub Organizations, plus a carve-out statewide maternal health allocation.
- **Administrative Services Organization (ASO)** — the fiscal back-office managing intake, subrecipient scopes, invoicing and compliance.
- **CRHSI / Rooted in New Mexico** — shared technical assistance and community programming.

Key project tags include Health Equity, Infrastructure and Maternal Deserts. The full breakdown is in New Mexico's budget narrative.

What has New Mexico procured so far, and what's open right now?

New Mexico has posted several major procurements. The **ASO RFP (#26-630-1000-0019)**, released April 30, 2026, seeks the fiscal anchor across four service domains (the federal RHTP is Domain 3); its deadline was extended to June 5, 2026 with award anticipated July 10. The **CRHSI RFP** closed June 12, 2026. The **Rural Health Innovation Fund RFP (#27-630-1000-0004)** made ~$47M available, with proposals due July 27, 2026 via Submittable and awards anticipated October 1, 2026 — notably, cost is not scored. The **Healthy Horizons RFA** for Regional Hubs was extended to July 6, 2026, and an **On-site Clinic RFP (#27-630-0700-0004)** with an optional rural mobile component was due August 1, 2026. The running record is in the dispatches below.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in New Mexico?

Recent key dates: RHIF proposals due **July 27, 2026** (evaluation July 28–August 17, finalist selection ~August 14, best-and-final offers August 20, awards as soon as October 1, 2026); On-site Clinic proposals due **August 1, 2026**; Healthy Horizons applications due July 6 with contracts starting September 1. As those windows close, new deadlines and webinars surface in the dispatches below and on HCA's open-RFP portal.

[NM HCA open RFPs →](https://www.hca.nm.gov/lookingforinformation/open-rfps/)

What legislation or state action enables New Mexico's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. New Mexico administers its award through the Health Care Authority. State law shapes how bids are scored: under **Section 13-1-21(J) NMSA 1978**, local (Resident, Veteran and Native American) preference points cannot be applied to federally funded work, so bidders on the federal RHTP domain compete strictly on merit and cost. The ASO also folds in state-funded streams including Senate Bill 3 behavioral health reform.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with New Mexico's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out as competitive RFPs where firms bid as **prime contractors** — the ASO, CRHSI and On-site Clinic procurements are examples (note Guidehouse, which wrote New Mexico's CMS application, is not precluded from bidding on implementation work). **Subgrants and subawards** flow to rural providers, Tribal entities, local public health, community-based organizations, local governments and academic institutions — and RHIF explicitly welcomes vendors, technology partners and equipment suppliers that can show a direct implementation role. This is where consultants most often engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners**.

Track the [HCA open-RFP portal](https://www.hca.nm.gov/lookingforinformation/open-rfps/), join the [RHTP updates and distribution list](https://forms.monday.com/forms/8e030d1aba2d00bf39f496544cea29ae?r=use1), and watch the [program hub](https://www.hca.nm.gov/rural-health-transformation-program/).

# New York Rural Health Transformation Program State Profile

New York's **$212,058,207.80** Rural Health Transformation Program award — the plan, the Department of Health administration, the Rural Community Health Integration procurement, its budget-period structure, with a dated log of official activity.

[New York’s official RHTP hub →](https://health.ny.gov/facilities/transforming_rural_healthcare/)

New York’s official Rural Health Transformation Program page — [health.ny.gov](https://health.ny.gov/facilities/transforming_rural_healthcare/), captured 2026-07-07.

## What New York committed to measure

The subjects New York’s funded application pledges to track and report to CMS — the yardsticks its progress will be measured against. Extracted from the state’s own project narrative; the detailed baselines and targets behind each are tracked in the [newsletter](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/).

preventable emergency visitshospital readmissionscancer screeningschool-based health centersPCMH recognitionchronic disease managementrural workforce pipelinetelehealth access pointseConsult specialty accesscybersecurity compliance

Source: New York’s CMS-approved RHTP project narrative. These are the state’s self-declared objectives; CMS weighs each state’s progress against its own commitments.

## Questions & answers

What is New York's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

New York's Year 1 award is **$212,058,207.80** from CMS/HHS, its share of the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program. The program is a five-year CMS cooperative agreement structured in budget periods. New York's first procurement, Rural Community Health Integration (RCHI), draws **$76,190,022** from Budget Period 1; notably, RCHI's implementation dollars don't flow in BP1 — they arrive in Budget Periods 2 through 5, with BP2 beginning November 1, 2026.

Which agency administers New York's RHTP, and who leads it?

The [New York State Department of Health (NYSDOH)](https://health.ny.gov/facilities/transforming_rural_healthcare/) administers the program, with questions routed to [RHTP@health.ny.gov](mailto:RHTP@health.ny.gov). RCHI applications and questions run through a dedicated program address, [rchi@health.ny.gov](mailto:rchi@health.ny.gov) (submissions are by email, not a portal).

What is New York's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

New York's plan is organized around four initiatives, the first and most developed of which is **Rural Community Health Integration (RCHI)** — building collaborative, implementation-ready integrated health networks anchored by a hospital in each rural community. The state prioritizes projects in **maternal-child health, maternity services, behavioral health integration, and substance use disorder prevention**, and holds applicants to at least one of three committed outcomes: reducing potentially preventable emergency visits, reducing hospital-wide readmissions, and increasing preventive care such as colorectal screening. Global Budget Pilots, Hospital Transition and Health Information Technology (HIT) are core project tags across the broader plan.

Where is the money going — which initiatives is New York funding, and at what share?

The first tranche is RCHI's **$76,190,022** in Budget Period 1, split into two tracks:

- **Planning grants** — up to $500,000 per county (per-county ceiling), stackable for multi-county applicants (three counties = up to $1.5M).
- **Implementation grants** — capped at $3,000,000 per application, covering up to three projects combined.

Administrative costs are held to a tighter **5%** in aggregate across the lead applicant and all partners/subcontractors, and capital/infrastructure spending is capped at 20%. The remaining initiatives — including global-budget pilots and hospital-transition work — are detailed in New York's project and budget narratives, with most implementation dollars scheduled for Budget Periods 2 through 5.

What has New York procured so far, and what's open right now?

New York's first live procurement is the **Rural Community Health Integration (RCHI)** funding guidance, released June 11, 2026. Through Addendum #1 (July 2) and Addendum #2 (July 6, a 375-question Q&A), the state extended the deadline, expanded the eligible-county map, and hardened the “located in” test. Award announcements are anticipated by the end of August 2026, with all contracts executed by September 30, 2026. This is the first of four planned initiatives; subsequent procurements will surface in later budget periods. Every dated dispatch covering New York is listed below, newest first.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in New York?

The RCHI application deadline, after two extensions, was **Tuesday, July 14, 2026 (4:00 PM EST)**, submitted by email to rchi@health.ny.gov. A webinar was held June 23. Award announcements are anticipated by end of August 2026, contracts executed by September 30, 2026, projects complete by June 30, 2027, funds fully expended by September 30, 2027, and final vouchers and reports due July 31, 2027. Future RCHI implementation guidance arrives across Budget Periods 2 through 5, with BP2 beginning November 1, 2026. Live windows surface first in the dated dispatches below and on the [NYSDOH rural-health page](https://health.ny.gov/facilities/transforming_rural_healthcare/).

What legislation or state action enables New York's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. In New York, the award is administered through the Department of Health under its CMS-approved project and budget narratives. Detailed allocation figures are set out in those narratives.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with New York's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** would go out as competitive procurements where firms bid as **prime contractors**. RCHI, however, flows as **subawards** with strict eligibility: each application needs a **lead applicant** — a registered 501(c)(3) not-for-profit or municipal hospital with a three-plus-year compliance history, **physically present or legally domiciled in one of the eligible rural counties** (the list stands at 47–49 counties across the addenda) — plus partner organizations and **at least one General Hospital or Rural Emergency Hospital**. Partners can sit anywhere, including out of state, as long as their work benefits eligible counties — the natural entry point for technology vendors and consultants engaging as **subcontractors or implementation partners** rather than direct grantees.

Track opportunities on the [NYSDOH Transforming Rural Healthcare hub](https://health.ny.gov/facilities/transforming_rural_healthcare/) and direct RCHI questions to [rchi@health.ny.gov](mailto:rchi@health.ny.gov).

[NYSDOH Transforming Rural Healthcare →](https://health.ny.gov/facilities/transforming_rural_healthcare/)

## At a glance

Tracker dispatches

14 dated briefs

## Questions & answers

What is North Carolina's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

North Carolina is receiving approximately **$213 million** in Year-1 funding under the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program. Year 1 is the first tranche of an approximately **$1 billion** five-year plan; the award is structured by CMS as an annual award across a five-year performance period.

Which agency administers North Carolina's RHTP, and who leads it?

The program is administered by the [NCDHHS Office of Rural Health](https://www.ncdhhs.gov/divisions/office-rural-health/rural-health-transformation-program), with new RHTP director **Maggie Woods** leading the effort. HHS Secretary Dev Sangvai and Governor Josh Stein have publicly championed it, and IT Secretary Nate Denny co-leads the digital-infrastructure work through NCDIT. Program contact: [corey.alford@dhhs.nc.gov](mailto:corey.alford@dhhs.nc.gov).

What is North Carolina's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

North Carolina is building its program around five regional **ROOTS Hubs** (Rural Organizations Orchestrating Transformation for Sustainability) — locally-governed networks covering all 100 counties across six Medicaid regions. The state is betting on existing infrastructure over net-new entities, with a repeated theme of "strengthen, expand, sustain." The hubs, not Raleigh, will award most subgrants once their needs assessments and governance are in place. Alongside the hubs, NC is investing in digital infrastructure — a statewide Health Information Exchange, digital health navigators, and a Rural Health Innovation Fund.

Where is the money going — which initiatives is North Carolina funding, and at what share?

Money is flowing through the ROOTS Hubs and several named initiatives:

- **Five ROOTS Hub leads:** Impact Health (western/Region 1), Trillium Health Resources (Regions 2 and 5), Vaya/VIA Health with Appalachian State and Partners Health Management (Region 3), UNC Health with Granville Vance Public Health and Piedmont Health Services (Region 4), and Access East, an ECU Health affiliate (Region 6).
- **Rural Health Innovation Fund** — $20 million a year for up to five years, launching this fall.
- **Mobile Integrated Health / EMS** — $10 million to 39 local EMS agencies.
- **Digital infrastructure** — connectivity to NC HealthConnex (the state HIE), onboarding 400+ rural providers, plus digital health navigators via NC 211.
- **Minority Diabetes Prevention Program** expansion and a School Health Centers expansion.

The full breakdown is in North Carolina's budget narrative and grant-opportunities postings.

What has North Carolina procured so far, and what's open right now?

North Carolina's flagship procurement was the **NC ROOTS Hub Lead RFA**, which named the five regional leads in May. Since then the state has posted a **Minority Diabetes Prevention Program** funding opportunity (extended via addendum), a **Mobile Integrated Health Grant**, and an invited-only **Expanding School Health Centers to Rural Areas** opportunity (questions due July 29, applications due 5 p.m. August 12, 2026). The Rural Health Innovation Fund is expected to open a provider-facing application this fall. Individual ROOTS Hubs are now issuing their own letters of interest and subgrant opportunities on their own timelines. Every dated dispatch covering North Carolina is listed below, newest first.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in North Carolina?

Concrete near-term dates include the **School Health Centers** opportunity (questions due July 29; applications due 5 p.m. August 12, 2026) and the **Rural Health Innovation Fund** fall launch. Because ROOTS Hubs are now setting their own subgrant windows and the state posts on a rolling basis, live dates surface first in the dated dispatches below and on the [NC RHTP Grant Opportunities](https://www.ncdhhs.gov/divisions/office-rural-health/rural-health-transformation-program/rural-health-transformation-program-grant-opportunities) page.

What legislation or state action enables North Carolina's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. North Carolina administers its award through the NCDHHS Office of Rural Health under its CMS-approved project and budget narratives, routing digital-infrastructure funds through the NC Department of Information Technology. A public advisory committee is convening to guide the program.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with North Carolina's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out as competitive RFAs, where firms bid as **prime contractors**. **Subgrants and subawards** flow to rural providers — hospitals, Rural Health Clinics, FQHCs, EMS agencies, school-based health centers, and county and community organizations — increasingly through the five ROOTS Hubs, and it is here that technology vendors and consultants most often engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners** rather than direct grantees. Because the hubs (not Raleigh) will award most subgrants, engaging early with the regional lead in your service area is the practical entry point.

Track opportunities on the [NC RHTP Grant Opportunities](https://www.ncdhhs.gov/divisions/office-rural-health/rural-health-transformation-program/rural-health-transformation-program-grant-opportunities) page and the [RHTP hub](https://www.ncdhhs.gov/divisions/office-rural-health/rural-health-transformation-program), and subscribe to the state's RHTP newsletter.

[Sign up for the NC RHTP newsletter →](https://ncdhhs.us4.list-manage.com/subscribe?u=58ec19aaea4630b1baad0e5e4&id=10ae728a96)
