# North Dakota Rural Health Transformation Program State Profile

**North Dakota**'s roughly **$198.9 million** Rural Health Transformation Program award — the plan, the administering agency, the four program pillars, the stack of live funding opportunities, with a dated log of official activity.

[North Dakota’s official RHTP hub →](https://www.hhs.nd.gov/rural-health-transformation)

North Dakota’s official Rural Health Transformation Program page — [hhs.nd.gov](https://www.hhs.nd.gov/rural-health-transformation), captured 2026-07-29.

## What North Dakota committed to measure

The subjects North Dakota’s funded application pledges to track and report to CMS — the yardsticks its progress will be measured against. Extracted from the state’s own project narrative; the detailed baselines and targets behind each are tracked in the [newsletter](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/).

provider retentionremote monitoring adoptionhealth professional shortage areasobesity and physical activitypreventive cancer screeningvalue-based payment participationchronic disease burdentelehealth encountersavoidable ED visitshealth data interoperability

Source: North Dakota’s CMS-approved RHTP project narrative. These are the state’s self-declared objectives; CMS weighs each state’s progress against its own commitments.

## Questions & answers

What is North Dakota's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

North Dakota's Year-1 award is approximately **$198.9 million**, its share of the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program. On February 25, 2026, CMS approved **$194,807,869.55** of North Dakota's year-one budget, with the remaining **$4,129,100** still under review to align the Notice of Award with the state's application. The program runs five years; Year-1 funds must be **obligated by October 30, 2026** and **fully spent by September 30, 2027**.

Which agency administers North Dakota's RHTP, and who leads it?

[North Dakota Health and Human Services (ND HHS)](https://www.hhs.nd.gov/rural-health-transformation) administers the program. In April 2026, ND HHS announced that **Vincent Roehr** and **Douglas A. McMillan** had joined the agency to help guide the RHTP. Program inquiries and vendor information go to [rhtp@nd.gov](mailto:rhtp@nd.gov).

What is North Dakota's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

North Dakota describes the RHTP as a five-year statewide investment to strengthen rural health care and help make North Dakota the healthiest state in the nation. ND HHS is prioritizing opportunities that build on existing infrastructure, partnerships and systems so it can move quickly within a tight spend-down window. The work is organized under four program pillars.

[North Dakota RHTP hub →](https://www.hhs.nd.gov/rural-health-transformation)

Where is the money going — which initiatives is North Dakota funding, and at what share?

- **Initiative 1 — Make North Dakota Healthy Again** ($17M total): behavioral health, wellness, and community programs (walking, gardens, Zero-Hour PE).
- **Initiative 2 — Strengthen and Stabilize the Rural Health Workforce**: retention, training, childcare, and workforce technology.
- **Initiative 3 — Bring High-Quality Healthcare Closer to Home**: telehealth, remote patient monitoring, mobile and facility-based care.
- **Initiative 4 — Connecting Technology, Data and Providers for a Stronger ND**.

Key project tags include EMS Sustainability, Tech Upgrades and Cardiac Care. The full allocation breakdown is set out in North Dakota's approved budget narrative.

What has North Dakota procured so far, and what's open right now?

North Dakota has been one of the most prolific states, releasing funding opportunities in rapid waves through the Qualtrics application system. Recent live opportunities include **Rural Ambulance Modernization (FO 210-342)** — about $22M, ~110 awards near $200,000, due August 9, 2026; **Technology as an Extender (FO 210-231)** — about $5M, ~20 awards near $250,000, due August 18, 2026; and the two **Clinics without Walls** opportunities, **Telehealth Infrastructure (FO 210-331)** (~$3.6M, due August 14) and **Remote Patient Monitoring (FO 210-334)** (~$1.6M, due August 14). Earlier rounds included the Rightsizing RFA (which names **Eide Bailly** as sole-source TA vendor), the $15M Ensuring Safety Net Service Delivery RFA, a $1.7M Behavioral Health Promotion Community Grant, wellness-equipment and workforce solicitations, and the initial Critical Access Hospital Workforce Retention RFA. The running record is in the dispatches below, newest first.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in North Dakota?

Deadlines are stacked in mid-August 2026: August 8 (Parents Lead), August 9 (Rural Ambulance Modernization), August 11 (Childcare for the Rural Health Workforce), August 14 (both Clinics without Walls opportunities) and August 18 (Technology as an Extender), most with technical-assistance calls in the days before. Across the program, Year-1 funds must be **obligated by October 30, 2026** and **fully spent by September 30, 2027**. Live dates surface first in the dated dispatches below and on the state's funding page.

[ND RHTP funding opportunities →](https://www.hhs.nd.gov/rural-health-transformation/funding)

What legislation or state action enables North Dakota's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. In North Dakota, CMS approved most of the state's year-one budget on February 25, 2026, allowing ND HHS to begin releasing funding opportunities in phases; the agency also hired dedicated RHTP program leads. Detailed allocation figures are set out in North Dakota's CMS-approved budget narrative.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with North Dakota's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out as competitive solicitations where firms bid as **prime contractors** (for example, sole-source technical-assistance roles like Eide Bailly's under the Rightsizing RFA). **Subgrants and subawards** flow to rural providers — hospitals, clinics, FQHCs, EMS and ambulance districts, tribes and tribal health organizations, public health units, schools and nonprofits — and it is here that technology vendors and consultants most often engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners**. North Dakota has confirmed that non-clinical systems (referral coordination, workforce tracking, reporting tools) may apply when aligned with RHTP goals.

Vendors can email product information to [rhtp@nd.gov](mailto:rhtp@nd.gov) to be added to the state's interested-vendor list. Track opportunities on the [ND RHTP hub](https://www.hhs.nd.gov/rural-health-transformation) and the [funding opportunities page](https://www.hhs.nd.gov/rural-health-transformation/funding).

Source: Ohio’s CMS-approved RHTP project narrative. These are the state’s self-declared objectives; CMS weighs each state’s progress against its own commitments.

## Questions & answers

What is Ohio's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Ohio received **approximately $202.0 million** in Year 1 funding under the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program. As with every state, the award is disbursed by CMS annually across five years, with each year's payment tied to performance; Ohio's solicitations are 100% federally funded by CMS/HHS.

Which agency administers Ohio's RHTP, and who leads it?

The [Ohio Department of Health (ODH)](https://odh.ohio.gov/know-our-programs/rural-health-transformation-program) administers the program. Program inquiries go to [RuralHealthTransformation@odh.ohio.gov](mailto:RuralHealthTransformation@odh.ohio.gov); procurement questions for its solicitations route separately to procurement@odh.ohio.gov.

What is Ohio's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

Ohio's plan centers on building durable rural health infrastructure — Rural Ohio Clinically Integrated Networks and Rural Health Innovation Hubs that rural hospitals commit to joining — alongside a statewide workforce pipeline, school-based health centers, chronic-disease prevention, and hospital financial sustainability. Tracked priorities include workforce housing, pharmacy, and behavioral health.

[Ohio RHTP hub →](https://odh.ohio.gov/know-our-programs/rural-health-transformation-program)

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Ohio funding, and at what share?

Named Ohio allocations so far: a **$10M** rural workforce pipeline (DOH59715, awarded in full to Ohio University to lead Health Workforce Ohio); a Clinically Integrated Networks and Rural Health Innovation Hubs RFP (DOH59718) with an estimated budget not to exceed **$61.7M** and at least **$30.3M per year** reserved for rural maternal care; plus a Chronic Disease RFP, a School-Based Health Center solicitation, and one-time Rural Hospital Peer Group funding. Tracked tags are workforce housing, pharmacy, and behavioral health. The full breakdown is in Ohio's budget narrative.

What has Ohio procured so far, and what's open right now?

Ohio runs an active procurement machine through its ODH solicitation-invitations page. Activity to date: DOH59715 (rural workforce pipeline, $10M, awarded to Ohio University July 10); DOH59718 (Rural Ohio Clinically Integrated Networks and Rural Health Innovation Hubs, up to $61.7M, multiple awards, closes September 1, 2026); DOH59808 (Healthier Ohio — Preventing and Addressing Chronic Disease, Track One, opened April 13, closed June 16); a School-Based Health Center competitive solicitation; and a one-time Rural Hospital Peer Group funding opportunity. The dispatch list below carries the running record.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Ohio?

The live deadline to watch is DOH59718 (Clinically Integrated Networks and Innovation Hubs): a bidders' conference was held **July 20** and proposals close **September 1, 2026**. Rural hospitals receiving Peer Group funding must commit to joining or forming a hub or clinically integrated network by **September 30, 2027**. Other early solicitations have closed. Live dates surface first in the dated dispatches below and on the [ODH solicitation-invitations page](https://odh.ohio.gov/know-our-programs/rural-health-transformation-program/solicitation-invitations/solicitation-invitations).

What legislation or state action enables Ohio's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. Ohio administers its award through ODH under its CMS-approved application and budget; no separate enabling state statute is named in the record.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Ohio's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out as ODH solicitations, where firms bid as **prime contractors** — note these are posted on ODH's own solicitation page rather than in OhioBuys, and inquiries route to procurement@odh.ohio.gov. **Subgrants and subawards** flow to rural providers — hospitals, Rural Health Clinics, FQHCs, EMS agencies, schools and community organizations — where technology vendors and consultants most often engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners**. Watch the downstream funnels: Ohio's $10M workforce award to Ohio University is now a subaward pipeline inviting employers, training institutions, and community partners to find funding at healthworkforceohio.org.

Join the RHT project listserv and track the ODH solicitation page for open opportunities.

[Ohio RHTP solicitations →](https://odh.ohio.gov/know-our-programs/rural-health-transformation-program/solicitation-invitations/solicitation-invitations) [Join the RHT listserv →](https://odh.ohio.gov/know-our-programs/rural-health-transformation-program/join-rht-project-listserv)

# Oklahoma Rural Health Transformation Program State Profile

Oklahoma's **$223,476,949** Rural Health Transformation Program award — the six-pillar plan, the administering agency, the budget split, live procurements, with a dated log of official activity.

[Oklahoma’s official RHTP hub →](https://oklahoma.gov/health/rhtp.html)

Oklahoma’s official Rural Health Transformation Program page — [oklahoma.gov](https://oklahoma.gov/health/rhtp.html), captured 2026-07-29.

Oklahoma’s own state-published rural map — Eligible-communities map (Project Narrative, Attachment A) — pop. <55,000, 75 counties. Source: [oklahoma.gov](https://oklahoma.gov/content/dam/ok/en/health/health2/aem-documents/health-promotion/rhtp/Project%20Narrative.pdf). See [how every state defines rural](/work/rht/states/rural-definitions/#map-oklahoma).

## What Oklahoma committed to measure

The subjects Oklahoma’s funded application pledges to track and report to CMS — the yardsticks its progress will be measured against. Extracted from the state’s own project narrative; the detailed baselines and targets behind each are tracked in the [newsletter](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/).

telehealth expansionmaternal health accesscommunity paramedicinebehavioral health integrationchronic disease preventionvalue-based care adoptionPACE and dual-eligible carerural workforce developmenthealth information exchangeEMS regionalization

Source: Oklahoma’s CMS-approved RHTP project narrative. These are the state’s self-declared objectives; CMS weighs each state’s progress against its own commitments.

## Questions & answers

What is Oklahoma's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Oklahoma received **$223,476,949** in Year 1 funding under the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program — the fifth-largest RHTP award in the country. As with every state, the award is disbursed by CMS annually across five budget periods (FY2026–FY2030), with each year's payment tied to performance. Year 1 (Budget Period One) runs December 28, 2025 through October 30, 2026.

Which agency administers Oklahoma's RHTP, and who leads it?

The [Oklahoma State Department of Health (OSDH)](https://oklahoma.gov/health/rhtp.html) administers the Oklahoma Rural Health Transformation Program. Program Directors **Lisa Rother** and **Jackie Kanak** run day-to-day operations, with Commissioner Keith Reed as the public face. General inquiries go to [OklahomaRHTP@health.ok.gov](mailto:OklahomaRHTP@health.ok.gov).

What is Oklahoma's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

Oklahoma's plan is built around **29 CMS-approved programs across six pillars** — innovating care models, growing talent, health data, rural maternal health, EMS stabilization, and a value-based payment shift, with behavioral health, chronic care, and provider stabilization threaded through. The state layers on a facilitator-led regional structure (Rural Regional Reorientation) so that funding maps to region-specific objective plans rather than a single statewide template.

[Oklahoma RHTP hub →](https://oklahoma.gov/health/rhtp.html)

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Oklahoma funding, and at what share?

Oklahoma has published a program-by-program map in its Program Quick Summary Guide. The largest bucket is Regional Collaboration at roughly **$75.1M** in Year 1, anchored by a **$43.1M** Provider Collaborative Network and a still-forming statewide Clinically Integrated Network. Other major lines: Rural Residency Programs (~$22.1M, six new training sites, co-administered by OU and OSU), a Technology Cooperative for primary-care and behavioral-health providers (~$13.8M), Rural Regional Reorientation (~$27.5M in the narrative, $20M in the first NOFO), Chronic Disease Management (~$15.3M), and School-Based Health Services (~$15.1M over five years). The full breakdown lives in the state's Quick Summary Guide and budget narrative.

What has Oklahoma procured so far, and what's open right now?

Oklahoma is front-loading procurement. Closed solicitations include Community-Led Wellness Hubs Microgrants (~$4M, 69 of 75 counties), Rural Regional Reorientation NOFO RHTP2026002 ($20M, closed June 12), Chronic Disease Management RHTP2026003 (~$15M, closed June 8), Behavioral Health Integration — MOUD/MAUD ($2.8M, closed July 10), and EMS & Community Paramedicine Vehicles ($3.7M, deadline extended to July 27). Also live this summer: the Expanding Care: Doulas NOFO (at least $2.5M, due July 27) and school-based grants through OSDE (ROOTS, School-Based Health Services). By mid-June OSDH reported ~70% of the Year-1 award obligated. Every dated dispatch covering Oklahoma is listed below, newest first.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Oklahoma?

Near-term dates: 16 in-person county-cluster kickoffs run **July 27–August 14, 2026**; Year-1 awards are due to be announced late July or early August; CMS holds a site visit **August 4–5**; and OSDH files its first annual report **August 30** — the document that determines Year 2 funding. The next competitive Rural Regional Reorientation NOFO is expected to open around **February 2027**. Subrecipients should note the BP1 spend-down rules: personnel, fringe and travel must be spent by October 30, 2026; all other BP1 funds spent and invoiced by July 31, 2027; and drawn down by OSDH by September 30, 2027. Live dates surface first in the dated dispatches below.

What legislation or state action enables Oklahoma's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. In Oklahoma, Governor Stitt signed **HB3066** on May 11, 2026, which creates the Oklahoma Rural Health Transformation Program inside OSDH and stands up a dedicated Rural Health Transformation Revolving Fund to manage the state's Year-1 award. The bill also ties the Health Care Workforce Training Commission's authority to RHTP grant parameters rather than treating the money as ordinary state appropriations.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Oklahoma's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out as competitive NOFOs (submitted through Smartsheet forms), where firms bid as **prime contractors**. **Subgrants and subawards** flow to rural providers — hospitals, Rural Health Clinics, FQHCs, Tribal health organizations, EMS agencies, counties and fire districts — and it is here that technology vendors and consultants most often engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners**. Note that many of Oklahoma's 29 programs move through inter-agency agreements (OU, OSU, OHCA, OSDE, CareerTech) and subrecipient channels such as the Oklahoma Hospital Association, without competitive solicitation.

Track open opportunities on the [RHTP funding page](https://oklahoma.gov/health/rhtp/rhtp-funding.html) and connect through the state's network of Regional Champions.

[Oklahoma RHTP funding page →](https://oklahoma.gov/health/rhtp/rhtp-funding.html)

# Oregon Rural Health Transformation Program — CMS award, lead agency, committed metrics & activity

# Oregon Rural Health Transformation Program State Profile

Oregon's **$197.3M** Rural Health Transformation Program award — the plan, the administering agency, where the money has actually landed, live procurements, with a dated log of official activity.

[Oregon’s official RHTP hub →](https://www.oregon.gov/oha/hpa/hp/pages/rural-health-transformation.aspx)

Oregon’s official Rural Health Transformation Program page — [oregon.gov](https://www.oregon.gov/oha/hpa/hp/pages/rural-health-transformation.aspx), captured 2026-07-17.

## What Oregon committed to measure

The subjects Oregon’s funded application pledges to track and report to CMS — the yardsticks its progress will be measured against. Extracted from the state’s own project narrative; the detailed baselines and targets behind each are tracked in the [newsletter](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/).

Regional partnershipsValue-based careHome visiting servicesBehavioral health and SUD treatmentTelehealth accessWorkforce recruitmentK-12 health career pathwaysHealth IT adoptionCybersecurity practicesRemote patient monitoring

Source: Oregon’s CMS-approved RHTP project narrative. These are the state’s self-declared objectives; CMS weighs each state’s progress against its own commitments.

## Questions & answers

What is Oregon's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Oregon's Year 1 award is **approximately $197.3 million** as its share of the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program, structured by CMS as a five-year program. CMS lifted restrictions on all Oregon RHTP funds on March 20, 2026 (previously only state staffing dollars were accessible), clearing the roughly $197M intended for subawardees to move; Oregon has since pushed more than $175 million out the door in 2026.

Which agency administers Oregon's RHTP, and who leads it?

The [Oregon Health Authority (OHA)](https://www.oregon.gov/oha/hpa/hp/pages/rural-health-transformation.aspx) administers the program through its Health Policy & Analytics division, with the **Oregon Office of Rural Health (ORH)** convening partners and running vendor engagement. Program questions go to [RHTP@oha.oregon.gov](mailto:RHTP@oha.oregon.gov).

What is Oregon's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

Oregon is moving money fast to hit the Year 1 metrics CMS will use to judge future funding, deploying dollars through a mix of one competitive round (the Catalyst Awards) and several non-competitive channels — direct Transformation Funds to rural providers, a Tribal Initiative set-aside, and OHA-selected Immediate Impact grants. Priorities span maternal and newborn care, workforce equity and pipeline development, behavioral health and substance use, chronic disease, remote monitoring, and cybersecurity.

[Oregon RHTP hub →](https://www.oregon.gov/oha/hpa/hp/pages/rural-health-transformation.aspx)

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Oregon funding, and at what share?

By mid-2026 Oregon had awarded roughly **$175.3 million**, most of it outside competitive procurement:

- **Catalyst Awards** — $80.1M in Budget Period 1 ($156.2M across two periods) to 85 organizations running 103 projects (the one competitive round).
- **Immediate Impact Awards** — $6.5M to 12 projects (April) plus $17M to 33 projects, non-competitive and OHA-selected.
- **Tribal Initiative set-aside** — $21.7M for the Nine Federally Recognized Tribes of Oregon.
- **Transformation Funds** (direct allocations) — $35M to rural hospitals, $10M to certified rural health clinics, $5M to local public health authorities.

What has Oregon procured so far, and what's open right now?

Oregon's one competitive round, the **Catalyst Awards RFGP** (posted on OregonBuys), closed and named winners July 8, 2026: 85 organizations, 103 projects, $156.2M across two budget periods. The strategic tell is that most of Oregon's newest money — the Transformation Funds, the Tribal set-aside, and two waves of Immediate Impact grants, roughly $95 million — went out **without a public RFP** an outside vendor could bid into. For vendors and consultants, the live opening is downstream: ORH is funding regional convenings (invitations available on request) to build the partnerships behind regionally identified applications by the end of Year 2, and is planning a vendor roadshow and an October vendor fair. The dispatch list below carries the running record.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Oregon?

- **End of August 2026** — Oregon's Year 1 federal progress report is due to CMS.
- **July 8, 2026** — Catalyst Award winners announced.
- **October 2026** — ORH's expanded rural health conference includes an RHTP vendor fair.
- **End of Year 2** — target for regionally identified RHTP grant applications.

With Catalyst closed, most remaining pathways are non-competitive; new dates surface first in the dated dispatches below.

What legislation or state action enables Oregon's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. In Oregon, CMS lifted restrictions on all RHTP funds on March 20, 2026 — previously only state staffing dollars were accessible while the roughly $197M for subawardees was frozen — which cleared the Catalyst Awards RFGP and the direct funding pathways to move. Detailed allocation figures are set out in Oregon's project and budget narratives.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Oregon's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out as competitive solicitations — principally the Catalyst Awards RFGP — where firms bid as **prime contractors**. But much of Oregon's money flows **non-competitively**: Transformation Funds go straight to rural hospitals, certified rural health clinics, and local public health authorities; a Tribal set-aside goes to the Nine Federally Recognized Tribes; and Immediate Impact grants are OHA-selected. Vendors and consultants most often engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners** to those subawardees rather than as direct grantees.

Complete OHA's [Vendor Interest Form](https://app.smartsheet.com/b/form/019c8c4dc64574cc8d9c0507aaba0e98) to be listed in the public directory, request an ORH regional convening invitation, and watch the [Catalyst Awards RFGP on OregonBuys](https://oregonbuys.gov/bso/external/bidDetail.sdo?docId=S-44300-00001537&external=true&parentUrl=close) and the [RHTP hub](https://www.oregon.gov/oha/hpa/hp/pages/rural-health-transformation.aspx).

# RHTP outlays by state

Every state runs its Rural Health Transformation Program on a federal cooperative agreement, and two numbers track the money: **obligated** — funds CMS has committed to the state — and **outlaid** — funds actually disbursed to date. This table records both for all 50 states, pulled weekly from USASpending.gov (federal program 93.798). As of 2026-09-18, states had drawn down **$118.1 million** of **$10.00 billion** obligated in Year 1 — about 1.2%. Federal award pages report each state’s outlays one grant at a time; this is a maintained side-by-side comparison of all 50. See [Methodology](/work/rht/states/methodology) for sourcing.

# Pennsylvania Rural Health Transformation Program State Profile

## Questions & answers

What is Pennsylvania's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Pennsylvania's Year-1 allocation is **approximately $193.3 million**, its share of the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program. CMS structures the program over five years, with a Year-1 allocation followed by additional annual funding. Pennsylvania is sequencing its Year-1 money into discrete channels — a broad $25M Rapid Response Stabilization round followed by targeted technology and provider-type payments — with awarded stabilization funds required to be expended by July 31, 2027.

Which agency administers Pennsylvania's RHTP, and who leads it?

The [Pennsylvania Department of Human Services (DHS)](https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dhs/programs-services/healthcare/rural-health/rural-health-transformation-plan) administers the program. Program contact is [klb520@psu.edu](mailto:klb520@psu.edu). DHS is standing up an **RHTP Advisory Council** of subject-matter experts and regional **Rural Care Collaboratives (RCCs)** as public planning bodies for the regions.

What is Pennsylvania's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

Pennsylvania's federally approved application is built around **six initiatives** — Aging and Access, Behavioral Health, Emergency Medical Services (EMS) and Transportation, Maternal Health, Technology and Infrastructure, and Workforce. A defining bet is interoperability: the state is using RHTP dollars to move its fragmented provider base onto a single state-controlled data spine, with five certified Health Information Organizations (HIOs) feeding one statewide hub, the Pennsylvania Patient and Provider Network (P3N) — a prerequisite for care coordination, maternal-health hubs, and remote behavioral health across the plan.

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Pennsylvania funding, and at what share?

Early Year-1 money has flowed through capped payment channels tied to the six initiatives. The **Rapid Response Stabilization** round put $25M toward one-time purchases (supplies, equipment, renovations, structural improvements, and ambulance enhancements) at $10,000–$1,000,000 per entity. Two technology tracks then targeted interoperability: a **$1.8M FQHC & FQHC Look-Alikes** payment (six awards of $300,000) and a **$25M EHR & HIO** payment for hospitals, long-term care, home health, behavioral health, and community/ICF providers — both funding CEHRT adoption and full P3N onboarding. Recurring focuses on record include rural budget expansion, health IT, EMS, and pharmacy. The full breakdown is in DHS's federally approved RHTP application.

What has Pennsylvania procured so far, and what's open right now?

Pennsylvania is running its technology money as **non-competitive, first-come, capped program payments** rather than scored RFPs, so speed and a complete submission matter more than a competitive proposal. Posted opportunities include the **Rapid Response Stabilization** round ($25M, eligibility certifications from midnight May 1, closed June 1), the **FQHC & FQHC Look-Alikes** EHR/HIO payment ($1.8M; applications July 27–August 7), and the broader **EHR & HIO interoperability** payment ($25M; applications July 27–August 14, or until the cap is met). The running record is in the dispatch list below.

[PA RHTP Funding Opportunities →](https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dhs/programs-services/healthcare/rural-health/rhtp-funding-opportunities)

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Pennsylvania?

Because these are first-come payments, windows move fast. The two technology tracks open together with a certification webform on **July 27, 2026**: the FQHC payment closes **August 7** and the EHR/HIO payment closes **August 14** (each “or until the funding cap is met, whichever comes first”). All Rapid Response Stabilization funds must be expended by **July 31, 2027**. Current per-opportunity dates surface first in the dated dispatches below and on the funding page.

What legislation or state action enables Pennsylvania's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. Pennsylvania administers its award through DHS under its federally approved RHTP application, and structures its technology program payments under **Section 203-H of the Fiscal Code**. Governance is being built through the RHTP Advisory Council and regional Rural Care Collaboratives.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Pennsylvania's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** would go out competitively with firms bidding as **prime contractors**, but much of Pennsylvania's early money instead flows as **capped program payments and subawards** to rural providers — hospitals, long-term care nursing facilities, home health agencies, behavioral health providers, community homes and ICFs, FQHCs, and EMS. Providers must be located in or serve HRSA-defined rural census tracts or rural county classes 4–8. For vendors and consultants, a key signal is on the record: DHS confirmed that RHTP dollars **can** pay a third-party consultant to guide an FQHC's CEHRT transition and P3N onboarding — explicitly allowable engagement as an implementation partner. Nominate for the Advisory Council/RCCs and subscribe for opportunity alerts.

[PA RHTP hub →](https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dhs/programs-services/healthcare/rural-health/rural-health-transformation-plan) [Subscribe for updates →](https://maestro.pa.gov/list/subscribe.html?mContainer=870&mOwner=G1j1d&mListId=HL%231142)

## What Rhode Island committed to measure

The subjects Rhode Island’s funded application pledges to track and report to CMS — the yardsticks its progress will be measured against. Source: Rhode Island’s CMS-approved RHTP project narrative. These are the state’s self-declared objectives; CMS weighs each state’s progress against its own commitments.

## Questions & answers

What is Rhode Island's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Rhode Island's Year 1 award is **$156,169,931.19**, its share of the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program, structured by CMS as a five-year program. The state has filed a **$142.7 million budget amendment** for SFY 2026–2027 reflecting its spending plan under the Year 1 award following final CMS approval.

Which agency administers Rhode Island's RHTP, and who leads it?

The [Rhode Island Executive Office of Health and Human Services (EOHHS)](https://eohhs.ri.gov/initiatives/rural-health-transformation-grant) leads the program, with all procurements managed by the Rhode Island Division of Purchases and rural health coordination run through RIDOH's Office of Primary Care and Rural Health. Program questions go to [RIDOH.OPCRH@health.ri.gov](mailto:RIDOH.OPCRH@health.ri.gov).

What is Rhode Island's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

Rhode Island's plan is built on five goals: making rural residents healthier by targeting chronic disease, behavioral health, substance use, and maternal, child and oral health; expanding sustainable access to urgent, primary, behavioral and specialty care; strengthening the rural health workforce; accelerating value-based and affordable care models; and integrating technology and HIT infrastructure into rural practice. It plans 13 initiatives in all.

[Rhode Island RHTP hub →](https://eohhs.ri.gov/initiatives/rural-health-transformation-grant)

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Rhode Island funding, and at what share?

Per Rhode Island's budget amendment, the top-line allocations are:

- **Value-based payment transition** — $32.2M.
- **Rural workforce** — $28.0M.
- **Health IT modernization** — $16.7M.
- **Hospital-at-home program** — $16.2M.

Additional initiatives span rural access data, provider recruitment, and telehealth; the full breakdown across the 13 planned initiatives is in the state's budget amendment.

What has Rhode Island procured so far, and what's open right now?

The first of Rhode Island's 13 planned initiatives to reach the street was the **Administrator for a Health Information Technology (HIT) Rural Infrastructure Fund** RFP — a single vendor to deliver technical assistance to rural providers across the state's 18 rural towns plus the Narragansett Indian Tribe and run the financial machinery to push many small subawards out the door. Responses closed July 10, 2026 and are under evaluation; the contract is slated to run September 1, 2026 through 2031, with the first provider subawards due by January 31, 2027. Next up is **RHT Recovery Community Centers (FY27)**. The dispatch list below carries the running record.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Rhode Island?

- **July 10, 2026** — HIT Rural Infrastructure Fund Administrator RFP closed (under evaluation).
- **September 1, 2026** — targeted start of the HIT Administrator contract (running through 2031).
- **January 31, 2027** — first round of provider subawards due out.

Future solicitations are posted on Ocean State Procures; new dates surface first in the dated dispatches below.

What legislation or state action enables Rhode Island's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. Rhode Island's $142.7 million SFY 2026–2027 budget amendment carries the state spending authority, and Governor Dan McKee endorsed the application in a letter to CMS. The award is tied to a state policy-reform package — rolling back Certificate of Need requirements, expanding scope of practice for pharmacists and dental hygienists, and joining interstate licensure compacts — all conditions to keep the full federal award flowing.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Rhode Island's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out as competitive solicitations through Ocean State Procures, where firms bid as **prime contractors** — as with the HIT Rural Infrastructure Fund Administrator role, which demands a vendor able to float $10 million-plus in provider subawards each year pending state reimbursement. **Subgrants and subawards** flow to rural providers across the state's 18 rural towns (each under 25,000 residents) and the Narragansett Indian Tribe; named early subrecipients include Block Island Health Services, the Care Transformation Collaborative of Rhode Island, the Hospital Association of Rhode Island, the RI League of Cities and Towns, and the Rhode Island Health Center Association. Vendors and consultants engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners**.

Register on [Ocean State Procures](https://webprocure.proactiscloud.com/wp-web-public/en/#/bidboard/search?customerid=46) (search “rural health”), complete the state's [interest survey](https://surveys.health.ri.gov/redcap/surveys/?s=CNJ3ADLPD4MRHLP3), and watch the [RHTP hub](https://eohhs.ri.gov/initiatives/rural-health-transformation-grant) and its Rural Stakeholder Advisory Council.

# How every state defines rural for its Rural Health Transformation Program

Source: https://www.civicoperator.com/work/rht/states/rural-definitions/

# How states define “rural”

Each state decides which communities count as “rural” for its Rural Health Transformation Program. This table records that choice for all 50 states — whether the state uses its **own definition**, a fixed **county list**, or the federal **HRSA/FORHP** default — alongside how rural the state is on a common federal baseline and a link to the state’s own source. **15 states publish an actual rural map** (gallery below); the rest define rural in text or defer to the federal standard. The *% rural* column is a single comparable yardstick — the share of the state’s counties (or census tracts) that are rural under the HRSA/FORHP standard — *not* the state’s own count, which often differs. It is a factual classification, not a ranking. See [Methodology](/work/rht/states/methodology) for how this is derived.

## What South Carolina committed to measure

The subjects South Carolina’s funded application pledges to track and report to CMS — the yardsticks its progress will be measured against. Extracted from the state’s own project narrative; the detailed baselines and targets behind each are tracked in the [newsletter](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/).

Chronic disease managementWorkforce recruitment and retentionProvider and patient experienceEHR interoperabilityTelehealth expansionRemote patient monitoringClosed-loop referralsMobile health unitsCommunity paramedicineHealth-tech startups

Source: South Carolina’s CMS-approved RHTP project narrative. These are the state’s self-declared objectives; CMS weighs each state’s progress against its own commitments.

## Questions & answers

What is South Carolina's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

South Carolina received **approximately $200.03 million** for the first budget period of the five-year Rural Health Transformation Program, its share of the federal $50 billion program, with additional annual awards expected in each funding year. The state is deploying the money largely through a subrecipient grant model organized around five core initiatives.

Which agency administers South Carolina's RHTP, and who leads it?

The **South Carolina Department of Health and Human Services (SCDHHS)** administers the program, branded **South Carolina Rural Health Transformation**, in coordination with the South Carolina Office of Rural Health. SCDHHS has contracted **BDO Government Services LLC** to conduct quarterly audits, monitor subrecipients, and manage CMS reporting, and has partnered with the **South Carolina Research Authority (SCRA)** to run the Tech Catalyst Fund. Program contact: [grants@scdhhs.gov](mailto:grants@scdhhs.gov); hub at [scorh.net](https://scorh.net/rural-health-transformation-fund/).

What is South Carolina's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

South Carolina has organized its transformation strategy into **five core initiatives**: **Connections to Care** (digital infrastructure — EHRs, remote patient monitoring, telehealth, a statewide resource database), **Leveling Up** (scaling chronic-disease and pediatric-care programs statewide), **Wellness Within Reach** (mobile health units, crisis-response teams, pop-up clinics), **Shoring Up to Sustainability** (workforce recruitment and retention, facility upgrades, provider training), and the **Tech Catalyst Fund** (non-dilutive seed funding for rural health-tech startups). Priority tags include digital regionalization, maternal care, hubs, EMS stabilization, CHW expansion, telehealth, and rural residency.

Where is the money going — which initiatives is South Carolina funding, and at what share?

- **Connections to Care (SCDHHS-26-001) — $75M Year 1**: Health IT modernization ($100K–$2M, or $5M–$10M for full EHR replacement) and remote patient monitoring / assistive technology ($250K–$5M). No more than 5% of the state award may go toward replacing an existing HITECH-certified EHR.
- **Leveling Up (SCDHHS-26-002) — $27M Year 1**: chronic-disease program expansion ($100K–$5M per award).
- **Wellness Within Reach (SCDHHS-26-003) — $27.7M Year 1**.
- **Shoring Up to Sustainability — workforce, facilities and training**.
- **Tech Catalyst Fund — $25M over five years** (about $5M and 4–6 subrecipients in Year 1, capped at $3M per company).

The full breakdown is in South Carolina's updated budget narrative.

What has South Carolina procured so far, and what's open right now?

For the first budget period SCDHHS released **four concurrent Requests for Applications** corresponding to four of its five initiatives — Connections to Care (SCDHHS-26-001), Leveling Up (SCDHHS-26-002), Wellness Within Reach (SCDHHS-26-003), and Shoring Up to Sustainability — posted in early April 2026. The fifth initiative, the **Tech Catalyst Fund**, runs on a separate track via SCRA; its first application window closed June 26, with about $5M expected to reach 4–6 startup subrecipients. SCDHHS is also separately procuring a consultant for a statewide rural needs assessment and dual-eligible managed-care transition. The dispatch list below carries the running record.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in South Carolina?

The four initiative RFPs opened in early April 2026 and the Tech Catalyst Fund's first window closed **June 26, 2026**. With that first cycle now largely past, new application windows and the next Tech Catalyst Fund stage surface first in the dated dispatches below and on the [SCDHHS grants page](https://scdhhs.gov/resources/grants). Subscribe to the [Office of Rural Health updates](https://public.govdelivery.com/accounts/ORHA/subscriber/new?topic_id=ORHA_209) to catch new postings.

What legislation or state action enables South Carolina's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. South Carolina administers its award through SCDHHS under its CMS-approved plan and updated budget narrative, using a competitive subrecipient grant model with BDO Government Services LLC monitoring overall program compliance.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with South Carolina's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out as competitive RFAs/RFPs where firms bid as **prime contractors** (and, separately, a state consultant for the rural needs assessment). **Subawards** flow to rural providers — rural hospitals, clinics, FQHCs, behavioral health and EMS organizations — where technology vendors and consultants most often engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners**. The **Tech Catalyst Fund** is the exception: it pays health-tech startups directly as non-dilutive capital (capped at $3M per company), administered through SCRA.

Track opportunities on the [SCDHHS grants portal](https://scdhhs.gov/resources/grants) and the [RHT hub](https://scorh.net/rural-health-transformation-fund/), subscribe to [Office of Rural Health updates](https://public.govdelivery.com/accounts/ORHA/subscriber/new?topic_id=ORHA_209), and direct questions to [grants@scdhhs.gov](mailto:grants@scdhhs.gov).

# South Dakota Rural Health Transformation Program — CMS award, lead agency, committed metrics & activity

Source: https://www.civicoperator.com/work/rht/states/south-dakota/

# South Dakota Rural Health Transformation Program State Profile

**South Dakota**'s **$189,477,607.26** Year-1 Rural Health Transformation Program award — the administering office, the initiatives, the run of live RFPs, with a dated log of official activity.

[South Dakota’s official RHTP hub →](https://doh.sd.gov/healthcare-professionals/rural-health/rural-health-transformation-project/)

South Dakota’s official Rural Health Transformation Program page — [doh.sd.gov](https://doh.sd.gov/healthcare-professionals/rural-health/rural-health-transformation-project/), captured 2026-07-29.

## At a glance

$189,477,607 · CMS obligated

## What South Dakota committed to measure

The subjects South Dakota’s funded application pledges to track and report to CMS — the yardsticks its progress will be measured against. Extracted from the state’s own project narrative; the detailed baselines and targets behind each are tracked in the [newsletter](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/).

EHR adoptionPreventive cancer screeningsRural workforce recruitmentCommunity health worker expansionBehavioral health CCBHC accessEMS response timesChronic disease managementMaternal and infant healthValue-based payment reformHealth Data Atlas usage

Source: [South Dakota’s RHTP project narrative](https://doh.sd.gov/media/lyfbrd2k/sd_rhtproject-narrative-final.pdf). These are the state’s self-declared objectives; CMS weighs each state’s progress against its own commitments.

## Questions & answers

What is South Dakota's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

South Dakota is working against a **$189,477,607.26** Year-1 CMS award (100% federally funded) — the opening tranche of an approximately **$1 billion**, five-year plan that runs through September 2031. Like all RHTP awards, it is structured by CMS as an annual award across a five-year performance period, and it is South Dakota's share of the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program.

Which agency administers South Dakota's RHTP, and who leads it?

The program is administered by the **South Dakota Department of Health (SD DOH)**, chiefly through its **Office of Rural Health and Emergency Services (ORHES)**, under Secretary of Health **Melissa Magstadt**. The Department of Social Services runs Medicaid-related components. Program hub and contact: [SD DOH Rural Health Transformation](https://doh.sd.gov/healthcare-professionals/rural-health/rural-health-transformation-project/), [DOH.Info@state.sd.us](mailto:DOH.Info@state.sd.us).

What is South Dakota's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

South Dakota's plan aims to build a sustainable rural healthcare system across workforce, digital modernization, maternal health, chronic disease, and Medicaid payment reform. A distinctive pattern has emerged: rather than build capacity in-house, SD DOH is contracting out the **management layer itself** — buying operators and integrators first, program delivery second. The plan aligns with the state's Strategic Analysis of South Dakota's Rural Healthcare Programs (2024).

Where is the money going — which initiatives is South Dakota funding, and at what share?

The largest visible commitment is the **Digital Health Modernization and Technology Grant Program** — a nearly **$480 million** multi-year program, with **$89,343,733** available in Cycle 1 (FFY26), structured around seven funding tiers (EHR adoption/upgrade/replacement, technology and equipment, digital security, workforce technology training, and Regional Innovation Centers). Other funded lines include a Sustainable Rural Healthcare Workforce initiative, Medicaid Primary Accountable Care Transformation (PACT), Chronic Disease Management, EMS Workforce and System Modernization, maternal health (doula workforce, access assessment), and Rural Health Forward, a statewide training hub. The full breakdown is in South Dakota's budget narrative.

What has South Dakota procured so far, and what's open right now?

South Dakota has moved fast on procurement. It has run multiple RFP rounds through its ESM Solutions posting board, including a first round of seven leadership/PM roles (Feb), a second round of three (doula workforce, maternal health assessment, Rural Health Forward), the **$89.3M Digital Health Modernization RFA (#26-09RHT-020)**, a **Recruitment & Retention RFP (#26-09RHT-024)** putting up to $6M on the table, and an invitation-only Grant & Project Management RFP (#27-09RHT-024). It has already awarded three program-management contracts: North Star Solutions ($1,462,802, Digital Health Modernization), Black Hills Special Services Cooperative (Chronic Disease PM), and Business Concepts & Applications ($500,000, DSS/Medicaid). The dispatch list below carries the running record.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in South Dakota?

Recent posted dates include the Digital Health Modernization RFA (#26-09RHT-020) — applications due June 30, 2026, awards anticipated by August 13, 2026 — and the invitation-only Grant & Project Management RFP (#27-09RHT-024) with proposals due August 4 and award expected August 14, 2026. Windows have been notably tight (some as short as 10 days), so live dates surface first in the dated dispatches below and on the state's [RHT posting board](https://postingboard.esmsolutions.com/3444a404-3818-494f-84c5-2a850acd7779/events).

What legislation or state action enables South Dakota's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. In South Dakota, Governor **Larry Rhoden** made RHT appropriations (**HB 1044**) the first bill he signed this session — a signal of how fast the state intends to move money — and the program operates under SD DOH's CMS-approved project and budget narratives.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with South Dakota's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out as competitive (and sometimes invitation-only) RFPs and RFAs on the state posting board, where firms bid as **prime contractors** — South Dakota's early buys have leaned heavily toward program-management and integrator roles. **Subgrants and subawards** flow to rural providers — FQHCs, Critical Access Hospitals, tribal clinics, community mental health centers, and other South Dakota healthcare providers — where technology vendors and consultants most often engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners**. Note that invitation-only solicitations (e.g., via the ESM Solutions / Central Bid Exchange board) restrict who can formally respond, so registering early matters. Digital Health Modernization applicants in Sioux Falls (Minnehaha) and Rapid City (Pennington) must explicitly show benefit to rural areas.

Track opportunities on the [RHT posting board](https://postingboard.esmsolutions.com/3444a404-3818-494f-84c5-2a850acd7779/events) and the [program hub](https://doh.sd.gov/healthcare-professionals/rural-health/rural-health-transformation-project/), and subscribe to the state's rural health listserv.

[Join the SD Rural Health listserv →](https://listserv.sd.gov/scripts/wa.exe?SUBED1=SDRURALHEALTH&A=1)

# Tennessee Rural Health Transformation Program — CMS award, lead agency, committed metrics & activity

Source: https://www.civicoperator.com/work/rht/states/tennessee/

# Tennessee Rural Health Transformation Program State Profile

Tennessee's **$206.9M** Rural Health Transformation Program award — the plan, the administering agency, the funding categories, the wave of live procurements, with a dated log of official activity.

[Tennessee’s official RHTP hub →](https://www.tn.gov/health/rural)

Tennessee’s official Rural Health Transformation Program page — [tn.gov](https://www.tn.gov/health/rural), captured 2026-07-09.

## At a glance

FY26 award (Year 1)

$206,888,882 · CMS obligated

Program name

Tennessee Rural Health Transformation

Official RHTP hub

[Tennessee program page](https://www.tn.gov/health/rural)

Program contact

[RuralHealth@TN.gov](mailto:RuralHealth@TN.gov)

[Funding opportunities](https://c2cre237.caspio.com/dp/4cdb40003c407a2328014c28a496)

Tracker dispatches

18 dated briefs

## What Tennessee committed to measure

The subjects Tennessee’s funded application pledges to track and report to CMS — the yardsticks its progress will be measured against. Extracted from the state’s own project narrative; the detailed baselines and targets behind each are tracked in the [newsletter](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/).

Rural service line expansionEmergency care and EMSBehavioral health integrationDental care accessMaternal and child healthValue-based paymentChronic disease preventionNon-emergency medical transportHealth information exchangeHealth workforce pipeline

Source: Tennessee’s CMS-approved RHTP project narrative. These are the state’s self-declared objectives; CMS weighs each state’s progress against its own commitments.

## Questions & answers

What is Tennessee's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Tennessee's Budget Period 1 award is **approximately $206.9 million** — above the $200 million baseline states were asked to apply for — as its share of the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program, structured by CMS as a five-year program with Year 1 funds obligated by October 31, 2026 and spent by September 30, 2027.

Which agency administers Tennessee's RHTP, and who leads it?

The [Tennessee Department of Health (TDH)](https://www.tn.gov/health/rural) administers the program, running solicitations out of its Division of Strategic Initiatives through the Department of General Services. Deputy Commissioner **JW Randolph** serves as the state's RHTP principal investigator. General program questions go to [RuralHealth@TN.gov](mailto:RuralHealth@TN.gov); the Competitive Procurement Director ([Competitive.Health@tn.gov](mailto:Competitive.Health@tn.gov)) is the sole point of contact for active RFAs.

What is Tennessee's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

Tennessee is building on its existing **Healthcare Resiliency Program (HRP)** model — which has deployed hundreds of millions and supported 110+ projects since 2022 — to expand preventive, behavioral-health, and substance-use care, address maternity deserts and memory care, modernize rural health technology, and extend the safety net into counties with no provider. Its flagship framing is “Make Rural Tennessee Healthy Again” (MaRTHA).

[Tennessee RHTP hub →](https://www.tn.gov/health/rural)

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Tennessee funding, and at what share?

- **Health Technology & Innovation (Long-Range)** — $59,380,009, the single biggest pool.
- **Health Technology & Innovation (Short-Range)** — $33 million.
- **Make Rural Tennessee Healthy Again (MaRTHA)** — $50 million.
- **Memory Care Assessment Network (MCAN)** — a dementia hub-and-spoke network.
- **Maternal & Child Health** — up to 100 awards ($1.25M small / $1.25M–$12.5M large).
- Plus Safety Net Expansion (>$60M), Rural FIMR ($4.5M), HART built-environment grants, and non-emergency medical transportation.

An EMR-replacement cap of 5% and a $225,700 salary cap apply across categories; the full breakdown is in Tennessee's budget narrative.

What has Tennessee procured so far, and what's open right now?

Tennessee is flooding the zone with solicitations. Between July 6 and July 20, 2026 TDH released six RFPs through the Department of General Services — a Statewide eConsult Platform, a CHANT call center, rural non-emergency transportation, a pregnancy/post-partum mobile app, and a Rural Health Innovation Catalyst. Named RFAs include Health Technology & Innovation Short-Range (#34320-20327, due July 27) and Long-Range (#34320-21427, $59.38M, due Aug 3), MaRTHA (#34320-20127, $50M, due Aug 3), and the Memory Care Assessment Network (#34320-19326, due July 20). Notably, for-profit health-tech companies are explicitly eligible as lead applicant. The dispatch list below carries the running record.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Tennessee?

- **July 20, 2026** — Memory Care Assessment Network applications due.
- **July 27, 2026, 2:00 p.m. CT** — Health Tech & Innovation (Short-Range) due; evaluation notice Aug 24, contract start Sept 1.
- **August 3, 2026, 2:00 p.m. CT** — Health Tech & Innovation (Long-Range) and MaRTHA due.
- **August 31, 2026** — MaRTHA evaluation notices; multiple RFPs carry October Notices of Intent to Award.

Live dates surface first in the dated dispatches below.

What legislation or state action enables Tennessee's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. In Tennessee, the state legislature is separately considering more than $100 million in complementary capital funding, and TennCare is investing $125 million of Shared Savings in targeted rural hospital and primary-care capital projects. Detailed allocation figures are set out in Tennessee's project and budget narratives.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Tennessee's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out as competitive RFAs and RFPs, where firms bid as **prime contractors** — and Tennessee has gone unusually far here, confirming repeatedly that **for-profit health-tech companies can be the lead applicant**, not just a subcontractor behind a hospital, with the only hard gate being Tennessee Secretary of State registration before contract execution. Assessments, workflow optimization, and technology roadmaps are fundable as the primary deliverable, opening the door to consulting and advisory firms. **Subgrants and subawards** also flow to rural providers — hospitals, FQHCs, and community-based organizations — where vendors engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners**. Note that awards are cost-reimbursement only, so applicants must be able to float costs.

Track opportunities on the [Tennessee RHTP hub](https://www.tn.gov/health/rural) and the [RHTP funding portal](https://c2cre237.caspio.com/dp/4cdb40003c407a2328014c28a496), and watch the Department of General Services RFP page for live solicitations.

# Test Run Pilot Rural Health Transformation Program — CMS award, lead agency, committed metrics & activity

Source: https://www.civicoperator.com/work/rht/states/test-run-pilot/

# Test Run Pilot Rural Health Transformation Program State Profile

Everything we track on Test Run Pilot's **~$55M** Rural Health Transformation Program award — the plan, the administering agency, live procurements, and every dispatch we've published, in a question-and-answer format.

## At a glance

FY26 award (Year 1)

~$55M

Program contact

[danielx@gmail.com](mailto:danielx@gmail.com)

Federal award data

[Search USAspending](https://www.usaspending.gov/search/?query=Rural%20Health%20Transformation)

Tracker dispatches

0 dated briefs

## Questions & answers

What is Test Run Pilot's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Test Run Pilot received approximately **$55M** in Year 1 Rural Health Transformation Program funding from CMS — its share of the federal $50 billion program. The exact award and five-year structure are set out in the state's CMS-approved project and budget narratives.

Which agency administers Test Run Pilot's RHTP, and who leads it?

Test Run Pilot's Rural Health Transformation Program is administered by the state's designated lead agency. Program contact: [danielx@gmail.com](mailto:danielx@gmail.com).

What is Test Run Pilot's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

We’re finalizing Test Run Pilot’s plan summary from its CMS-approved project narrative narrative pending. In the meantime, read the state’s official Rural Health Transformation plan and priorities on its program hub.

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Test Run Pilot funding, and at what share?

Test Run Pilot’s initiative and budget breakdown is being summarized from its approved budget narrative breakdown pending.

What has Test Run Pilot procured so far, and what's open right now?

Live procurements and awards for Test Run Pilot appear in the dispatch list below as we publish them. The state's official funding-opportunities page is the authoritative source for open solicitations.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Test Run Pilot?

Upcoming deadlines, technical-assistance calls and webinars surface first in the dated dispatches below, and on the state's funding-opportunities page.

What legislation or state action enables Test Run Pilot's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. Test Run Pilot administers its award through its state-designated agency under CMS-approved project and budget narratives.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Test Run Pilot's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out as competitive RFPs where firms bid as **prime contractors**; **subgrants and subawards** flow to rural providers — hospitals, Rural Health Clinics, FQHCs, Tribal health organizations, EMS agencies, counties and fire districts — where technology vendors and consultants most often engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners** rather than direct grantees.

# Texas Rural Health Transformation Program — CMS award, lead agency, committed metrics & activity

Source: https://www.civicoperator.com/work/rht/states/texas/

# Texas Rural Health Transformation Program State Profile

Texas's **$281.3M** first-year Rural Health Transformation Program award — the "Rural Texas Strong" plan, the HHSC team running it, the initiative rounds, the live RFAs, with a dated log of official activity.

[Texas’s official RHTP hub →](https://pfd.hhs.texas.gov/rural-health-transformation-program)

Texas’s official Rural Health Transformation Program page — [pfd.hhs.texas.gov](https://pfd.hhs.texas.gov/rural-health-transformation-program), captured 2026-06-24.

## At a glance

FY26 award (Year 1)

$281,319,361 · CMS obligated

Program name

Rural Texas Strong: Supporting Health and Wellness

Official RHTP hub

[Texas program page](https://pfd.hhs.texas.gov/rural-health-transformation-program)

Tracker dispatches

4 dated briefs

## Questions & answers

What is Texas's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Texas received **approximately $281.3 million** in its first-year award from the CMS Rural Health Transformation Program — its share of the federal $50 billion program — with an estimated $1.4 billion expected to flow to Texas over the five-year performance period. Additional annual awards are expected in each funding year.

Which agency administers Texas's RHTP, and who leads it?

The [Texas Health and Human Services Commission (HHSC)](https://pfd.hhs.texas.gov/rural-health-transformation-program) administers the program, branded **Rural Texas Strong: Supporting Health and Wellness**, with Governor Greg Abbott's office announcing major funding rounds. Applications run through the HHSC Grants Management System (GMS), which requires active IAMOnline accounts. Program contact: [RuralTexasStrong@hhs.texas.gov](mailto:RuralTexasStrong@hhs.texas.gov).

What is Texas's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

The federally approved Rural Texas Strong plan is organized around numbered initiatives with a strong "Make Rural Texans Healthy Again" thrust — community-based prevention, wellness and nutrition programs to combat chronic disease, alongside a rural workforce pipeline ("The Next Generation of the Small Town Doctor and Team"). Named priority tags include putting **patients in the driver's seat**, **remote patient monitoring**, and **health data exchange**.

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Texas funding, and at what share?

Money moves through initiative rounds rather than a single published percentage split. Early deployment centered on chronic disease: a **$56 million competitive grant** for public and private rural hospitals (community prevention, wellness and nutrition) layered on top of **$60 million in direct awards** to rural hospital districts — together a roughly **$116 million** "Make Rural Texans Healthy Again" push. Initiative 4 (rural workforce pipeline) is running in rounds. The full breakdown sits in Texas's budget narrative; named project tags are patients-in-the-driver's-seat, RPM, and health data exchange.

What has Texas procured so far, and what's open right now?

Currently open: **Rural Texas Strong Initiative 4, Round 2 — "The Next Generation of the Small Town Doctor and Team" (RFA No. HHS0017618)**, which opened the competitive application process July 15, 2026 and funds mid-level practitioners and allied health professionals around rural physicians. Entities receiving funds under the companion RFA No. HHS0017212 are not eligible under this one, and prior applications will not carry over — a new application is required. Earlier, HHSC launched the **$56M chronic-disease competitive grant** for rural hospitals (applications due June 4). The dispatch list below carries the running record.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Texas?

The key open deadline: **Initiative 4, Round 2 (RFA No. HHS0017618) applications are due August 26, 2026 at 10:30 a.m. Central Time**, submitted through the HHSC Grants Management System — late submissions are not considered, so organizations need active IAMOnline accounts and GMS access in place beforehand. Texas remains in a pre-procurement blackout (no vendor meetings until postings go live), so new postings themselves are the signal to watch on the [ESBD portal](https://www.txsmartbuy.gov/esbd?page=1&keyword=rural%20health%20transformation); live dates surface in the dispatches below.

What legislation or state action enables Texas's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. Texas administers its award through HHSC under its CMS-approved Rural Texas Strong plan and budget, with Governor Greg Abbott's office announcing major funding rounds.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Texas's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out as competitive RFAs through the HHSC Grants Management System, where firms bid as **prime applicants** — though eligibility for the current workforce RFA is limited to **rural healthcare providers and rural hospitals**. **Subawards and direct hospital awards** flow to rural providers — rural hospital districts, Critical Access and rural hospitals, clinics and EMS — where technology vendors and consultants most often engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners**. Note the pre-procurement blackout: no vendor meetings occur until a posting goes live.

Register for an IAMOnline account and GMS access ahead of postings, watch the [ESBD funding portal](https://www.txsmartbuy.gov/esbd?page=1&keyword=rural%20health%20transformation) and the [Rural Texas Strong hub](https://pfd.hhs.texas.gov/rural-health-transformation-program), subscribe to [HHSC updates](https://public.govdelivery.com/accounts/TXHHSC/subscriber/new?topic_id=TXHHSC_1016), and direct questions to [RuralTexasStrong@hhs.texas.gov](mailto:RuralTexasStrong@hhs.texas.gov).

# Utah Rural Health Transformation Program — CMS award, lead agency, committed metrics & activity

Source: https://www.civicoperator.com/work/rht/states/utah/

# Utah Rural Health Transformation Program State Profile

Utah's **$195,743,566.29** first-year Rural Health Transformation Program award — the seven-initiative plan, the DHHS team running it, the four-bucket budget split, the fast-moving RFGA calendar, with a dated log of official activity.

[Utah’s official RHTP hub →](https://dhhs.utah.gov/ruralhealth/)

Utah’s official Rural Health Transformation Program page — [dhhs.utah.gov](https://dhhs.utah.gov/ruralhealth/), captured 2026-07-21.

## At a glance

FY26 award (Year 1)

$195,743,566 · CMS obligated

Official RHTP hub

[Utah program page](https://dhhs.utah.gov/ruralhealth/)

Program contact

[ruralht@utah.gov](mailto:ruralht@utah.gov)

Funding / RFP portal

[Funding opportunities](https://dhhs.utah.gov/ruralhealth/funding-opportunities/)

Governor's newsroom

[Press releases](https://governor.utah.gov/category/press-release/)

Key project focus

Tech-Enabled Solutions, Chronic Care, Retention

[Utah Department of Health and Human Services](/work/rht/states/agencies/)

Rural geography

[Uses its own rural definition](/work/rht/states/rural-definitions/)

[View federal award](https://www.usaspending.gov/award/ASST_NON_RHTCMS332051_075/)

Tracker dispatches

22 dated briefs

## What Utah committed to measure

The subjects Utah’s funded application pledges to track and report to CMS — the yardsticks its progress will be measured against. Extracted from the state’s own project narrative; the detailed baselines and targets behind each are tracked in the [newsletter](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/).

Rural obesity and chronic diseaseBehavioral health and suicideMaternal and infant careAccess and appointment wait timesHealthcare workforce stabilityPreventable hospitalizations and readmissionsTelehealth utilizationData interoperability and cybersecurityFinancial sustainability of rural facilitiesEMS capacity

Source: [Utah’s RHTP project narrative](https://dhhs.utah.gov/wp-content/uploads/Utah-RHTP-Revised-Project-Narrative_v.1.28.26.pdf). These are the state’s self-declared objectives; CMS weighs each state’s progress against its own commitments.

## Questions & answers

What is Utah's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Utah received **$195,743,566.29** in first-year (Budget Period 1) funding, 100% funded by CMS/HHS, as its share of the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program. The program runs five years (FY2026–FY2030), with additional annual awards expected in each funding year. Utah has mapped Year 1 into four buckets: **Competitive & Community Grants $115.5M (59.1%)**, **State & Public Entity Agreements $75.4M (38.5%)**, Data Evaluation & Mapping $1.7M (0.9%), and State Administration & Reserves $3.0M (1.5%).

Which agency administers Utah's RHTP, and who leads it?

The [Utah Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS)](https://dhhs.utah.gov/ruralhealth/) administers the award, with the program run out of the DHHS Commissioner's Office. **Krisann Humphreys** took over as RHTP Director the week of June 29, 2026, succeeding Brittney Okada, who stood the program up. General questions go to [ruralht@utah.gov](mailto:ruralht@utah.gov); the Office of Primary Care and Rural Health ([opcrh@utah.gov](mailto:opcrh@utah.gov)) handles the preceptor-stipend track.

What is Utah's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

Utah organizes its work under **seven named initiatives**: RISE (workforce recruitment and retention), PATH (behavioral health–primary care integration), SHIFT (capital infrastructure), FAST (value-based care), LIFT (telehealth), SUPPORT (EHR modernization, cybersecurity and AI), and LINCS (interoperability). The through-lines are tech-enabled solutions, chronic care, and clinician retention — increasingly delivered through consortium "administrative partners" that receive funds and re-release them as downstream subawards to rural providers.

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Utah funding, and at what share?

- **Competitive & Community Grants — $115.5M (59.1%)**, across 11 opportunities and 20 key actions, administered by DHHS.
- **State & Public Entity Agreements — $75.4M (38.5%)**, across 7 agreements with sister agencies (UDAF, USBE, UDOT, USHE, DPS, UETN, DEQ).
- **Data Evaluation & Mapping Contracts — $1.7M (0.9%)**.
- **State Administration & Reserves — $3.0M (1.5%)**.

The single largest solicitation is SPRINT (up to $59.2M in Year 1). The full activity-level breakdown is in Utah's approved Project and Budget Narratives.

What has Utah procured so far, and what's open right now?

Utah is running one of the most granular procurement programs of any state. Recent and active solicitations include the **SPRINT Consortium RFGA** (URHTP-2858-2026, up to $59.2M Year 1 / $291.8M over five years), **LINCS 7.3–7.4** (URHTP-2694-2026, $11M Year 1), **LIFT 5.1 Scalable Telehealth** (run by UETN under a $26.5M subaward, $23.7M Year 1), **RISE 2.5 Recruit and Retain** ($20M Year 1), **SHIFT 3.2 Rural Health Provider Networks** (up to $18.5M over five years), a cross-listed **Food Security Grant** (up to $9.27M), and **FAST 4.1 Value-Based Care** ($15M). Earlier PATH 1.5 and RISE 2.2 preceptor rounds have closed. The dispatch list below carries the running record.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Utah?

Near-term deadlines to hold: the **SPRINT** mandatory letter of intent is due **July 27** with applications due **August 7**; **LINCS 7.3–7.4** applications close **August 7** (award by August 26); **SHIFT 3.2** is due **August 14**; and the **Food Security Grant** runs July 21–**August 31**. Confirm each on Utah's [funding-opportunities page](https://dhhs.utah.gov/ruralhealth/funding-opportunities/); live dates surface first in the dated dispatches below.

What legislation or state action enables Utah's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. Utah's participation is administered through DHHS under its CMS-approved Year 1 application and budget, with 100% of costs funded by CMS/HHS. Detailed allocation figures are set out in Utah's approved Project and Budget Narratives.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Utah's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out as competitive RFGAs, where firms bid as **prime contractors** — and many Utah solicitations are written narrowly, favoring Utah-based organizations, 501(c)(3)s, ACOs, CINs, or consortiums with deep rural health-systems expertise and existing rural relationships. **Subgrants and subawards** flow to rural providers — rural hospitals, FQHCs, Rural Health Clinics, Tribal (I/T/U) facilities, behavioral health authorities, EMS and long-term care — where technology vendors and consultants most often engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners**. Awardees must register as State of Utah vendors, typically within 14 days of selection.

Track opportunities on the [Utah RHTP hub](https://dhhs.utah.gov/ruralhealth/) and the [funding-opportunities portal](https://dhhs.utah.gov/ruralhealth/funding-opportunities/), and join the RHTP contact list for new-opportunity alerts by emailing [ruralht@utah.gov](mailto:ruralht@utah.gov).

# Vermont Rural Health Transformation Program — CMS award, lead agency, committed metrics & activity

Source: https://www.civicoperator.com/work/rht/states/vermont/

# Vermont Rural Health Transformation Program State Profile

Vermont's **$195,053,740** Year-1 Rural Health Transformation Program award — the five-initiative plan, the administering agency, live RFPs and NOFOs, with a dated log of official activity for vendors, providers, and consultants tracking the program.

[Vermont’s official RHTP hub →](https://healthcarereform.vermont.gov/hr1rural-health-transformation-fund)

Vermont’s official Rural Health Transformation Program page — [healthcarereform.vermont.gov](https://healthcarereform.vermont.gov/hr1rural-health-transformation-fund), captured 2026-07-18.

## At a glance
