## What Vermont committed to measure

The subjects Vermont’s funded application pledges to track and report to CMS — the yardsticks its progress will be measured against. Extracted from the state’s own project narrative; the detailed baselines and targets behind each are tracked in the [newsletter](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/).

ED follow-up careHospital readmissionsHospital transformation plansCritical access hospital marginsCommunity paramedicineTelehealth and remote monitoringChronic disease controlDepression screeningPrimary care engagementHealth workforce FTEsHealth care cost growth

Source: Vermont’s CMS-approved RHTP project narrative. These are the state’s self-declared objectives; CMS weighs each state’s progress against its own commitments.

## Questions & answers

What is Vermont's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Vermont's Year-1 award is **$195,053,740.44**, 100% CMS-funded under Notice of Award **#RHTCMS332047-01-00**. It is Vermont's share of the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program, which CMS structures as a five-year initiative (roughly one-fifth of the national $50B is distributed to states in Year 1, with additional annual allocations across the five-year period).

Which agency administers Vermont's RHTP, and who leads it?

The [Vermont Agency of Human Services (AHS)](https://healthcarereform.vermont.gov/hr1rural-health-transformation-fund) administers the award, with the Department of Vermont Health Access (DVHA) running much of the procurement. The Project Director named on the CMS Notice of Award is **Jill Olson**, Executive Director for Medicaid at DVHA. General program contact is the State Office of Rural Health at [AHS.VDH\_SORH@vermont.gov](mailto:AHS.VDH_SORH@vermont.gov); individual solicitations name their own contacts (for example, Kristin Seiffert at [ahs.contracts@vermont.gov](mailto:ahs.contracts@vermont.gov)).

What is Vermont's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

Vermont organizes its entire award into five named Strategic Initiatives — **Regionalization, Shared Services, Primary Care, Workforce Development, and Price Transparency** — broken into 35 discrete activities. The thrust is to build stronger rural health networks, improve technology and shared operations, strengthen the rural workforce, and ensure Vermonters get the right care at the right time at an affordable cost. Initiatives 3 (Primary Care) and 4 (Workforce Development) are the largest by activity count and, as of mid-2026, carried the clearest forward procurement pipeline.

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Vermont funding, and at what share?

The plan funds thirty grant subrecipient activities plus consultant and contractor procurements across the five initiatives. Key project focuses on record include **AHEAD integration, rural health information technology, and workforce housing**, alongside mobile dental and MH/SUD units, community paramedicine, a shared EHR/EMR platform, a shared HRIS, a statewide closed-loop referral system, e-Consult, remote patient monitoring, telehealth, a Family Medicine residency, and pharmacist test-to-treat scope expansion. The full activity-by-activity budget breakdown lives in Vermont's approved Project Narrative and Budget Narrative.

What has Vermont procured so far, and what's open right now?

Vermont has moved fast, releasing tight single-purpose grants and RFPs in rapid succession through the Vermont Business Registry. Named solicitations include the first RFP for SUD Recovery Residences (March 9, up to $500,000), Mobile Health Care Clinics, Pharmacy Test-to-Treat, Mobile Integrated Health, a Stakeholder Engagement / Statewide Health Care Delivery Strategic Plan RFP, an AI Transcription/Scribe NOFO, Remote Patient Monitoring, Telehealth, and E-Consult NOFOs, five DVHA Blueprint capacity-building RFPs, Shared EHR and Shared HRIS NOFOs, an independent program-evaluator RFP (Year-1 ceiling **$1,000,000**), a Green Mountain Care Board Health Data Infrastructure Transformation RFP, a statewide Closed-Loop Referral System RFP, paired Regional Care Redesign and Facility Upgrades NOFOs (Facility Upgrades $50,000–$2,000,000), a Mental Health Urgent Care RFP for Rutland County, and a Centralized Interfacility Transfer NOFO. The running record of every posting is in the dispatch list below.

[Vermont RHT RFPs & NOFOs →](https://healthcarereform.vermont.gov/rht-program-rfps-nofos)

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Vermont?

Vermont uses rolling application windows: applications received by 7/17 (10 p.m.) were considered for a September 1 start, and applications received by **8/17 (10 p.m.)** are considered for an anticipated October 1 start — making August 17 the next live cutoff at the time of writing. Subrecipient contracts are anticipated to start August 1, 2026 on a 14-month base period through September 30, 2027, with up to four one-year extensions. The state has committed to a weekly Friday email summarizing newly posted opportunities; specific per-solicitation deadlines surface first in the dated dispatches below and on the funding page.

What legislation or state action enables Vermont's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. Vermont administers its award through AHS under CMS-approved project and budget narratives. A key state action is **Act 68 of 2025**, which underpins the Stakeholder Engagement and Statewide Health Care Delivery Strategic Plan work at the center of Initiative 1 (Regionalization). Vermont has also attached two notable state guardrails to its subrecipient grants: a federal clinician non-compete clause (funds may not support clinician wages at facilities that impose non-competes) and AHS Attachment F, which requires written permission before AHS-funded service data can be used to train AI technologies.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Vermont's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out as competitive RFPs (for example, program evaluation, data infrastructure, and consulting engagements), where firms bid as **prime contractors**. **Subrecipient grants and NOFOs** flow to rural providers — hospitals, FQHCs and health centers, independent provider groups, home health, long-term care, community-paramedicine agencies, and community service providers — and it is here that technology vendors and consultants most often engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners**. Many provider grants are gated to rural ZIP codes (2020 RUCA score ≥ 2), and all subrecipients must hold an active SAM registration and valid UEI before award.

[Vermont RHT hub →](https://healthcarereform.vermont.gov/hr1rural-health-transformation-fund) [Join the RHT list →](https://list.vermont.gov/mailman/listinfo/vt.rht)

# Virginia Rural Health Transformation Program — CMS award, lead agency, committed metrics & activity

# Virginia Rural Health Transformation Program State Profile

Virginia's **$189,544,888.14** first-year Rural Health Transformation Program award — the "VA Rural Vitality" plan, the DMAS-led partner model, the workforce and tech initiatives, with a dated log of official activity.

[Virginia’s official RHTP hub →](https://www.ruralhealthtransformationva.virginia.gov/)

Virginia’s official Rural Health Transformation Program page — [ruralhealthtransformationva.virginia.gov](https://www.ruralhealthtransformationva.virginia.gov/), captured 2026-04-10.

Virginia’s own state-published rural map — Map of Virginia's rural regions (Figure 2, p3) — the six-region rural horseshoe. Source: [dmas.virginia.gov](https://dmas.virginia.gov/media/visgijnd/rhc-transformation-project-narrative.pdf). See [how every state defines rural](/work/rht/states/rural-definitions/#map-virginia).

## What Virginia committed to measure

The subjects Virginia’s funded application pledges to track and report to CMS — the yardsticks its progress will be measured against. Extracted from the state’s own project narrative; the detailed baselines and targets behind each are tracked in the [newsletter](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/).

Chronic disease ratesSubstance use disordersMaternal and infant healthPrimary care accessAvoidable ED visitsHealthcare workforce pipelineProvider technology adoptionRemote patient monitoringCommunity paramedicineFood as medicine

Source: Virginia’s CMS-approved RHTP project narrative. These are the state’s self-declared objectives; CMS weighs each state’s progress against its own commitments.

## Questions & answers

What is Virginia's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Virginia secured a confirmed federal award of **$189,544,888.14** for the first budget period of the five-year Rural Health Transformation Program — its share of the federal $50 billion program. Branded **"VA Rural Vitality,"** the effort is a five-year strategic investment plan, with additional annual awards expected in each funding year.

Which agency administers Virginia's RHTP, and who leads it?

The [Department of Medical Assistance Services (DMAS)](https://dmas.virginia.gov/data-reporting/programs-services/rural-health-transformation/) is the lead state agency and primary recipient of the CMS cooperative agreement, providing oversight and ensuring federal compliance. Virginia uses a **named subrecipient model**, delegating administration of specific funding streams to "Key Implementation Partners" that release downstream RFAs. Program contact: [ruralhealth@vdh.virginia.gov](mailto:ruralhealth@vdh.virginia.gov); hub at [ruralhealthtransformationva.virginia.gov](https://www.ruralhealthtransformationva.virginia.gov/).

What is Virginia's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

VA Rural Vitality targets Virginia's **76 rural counties** — the "rural horseshoe," 57% of the Commonwealth's counties and about 1.5 million residents. The plan front-loads workforce development to address clinician shortages and pairs it with a major technology-modernization push, delivered through established implementation partners rather than a single central office. The named tags are clinical transformation, rural residency, and mobile primary care.

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Virginia funding, and at what share?

- **Workforce Development — "Homegrown Health Heroes," proposed at $132.0M over five years**: physician residency (via the Virginia Hospital Research and Education Foundation, targeting 80–100 slots in OB/GYN, Family Medicine and Psychiatry), allied-health degrees (via the VCCS Foundation's hub-and-spoke model with mobile simulation labs), apprenticeships (Virginia Works "Earn to Learn," ~1,500 slots over five years), and K-12 pipelines (VDOE health academies and CTE).
- **Tech Innovation — "CareIQ," proposed at $282.6M**: modernizing rural legacy infrastructure.

These are multi-year proposed budgets; the full Year-1 breakdown is in Virginia's project and budget narratives on the funding page.

What has Virginia procured so far, and what's open right now?

Virginia runs a partner-led model in which Key Implementation Partners — the Virginia Hospital Research and Education Foundation, the VCCS Foundation, Virginia Works, and the Virginia Department of Education — issue downstream RFAs to local providers and organizations. As of mid-2026 the state is transitioning from Phase 1 (partners established and contracting) to Phase 2 (identifying administrators for its access and wellness initiatives). Specific solicitation numbers and amounts had not yet been detailed publicly; the dispatch list below carries the running record.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Virginia?

Virginia has not published concrete application windows in the sources on record; because RFAs are released by the individual implementation partners as the state moves from Phase 1 to Phase 2, deadlines surface first in the dated dispatches below and on the DMAS [Rural Health Transformation page](https://dmas.virginia.gov/data-reporting/programs-services/rural-health-transformation/).

What legislation or state action enables Virginia's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. Virginia administers its award through DMAS as the primary recipient of the CMS cooperative agreement, delegating funding streams to named Key Implementation Partners under its CMS-approved plan.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Virginia's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts and partner agreements** position Key Implementation Partners (VHREF, the VCCS Foundation, Virginia Works, VDOE) as the entities receiving and re-releasing funds, and firms can bid as **prime contractors** where the state or a partner competes work. **Subawards** flow through those partners to rural providers — rural hospitals, residency sponsors, community colleges, apprenticeship employers and local organizations across the 76-county rural horseshoe — where technology vendors and consultants most often engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners**.

Track opportunities on the [VA Rural Vitality hub](https://www.ruralhealthtransformationva.virginia.gov/) and the DMAS [Rural Health Transformation page](https://dmas.virginia.gov/data-reporting/programs-services/rural-health-transformation/), and direct questions to [ruralhealth@vdh.virginia.gov](mailto:ruralhealth@vdh.virginia.gov).

## What Washington committed to measure

The subjects Washington’s funded application pledges to track and report to CMS — the yardsticks its progress will be measured against. Extracted from the state’s own project narrative; the detailed baselines and targets behind each are tracked in the [newsletter](https://www.ruralhealthtransformation.life/).

Advanced payment modelsObstetric unit accessMobile health utilizationCommunity health workersRural workforce residenciesBehavioral health accessTribal health careTelehealth utilizationAI and population health toolsCare coordination

Source: Washington’s CMS-approved RHTP project narrative. These are the state’s self-declared objectives; CMS weighs each state’s progress against its own commitments.

## Questions & answers

What is Washington's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

CMS approved Washington a Year 1 budget of **approximately $181.3 million** as its share of the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program. During the original application CMS suggested states budget for $200 million per year; Washington's revised budget, approved February 26, 2026, brought the Year 1 figure to about $181 million **without eliminating any of the six approved activities**, instead front-loading projects ready for rapid implementation. The program runs on a five-year period of performance.

Which agency administers Washington's RHTP, and who leads it?

The [Washington Health Care Authority (HCA)](https://www.hca.wa.gov/about-hca/programs-and-initiatives/value-based-purchasing/rural-health-transformation-program) is the lead agency, working in partnership with the Department of Health (DOH) and the Department of Social and Health Services (DSHS) in support of the Governor's Office. The program is led by RHT Program Director **Priya Helweg**, a 20-year federal health-policy veteran of HHS and CMS who started April 16, 2026. Program questions go to [ruralhealth@doh.wa.gov](mailto:ruralhealth@doh.wa.gov).

What is Washington's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

Washington is delivering on **six CMS-approved initiatives** and, per its project leaders, cannot add new activities to the plan. The thrust spans integrated behavioral health, a community health center model, rural provider technology adoption, and cybersecurity, with Year 1 focused on projects that leverage existing partnerships for rapid implementation.

[Washington RHTP hub →](https://www.hca.wa.gov/about-hca/programs-and-initiatives/value-based-purchasing/rural-health-transformation-program)

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Washington funding, and at what share?

- **Rural Health Provider Technology Fund (RFA 2026HCA12)** — $11.5 million in Budget Period 1 (another $11.5M anticipated for Period 2, pending CMS), with individual awards of $200,000–$500,000 for telehealth, remote patient monitoring, wearables, and AI-enabled administrative tools.
- **OTP Workforce Incentive Program (RFA 2026HCA9)** and **Rural Hospitals: Maternal, Emergency & Specialty Services (RFA 2026HCA14)**.
- Program-wide caps: administrative overhead 10%, EMR replacement 5%, provider payments 15%; no new construction, lobbying, or supplanting.

The full breakdown is in Washington's CMS-approved budget.

What has Washington procured so far, and what's open right now?

HCA has moved several RFAs to the street. The **Provider Technology Fund (2026HCA12)** opened July 15 ($11.5M, awards $200K–$500K, due Aug 13); Amendment 1 widened eligibility to name RHCs, FQHCs, hospitals, behavioral-health and dental providers, EMS, Tribes, CBOs, associations, coordinated care organizations, and school and educational service districts. The **OTP Workforce Incentive Program (2026HCA9)** and **Rural Hospitals: Maternal, Emergency & Specialty Services (2026HCA14)** (due Aug 20) are also live. A structural note: these are RFAs, not RFPs — HCA is funding providers to buy their own technology, not buying it directly. The dispatch list below carries the running record.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Washington?

- **2026HCA12 (Provider Technology Fund):** questions July 23, answers July 30, applications Aug 13 (2:00 p.m. PT), evaluation through Aug 31, awards from Sept 1, contracts executed by Oct 30.
- **2026HCA14 (Rural Hospitals):** questions July 30, HCA responses Aug 7, applications Aug 20 (2:00 p.m. PT), evaluation Aug 20–Sept 14, award notification Sept 16.
- Next program update webinar: **September 16, 2026, 1:00–1:45 p.m.**

Live dates surface first in the dated dispatches below.

What legislation or state action enables Washington's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. In Washington, CMS approved the state's revised Year 1 budget on February 26, 2026, and the program is delivered jointly by HCA, DOH, and DSHS in support of the Governor's Office. Detailed allocation figures are set out in Washington's CMS-approved budget.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Washington's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out as competitive solicitations where firms bid as **prime contractors**. But much of Washington's early money moves through **RFAs** that hand rural providers grant funds to buy their own technology — so if you sell telehealth, remote patient monitoring, analytics, or cybersecurity tooling, **your customer is the applicant** and you engage as a supplier or **implementation partner**. Eligibility is wide (RHCs, FQHCs, hospitals, behavioral-health and dental providers, EMS, Tribes, nonprofits, CBOs, associations, coordinated care organizations, and educational service and school districts), and an applicant need not be based in a rural community — only demonstrate benefit to rural Washingtonians.

Register on Washington's **Electronic Business Solution (WEBS)** to be notified of bids, and track the [HCA Bids & Contracts](https://www.hca.wa.gov/about-hca/bids-and-contracts) page and the [RHTP hub](https://www.hca.wa.gov/about-hca/programs-and-initiatives/value-based-purchasing/rural-health-transformation-program).

## What West Virginia committed to measure

The subjects West Virginia’s funded application pledges to track and report to CMS — the yardsticks its progress will be measured against. Telehealth accessRemote patient monitoringAvoidable ED visitsNon-emergency medical transportationHealthcare workforce pipelineValue-based care adoptionReturn-to-work programsChronic disease preventionMaternal and infant healthHealth tech innovation

Source: West Virginia’s CMS-approved RHTP project narrative. These are the state’s self-declared objectives; CMS weighs each state’s progress against its own commitments.

## Questions & answers

What is West Virginia's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

West Virginia secured approximately **$199.5 million** in Year-1 funding under the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program. Year 1 is the first tranche of an estimated **$1 billion** five-year plan; like every RHTP award, the funding is structured by CMS as an annual award across a five-year performance period, and it is roughly 100% federally funded.

Which agency administers West Virginia's RHTP, and who leads it?

The **West Virginia Department of Health** administers the program, coordinated through the [WV State Office of Rural Health](https://health.wv.gov/rural-health-transformation-program) ([wvsorh@wv.gov](mailto:wvsorh@wv.gov)). Secretary of Health **Dr. Arvin Singh** leads the effort, with **Dr. Carrie Jeffries** serving as Director of RHTP. Procurement runs through the Office of Shared Administration.

What is West Virginia's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

West Virginia is taking a distinctly economic approach it calls **"Health to Prosperity."** Rather than primarily propping up hospital margins, the state aims to create a "virtuous circle" between health and work — targeting a move in the state's workforce participation rate from 54.3% to at least 56.3%. The plan is organized as a flywheel across seven flagship pillars: Connected Care Grid, Rural Health Link, Mountain State Care Force, Smart Care Catalyst, Health to Prosperity Pipeline, Personal Health Accelerator, and HealthTech Appalachia.

Where is the money going — which initiatives is West Virginia funding, and at what share?

West Virginia disclosed its Year-1 pillar allocations for the first time at its July 9 webinar:

- **Connected Care Grid** — $45.9M
- **Smart Care Catalyst** — $45.6M
- **Personal Health Accelerator** — $29.0M
- **HealthTech Appalachia** — $18.8M
- **Mountain State Care Force** — $15.2M
- **Rural Health Link** — $13.8M
- **Health to Prosperity** — $13.4M

Administrative costs are excluded, so the pillar figures don't sum to $199.5M. The state has set hard cost caps: administrative costs at 10%, provider payments at 15%, EMR replacement at 5%, and the Rural Tech Catalyst Fund at 10% or $20M (whichever is lower).

What has West Virginia procured so far, and what's open right now?

West Virginia is running the fastest procurement cadence in the RHTP — it reported 20+ funding opportunities released with 10+ more coming this summer. Named solicitations include the Connected Care Grid **Data Spine RFP** (RHT26\*4, sealed bids opened July 7), the **Workforce Catalyst Program AFA** ($500K, due Aug 5), **Mountain State Care Force Provider Rotational Staffing Pools** ($1.8M, due July 28), multiple CCG telehealth and mobile-unit AFAs, and the $24.1M Personal Health Accelerator nutrition-and-lifestyle solicitation. All applications route through the **wvOASIS Vendor Self Service** portal. Every dated dispatch covering West Virginia is listed below, newest first.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in West Virginia?

West Virginia's solicitation deadlines move quickly and many have already passed; the most recent is the **Workforce Catalyst Program AFA, due August 5, 2026**. Because the state releases opportunities on a rolling basis with tight windows, live dates surface first in the dated dispatches below and on the [grant opportunities](https://health.wv.gov/grant-opportunities) portal. Vendor questions on most solicitations route to procurement officer Mike Sheets ([mike.sheets@wv.gov](mailto:mike.sheets@wv.gov)) within three business days of posting.

What legislation or state action enables West Virginia's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. To maximize its CMS merit score, West Virginia committed to specific state policy changes, including passing the **Make West Virginia Healthy Act of 2026** (satisfying the CMS Presidential Fitness Test requirement), enacting a SNAP waiver prohibiting the purchase of soda with benefits, and moving to require nutrition-focused Continuing Medical Education for physicians. The state also established a statewide Advisory Panel and a specialized HealthTech panel to govern the program.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with West Virginia's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out as competitive RFPs and Announcements of Funding Availability (AFAs), where firms bid as **prime contractors** — the Data Spine, provider directory, and platform solicitations are examples. **Subgrants and subawards** flow to rural providers — hospitals and critical-access hospitals, FQHCs and community health centers, rural health clinics, behavioral health providers, EMS agencies, and long-term/post-acute care — and it is here that technology vendors and consultants most often engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners**. West Virginia signals clear preferences: multi-system collaborations, in-state hiring and local operational presence (a "flywheel effect"), and mandatory integration with the state's Connected Care Grid Data Spine; it steers away from consulting-heavy models, academic pilots, and standalone apps.

Track opportunities on the [WV RHTP hub](https://health.wv.gov/rural-health-transformation-program) and the [grant opportunities](https://health.wv.gov/grant-opportunities) portal, submit through wvOASIS, and subscribe to the state's RHTP listserv.

[Join the WV RHTP listserv →](https://health.wv.gov/rhtp-listserv)

## Questions & answers

What is Wisconsin's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Wisconsin's first-year award is **approximately $203.7 million**, its share of the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program. The program is a five-year CMS cooperative agreement; CMS has not yet announced award amounts for the subsequent four years. Wisconsin is sequencing its money in rounds — for example, its Rural Technology Transformation Fund is designed as formula-based allocations of an estimated $209 million over five years (pending CMS approval), delivered in two rounds, with Round 1 in 2026 and the larger Round 2 in 2027.

Which agency administers Wisconsin's RHTP, and who leads it?

The [Wisconsin Department of Health Services (DHS)](https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/business/rhtp.htm) administers the program, with questions routed to [aaron.larson@dhs.wisconsin.gov](mailto:aaron.larson@dhs.wisconsin.gov). A dedicated [RHTP Advisory Council](https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/business/rhtpac.htm) provides strategic guidance and input, and the University of Wisconsin provides application technical assistance ([RHTP-evaluation@wisc.edu](mailto:RHTP-evaluation@wisc.edu)).

What is Wisconsin's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

Wisconsin's plan is focused on improving the health and wellbeing of rural communities by **expanding access, improving quality, and ensuring sustainable solutions**. A defining feature is its technology ambition: DHS is pursuing a single **statewide electronic health records (EHR) system** so rural organizations can achieve economies of scale through one procurement — a shared clinical and billing system with longitudinal records, a patient portal and a closed-loop referral network. Alongside that, the plan invests in care coordination across systems and sectors, community health workers, and rural dental efficiency and access. RHC Network, Quality Initiatives and Pharmacy Hubs are core project tags.

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Wisconsin funding, and at what share?

Wisconsin's marquee vehicle is the **Rural Technology Transformation Fund**:

- **Round 1 — $61M over three years**, an invitation-only competition limited to the 12 FQHC organizations and 28 Rural Health Clinic organizations named in the state's Exhibit 4 (RHCs see $28M in Year 1, ~$1.01M average per org; FQHCs see $15M, ~$1.26M average).
- **Round 2 — an estimated $148M** in 2027, reaching hospital systems (44), local health departments (69), Tribal clinics (14), and free/charitable and opioid-treatment facilities (26).

A separate June batch put **$40M** into three grants — Care Coordination (up to $10M planning), Community Health Worker ($20M), and Rural Dental Efficiency and Access ($10M). Eligible technology buys are broad and hardware-specific — EHR/IT upgrades, data-analytics subscriptions, Bluetooth blood-pressure cuffs, continuous glucose monitors, ambient AI scribes, even robotic surgical systems — within federal caps (EHR replacement 5%, administrative 8%, minor renovations 20%; no new construction).

What has Wisconsin procured so far, and what's open right now?

Wisconsin has moved on several fronts. It issued a **statewide EHR RFP** (eSupplier event S-FMF1944 OGM-26 / Event 14009, proposals due April 20) for a vendor to design, host and manage a full-service shared EHR, following an EHR Readiness and Interest survey. It opened the **Rural Technology Transformation Fund Round 1 ($61M)** in July, and released a June batch of three grants ($40M) for care coordination, community health workers and rural dental. Round 2 of the technology fund and its eligible-organization list won't post until 2027. Every dated dispatch covering Wisconsin is listed below, newest first, and it carries the running procurement record.

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Wisconsin?

Recent grant deadlines from the June batch: **Rural Dental Efficiency and Access due July 27**, **Community Health Worker due August 7** (letters of intent recommended by July 1), and **Care Coordination due August 21**. The statewide EHR RFP set proposals due April 20. Grant windows generally run about 10 weeks. Round 2 of the Rural Technology Transformation Fund is expected to open in 2027, with funds beginning summer or fall of that year. Live windows surface first in the dated dispatches below and on the [DHS grant funding opportunities page](https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/business/solicitations-list.htm).

What legislation or state action enables Wisconsin's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. In Wisconsin, the award is administered through DHS, with strategic input from the RHTP Advisory Council. Detailed allocation figures are set out in Wisconsin's approved project and budget narratives.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Wisconsin's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out as competitive RFPs through Wisconsin's **eSupplier** portal, where firms bid as **prime contractors** — the statewide EHR system is the flagship example, and technology vendors compete for that build directly. **Subgrants and subawards** flow to rural providers — FQHCs, Rural Health Clinics, hospital systems, local health departments, Tribal clinics and free/charitable facilities — and here vendors and consultants most often engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners**. Note Wisconsin's Rural Technology Transformation Fund is invitation-only against a pre-identified list; being named guarantees nothing, and DHS negotiates each award individually. Group purchasing is encouraged so smaller organizations can reach scale on shared software or big-ticket equipment.

Track opportunities on the [DHS grant funding opportunities page](https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/business/solicitations-list.htm), review the [Advisory Council](https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/business/rhtpac.htm), and [sign up for RHTP email updates](https://public.govdelivery.com/accounts/WIDHS/subscriber/new?topic_id=WIDHS_75).

[Wisconsin DHS Rural Health Transformation Program →](https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/business/rhtp.htm)

# Wyoming Rural Health Transformation Program — CMS award, lead agency, committed metrics & activity

Source: https://www.civicoperator.com/work/rht/states/wyoming/

# Wyoming Rural Health Transformation Program State Profile

Wyoming's **$205.0M** Rural Health Transformation Program award — the infrastructure-stabilization plan, the administering agency, its RFA portal and tech-vendor RFPs, with a dated log of official activity for vendors, providers, and consultants tracking the program.

## Questions & answers

What is Wyoming's Rural Health Transformation Program allocation, and how is the funding structured?

Wyoming's award is **approximately $205.0 million** in Year-1 funding, its share of the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program. CMS structures the program as a five-year, spend-down initiative — a point Wyoming learned firsthand when CMS rejected the state's proposed perpetuity/endowment fund (which had aimed to stretch an anticipated ~$1 billion over five years for decades). Wyoming refiled a revised plan without the fund, which CMS approved in May 2026.

Which agency administers Wyoming's RHTP, and who leads it?

The [Wyoming Department of Health (WDH)](https://health.wyo.gov/admin/rural-health-transformation-program/) administers the program; WDH Director **Stefan Johansson** has represented the plan to state lawmakers. Program contact is [wdh-primarycare-ruralhealth@wyo.gov](mailto:wdh-primarycare-ruralhealth@wyo.gov). The plan was shaped by extensive community town-hall feedback documented in a state-maintained shared drive.

What is Wyoming's rural health transformation plan trying to accomplish?

Wyoming's plan focuses on **stabilizing essential rural healthcare infrastructure** rather than funding temporary programs or unneeded specialty services. Driven by the fundamentals of high fixed costs and low patient volumes across its frontier regions, the state prioritizes access to foundational care — emergency departments, reliable ambulances, and primary care — and building a durable workforce pipeline, alongside longer-term population-health investments.

Where is the money going — which initiatives is Wyoming funding, and at what share?

- **Emergency medical care access — roughly 48% of the budget**, the largest share. Includes the “Critical Access Hospital – Basic” (CAHB) incentive rewarding small hospitals for maintaining 24/7 emergency departments, stroke/trauma imaging, and local ambulance service; EMS regionalization incentives; and “BearCare,” a public major-medical plan for residents priced out of comprehensive insurance.
- **Workforce pipeline — over 25% of the budget**, funding educational support and post-graduate medical slots for physicians, nurses, and EMS personnel in exchange for five-year rural service commitments.
- **Population health** — longer-term investments to improve rural health outcomes.

Recurring focuses on record include EMS stabilization, robotics, pharmacy, and high-risk care. The full breakdown is in Wyoming's approved plan.

What has Wyoming procured so far, and what's open right now?

Wyoming opened its RHT application portal on July 1, 2026, hosted on Submittable, where applicants apply for the program's Request for Application (RFA) sub-initiatives. Separately, three technology-vendor procurements run through the standard state process on Public Purchase as competitive **RFPs**: **3.2 Statewide telespecialist platform, 3.3 Non-emergency transportation coordination, and 3.4 Centralized billing capacity** — two of the three were linked as of July 11, 2026. The running record is in the dispatch list below.

[Wyoming RHT Application Portal →](https://wyrhtp.submittable.com/submit)

What are the key upcoming dates and deadlines in Wyoming?

The key date on the record is the RFA application close: **midnight on August 2, 2026** (the Submittable portal lists the required 0.1 Applicant Eligibility Information form ending early on August 3). Everyone applying for any initiative (except those marked “information only”) must complete that **0.1 Applicant Eligibility Information** form first. The three tech-vendor RFP deadlines post on Public Purchase; current dates surface first in the dated dispatches below and on the portal.

What legislation or state action enables Wyoming's RHTP?

The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by **Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)** and is administered federally by CMS. Wyoming administers its award through the Wyoming Department of Health. A defining piece of state action was Wyoming's attempt to establish a **perpetuity/endowment fund** to stretch the funding beyond five years; CMS rejected that mechanism, treating the RHTP as a spend-down (not stretch-down) program, and Wyoming's approved plan proceeds without it.

How can vendors, providers, or consultants engage with Wyoming's program?

Eligibility runs on two tracks. **Subgrants/subawards** flow to rural providers — hospitals (including Critical Access Hospitals), EMS agencies, clinics, and other rural health entities — who apply for the RFA sub-initiatives through the Submittable portal, and it is here that technology vendors and consultants most often engage as **subcontractors or implementation partners**. **Direct-to-state contracts** go out as the three competitive technology-vendor RFPs on Public Purchase (statewide telespecialist platform, non-emergency transportation coordination, centralized billing capacity), where firms bid as **prime contractors**. Any applicant should start with the required 0.1 Applicant Eligibility Information form.

[Wyoming RHTP hub →](https://health.wyo.gov/admin/rural-health-transformation-program/) [RFA application portal →](https://wyrhtp.submittable.com/submit)
